qa-educators-students:
Question-Answer session with Educators & Students regarding ‘Human Values’ and ‘Life Spiritual’

– Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh

–

(A) Questions from Educators

1. What is the relation between Education and values?

Answer: The very purpose of education is inculcation and strengthening of values OR to make life more valuable and worthwhile.

This is clear by the very meaning of the words involved. The new Webster Dictionary explains `education' as "instruction or training by which people learn to develop and use their mental, moral and physical powers" and the same dictionary explains `value' as "the measure of how strongly something is desired for its physical or moral beauty, usefulness, rarity, etc". Paying particular attention to `mental powers' in the definition of education we find the same dictionary stating that `mental' means "of or pertaining to the mind", and `mind' means "the seat of consciousness, thought, feeling and will".

If we combine all these definitions we find that education is that instruction or training by which people learn to develop their powers of thought, feeling and will as well as moral or physical powers, thereby making their life more and more valuable and worthwhile to themselves and to society at large.

2. What is your reading of the present scenario?

Answer: We are passing through darkest period where education has become totally divorced from its own meaning.

It seems that the we have totally forgotten the purpose of education and as a result we are facing steep decline of moral values, rise and dominance of anti-values like corruption, apathy towards neighbours and nation, etc. etc. and drifting towards chaos.

The present education has totally neglected moral training as well as training of feeling and will, and is only concerned with intellectual gathering of information. Thus we get so-called knowledge without wisdom,-- and man, instead of being transformed from animal to human and human to divine, becomes a learned animal or a skilled criminal. Drastic remedial measures are called for from all concerned, especially from the Government.

3. What is the Government’s responsibility?

Answer: The Government is primarily responsible for a) Media; b) Syllabus and Course contents in general; c) Syllabus and Course content of Teachers' Training Programmes.

The educators for any person are

(i) Parents, (ii) Educational Institutions, (iii) Society and (iv) Media.

The Media in turn goes on educating the parents and the society.

Hence the Government should see that the media, the course content in Education in general and in the Teachers' Training programmes should be flooded with positive ideas of development of thought, feeling, will, and moral and physical strength.

4. What values are universally accepted and really conducive to man-making?

Answer: The Supreme values are :-- i) Awareness of potential divinity in oneself resulting in real stable Self-Confidence and healthy positive attitude.

ii) Awareness of potential divinity in others resulting in love and respect for all others irrespective of their caste, creed or nationality.

We can also add :

a. Fearlessness / Boldness b. Purity of Heart c. Constant Pursuit of Higher Values d. Austerity and Struggle for Perfection e. Steadfastness in the pursuit of knowledge.

f. Self-control g. Truthfulness / Uprightness h. Tranquillity / Steadiness / Even-mindedness i. Charity / Nobility / Spirit of sacrifice j. Kindness to Beings k. Humility / Gentleness / Modesty l. Forgiveness / Forbearence / Fortitude m. Cleanliness n. Dignity of manual labour o. Reverence to the teacher p. Introspection q. Non-attachment r. Faith and love for the Almighty God s. Absence of Jealousy, ill-feeling and hatred t. Freedom from Slander u. Absence/Control over Anger v. Non-craving for Enjoyments or Absence of Self-Indulgence w. Absence of Greed x. Absence of Conceit y. Absence of Arrogance and Rudeness.

z. Absence of Ostentation

5. What methods of implementation do you suggest at school, college and University levels?

Answer: We should orient the entire education system towards it so that education becomes true education.

a) For example, the very appearence and upkeep of the educational institutions and their Surroundings must be thought of as integral parts of `education'.

(i) The campus and buildings in every educational institution have to be kept spotlessly clean and most of the cleaning should be done by the staff and the students supervised by the Principal to inculcate (a) dignity of manual labour, (b) love and regards for that section of the society who keep our city etc. clean, ( c) Cleanliness as a value, and (d) mental and moral benefits derived from cleanliness.

(ii) Great and noble thoughts should be prominently displayed in all possible places.

b) Similarly, we should use all direct and indirect methods of inculcating and strengthening values.

c) At least at school level there should be teacher-parent association -- a forum where values should be discussed and encouraged.

d) At college level groups should be formed under a tutor or counseller to discuss ways and means of imbibing values.

The approach must necessarily be multi-dimensional e) Some of the means suggested are i) compulsory class on moral education at every level ii) the course content, especially of language and literature topics must contain inspiring passages from the lives and teachings of great men of all countries whose lives have been shining examples of values leading to real success and glory of life.

iii) Teachers should be trained for counselling and this must be introduced in all educational institutions for guiding individuals.

iv) Activities like Boy-scouts, N.S.S., etc. should be made a part of education.

(B) Questions from Students

Q. 1 What should be the basic guidelines of life?

Answer : 1. Conviction of one’s own and others potential divinity should be the first principle.

2. Faith in oneself, which directly follows from the above conviction.

3. The four cardinal virtues : i. Unselfishness; ii. Deep devotion to God, the Universal Infinite, worshipped in any form or manner; iii. Self-control; iv. Rational understanding of the ultimate nature of things.

4. Devotion to Duty

5. Regularity of spiritual practice.

6. Planned and disciplined life.

7. Zest for knowledge.

8. Following everything that makes oneself strong physically, mentally, morally, spiritually, and avoiding everything which weakens.

9. If one is cent per cent sure about a thing being right, one must have the courage to follow it.

Q. 2 Is meditation and long prayers, the only way to reach God?

What should the children do whose first and primary Goal is to study?

Answer : Let us first think of ‘studies’ and the various motivations etc. involved in it. I was once amidst students of the higher secondary (11th & 12th standard) classes who told me that their parents enjoyed watching T.V. but did not allow them to do so and told them -- "Now you go on studying so that later on you can enjoy these pleasures." They then asked me (I don’t know whether they asked the same question to their parents or not) -- "Why should we not enjoy pleasures now itself? What would happen if we die tomorrow?" I exclaimed -- "Alas! How wrong to motivate towards study by telling that it would give them the route passage (through money?) for the enjoyment of pleasures (which a pig can do best without any education)! Why not tell them that the process of education will help them become well developed individuals by increasing their power of thinking, the capacity of understanding the world and themselves better and better, and by giving them the ability to work in different fields of human endeavor and express their respective potentials fully and properly. Side by side they should develop their physical abilities and skills, develop their feelings in the right direction and learn to control passions and self-destructive emotions etc. They should become wiser and wiser and abler and abler. On the other hand indulging in fleeting pleasures of the senses which titillate (the nerves) and fritter away their energy will hamper their capacity to improve. If we run after enjoyments, we shall not have the power to improve ourselves and those enjoyments will also slip away from us like shadows, but if we continually struggle for self-improvement then happiness will follow us. Of course, we must have some enjoyments or pleasures in a planned and disciplined way

so that we become ‘re-freshed’ when we are fatigued by the constant struggle for improvement and that is why these types of activities are called ‘recreation’ which is an essential part of the science of struggle for improvement which is called ‘education’. And of course we can derive abundant pleasures from creative cultural activities, along with games and sports and useful hobbies. So we find some students engaged in ‘meditation and long prayers’ and yet coming up very well in their studies and some others using meditation and ‘short’ prayers to improve their power of self-discipline, peace of mind and concentration so that they do their studies easily and successfully. It all depends on individual ‘temperament’, but the important point is to be aware of the Goal of life which is not only to be a really well-developed man or woman in whom all available faculties are properly used and groomed, but also to go towards becoming like God.

Q. 3 Does one have to think of the society every time he wants to do something ?

Answer : There are two basic tendencies in the human mind -- the lure of enjoyment and the struggle for improvement. These are also called the pull of the ‘pleasurable’ and the pull of the ‘ultimately beneficial’. If the first pull is left unchecked it leads to ultimate ruination, while the second pull or struggle if checked will stagnate our life. Thinking of society is useful to check the downslide of life resulting from the first temptation. On the other hand, if one is absolutely sure that one is trying to improve oneself then he/she should not allow himself/herself to be checked by society. It is of course always useful to get one’s course of action approved by some really wise person.

Q. 4 What is the importance of good behavior?

Q. 5 Is culture to be shown to everyone or it is enough if we have it in us ?

Answer : We must first understand the subtle difference between character and conduct or behaviour. Character is what we really are ourselves and conduct is how we appear to others. If character is perfect it reflects in good behavior. Otherwise good behavior can also be a ‘mask’. In any case the effect of good behavior is that others become pleased. The effect on ourselves varies -- (i) If it is an expression of good character, then good behavior strengthens it. (ii) If behavior is only a mask, then it may make our life artificial.

Similarly, if we really have the culture in us, it will come out even in our dealing with others. Hence if it is not coming out in that manner, we should know that we do not have it fully developed in us as yet, and hence we must strive hard to develop it more and more on the inside. On the other hand if we try to show or are merely taught to show culture to everyone without really having it in ourselves, we are likely to turn into hypocrites and will never be at ease with ourselves nor with others.

Q. 6 What is a friend? Why does the human heart wish to have a friend?

Please give guidelines for being a friend.

Answer : This is an extremely important question in actual life of any individual human being.

(a) ‘A friend in need is a friend indeed’ is the old proverb.

(b) Really ‘God’ alone is our best friend. The great sage Shankaracharya says that a ‘friend’ is a ‘friend’ usually only so long as we are nice to him, but God is our friend always and ever. (Commentary on Gita 9,18)

(c) This God, who is the Ultimate Reality -- One only, without a second -- manifests Himself in innumerably unique ways through the infinite variety of human beings created by Him out of Himself. This leads to a situation where each individual finds himself/herself different from others, separate from others, limited, and hence, to complete himself/herself, he/she craves for a friend who is an expression of the same common Reality and yet is differently constituted. So much so that many of us feel totally at a loss to cope up with life without a proper friend or friends.

(d) If we can be always aware that friendship is based on two factors -- variety outside, and yet sharing the common background and support of same Universal Reality called God so that the third

friend God is always available in case of our falling out with each other due to misunderstandings etc. -

- we can be true friends always.

(e) The purpose of friendship is to compliment and supplement each other and help each other to strive for perfection. When perfection is reached we are not in need of anyone to help us, and then we can be real friends because we really feel the same God in us and in others.

(f) Friendship should be based on giving and not expecting.

(g) Friendship should lead to more and more improvement together. It should never be against anybody and never lead to common disaster by doing anything bad together!

(h) Friendship is destroyed by imposing and expecting. It is really built up in freedom.

(i) Select your friends very carefully in such a way that every merit in you gets a boost and not the demerits or evil passions.

( j ) Friendship is sustained by each one struggling to be a better and better individual and by always helping each other.

Q.7 What is there in God that we call him God?

Answer : This question asks us to ‘define’ God. Let us try.

(a) God is Absolute Infinite Undivided Eternal Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (Sat-chit-Ananda).

(b) God is both the efficient and material cause of creation (or projection or appearance), preservation (or sustenance or continuation) and dissolution (or disappearance) of the world. [When a potter makes a pot from clay, he is said to be the efficient cause of the pot while clay is the material cause. In case of the world, God is both the efficient and material cause, i.e. God projects the world from within himself by his own will.]

(c) God is the one Ruler of this universe (nobody has the power to overrule him).

(d) God is Eternally pure, All-pervading, Ever-free, Almighty, All-knowing, All-merciful, Teacher of all teachers.

(e) God is inexpressible LOVE and BLISS.

(f) God is Absolutely Perfect. God is the repository of infinite number of blessed qualities.

(g) God is our Father, Mother, Friend, Lover, Beloved, Support, Innermost Reality, Life of our life, and what not.

Q.8 Why do we respect God so much?

Answer : (a) (i) We respect anyone for his/her merits or superior qualities. But all the possible merits and superior qualities in all respects are in God to an infinite degree.

(ii) We respect parents and other elders as they are ‘older’ in this world and are supposed to be wiser and know more about the world and about human life than us. But God is the ‘Oldest’ -- pre-existing before the world itself. God is the wisest and knows ‘everything’ about the world and about ‘life’.

(iii) Parents are also respected because they are like ‘causes’ and we are ‘effects’. But God is the ‘Ultimate Cause’ and everything and everybody is an ‘effect’ coming out of God. That is why we respect God ‘so much’, though it is much less than as much we should respect God.

(b) God is also the source of any good merit found anywhere. Hence when we respect anyone we are respecting God reflected in that person. If we know this, we will love and respect God with all our heart and soul.

Q.9 Where is the existence of God?

Answer : (a) God exists everywhere, permeates every atom; is also beyond everything in his own nature.

(b) God is ever present -- hidingly -- in the heart-cave of every living being.

Q.10 If there is a God, why don’t we see Him?

Answer : (i) Becouse God is the innermost Reality of everything while we are normally constituted seeing things from outside and require very special training to be able to see the inside.

(ii) Becouse we do not have the needed all comprehensive yearning, One great sage always used to say that God is the abiding reality in all of us. So, some times people asked him, "You say that God is the abiding reality, then why don’t we see Him?" He used to reply spontaneously repeating the same question in a different tone. He used to say -- "What a pity! Though God is the abiding reality, why don’t we see Him?" The ‘meaning’ of this reply is that the question should be asked neither as a challenge nor as doubt but as yearning and pathos!

(iii)Because we have not followed any of the various prescribed methods to do so, and

(iv) Becouse we lack the purity which is absolutely necessary to develop the penetrative vision to see God. "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" -- says Jesus Christ.

Q.11 Is it true that God lives in Param Dham (above the sky)?

Answer : Let us try to understand what is Param Dham and also what is meant by ‘above the sky’.

(a) When we say ‘above’, the crudeness of our thinking makes it appear as if it is something on a great physical hight. Removing this crude idea that in ‘above’ two ideas are mixed up -- (i)’Beyond’ and (ii) Superior -- but both of them may really mean -- ‘inside’. (b) Some people say that God is beyond the 9th ‘cloud’. These ‘clouds’ are the layers of ignorance in our own heart. So beyond all of them means absolutely ‘inside’. (c) Dham means place or location and Param means Supreme, most superior etc. So God lives in Param Dham means God lives in the deepest recesses of human heart -- untouched by all good and bad in the externalised mind of man. Hence Saint Kabir sings: "Lift the layers of the veil to see the most beloved." (d) Let us try to understand in another way. Whenever we see objects outside -- they are located in ‘space’ outside. But when we ‘see’ mental objects like Anger, Hatred, Love, Peace they are located in the space of the mind. But when we directly perceive God who is the very source of all perception -- being the source of our consciousness and who is of the very nature of consciousness, that undivided consciousness itself is the location to see God and hence it is called the supreme sky or supreme space or supreme location.

Q.12 How did people get the idea of praying to the Idols?

Q.13 Is it correct to worship idols?

Q.14 Should we believe in idol-worship?

Answer : Some funny confusion seems to have engulfed the Indians due to modern education, grossness of the mind, and ignorance of the ways of mind.

(a) Let us see what Swami Vivekananda has to say.

It was in Rajasthan that Thakur Mangal Singhji, the Maharaja of Alwar, who had become much anglicised, asked, "Well, Swamiji Maharaj, I have no faith in idol worship. What is going to be my fate?" He smiled as he spoke ..."You see, I really cannot worship wood, earth, stone or metal like other people. Does this mean that I shall fare worse in the life hereafter?" The Swami answered, "Well, I suppose every man should follow the religious ideal according to his own faith."... his eyes lighted on a picture of the Maharaja which was hanging on the wall. The Swami commanded the Dewan: "spit on it" ... The Dewan cried out, "What, Swamiji! What are you asking me to do? This is the likeness of our Maharaja! How can I do such a thing?" ... Turning to the Maharaja the Swami continued, "See, your Highness; though this is not you in one sense, in another sense it is you. That was why your devoted servants were so perplexed when I asked them to spit on it. It is a shadow of you; it brings you into their minds. One glance at it makes them see you in it; therefore they look at it with as much respect as they would have in looking at your own person. Thus it is also with the devotees who worship stone and metal images of gods and goddesses. It is because an image brings to their minds their Ishta (that particular aspect of God which is most suitable for that individual), or some special forms and attributes

of the Divinity, and helps them to concentrate, that the devotees worship God in an image. They do not worship the stone or the metal as such.

"I have travelled in many places, but nowhere have I found a single Hindu worshipping an image, saying, ‘O Stone, I worship Thee. O Metal, be merciful to me.’ Everyone, Maharaja, is worshipping the same one God who is the Supreme Spirit, the Soul of Pure Knowledge. And God appears to all according to their understanding and their representation of Him. Prince, I speak for myself. Of course, I cannot speak for you."

Mangal Singhji, who had been listening attentively all this time, said, with folded hands, "Swamiji, I must admit that, looking at image worship in the light you have thrown on it, I have never met anyone who worshipped stone, or wood, or metal. Before this I did not understand its meaning. You have opened my eyes. ..." (Life of SW.V. Vol.I P.268-270)

(b) And hence says Swami Vivekananda -- (i) All men are born idolaters. The lowest man is an animal. The highest man is perfect. And between these two, all have to think in sound and colour, in doctrine and ritual. The test of having ceased to be an idolater is : when you say ‘I’, does the body come into your thought or not? If it does, then you are still a worshipper of idols. (C.W.of Sw.V.,Vol.8, P.229-230)

(ii) The man who is bowing down before the idol; ... It is peculiar to the Hindus. The man is before the idol, and he shuts his eyes and tries to think, "I am He; I have neither life nor death; I have neither father nor mother; I am not bound by time or space; I am Existence infinite, Bliss infinite and Knowledge infinite; I am He, I am He." ... this he repeats and then says, "O Lord, I cannot conceive Thee in myself; I am a poor man." ... You may take the most learned man you have and ask him to think of spirit as spirit; he cannot ... It is impossible to think of spirit without training. (Vol.8,P 210-211)

(iii) Among the Jews, idol worship is condemned, but they had a temple in which was kept a chest which they called an ark, in which the Tables of the Law were preserved, and above the chest were two figures of angels with wings outstretched, between which the Divine Presence was supposed to manifest itself as a cloud. That temple has long since been destroyed, but the new temples are made exactly after the old fashion, and in the chest religious books are kept. The Roman Catholics and the Greek Christians have idol-worship in certain forms. The image of Jesus and that of his mother are worshipped. Among Protestants there is no idol-worship, yet they worship God in a personal form, which may be called idol-worship in another form. Among Parsees and Iranians fire-worship is carried on to a great extent. Among Mohammedans the prophets and great and noble persons are worshipped, and they turn their faces towards the Caaba when they pray. These things show that men at the first stage of religious development have to make use of something external, and when the inner self becomes purified they turn to more abstract conceptions. "When the Jiva is sought to be united with Brahman it is best, when meditation is practised it is mediocre, repetition of names is the lowest form, and external worship is the lowest of the low." But it should be distinctly understood that even in practising the last there is no sin. Everybody ought to do what he is able to do; and if he be dissuaded from that, he will do it in some other way in order to attain his end. So we should not speak ill of a man who worships idols. He is in that stage of growth, and, therefore, must have them; wise men should try to help forward such men and get them to do better. But there is no use in quarrelling about these various sorts of worship. (Vol.3, P.362-363)

(iv) It has become a trite saying that idolatry is wrong, and every man swallows it at the present time without questioning. I once thought so, and to pay the penalty of that I had to learn my lesson sitting at the feet of a man who realised everything through idols; I allude to Ramakrishna Paramahansa. If such Ramakrishna Paramahansas are produced by idol worship, what will you have -- the reformer’s creed or any number of idols? I want an answer. Take a thousand idols more if you can produce Ramakrishna Paramahansas through idol-worship, and may God speed you! Produce such noble natures by any means you can. Yet idolatry is condemned! Why? Nobody knows. Because some hundreds of years ago some man of Jewish blood happened to condemn it? That is, he happened to condemn everybody else’s idols except his own. If God is represented in any beautiful form or any

symbolic form, said the Jew, it is awfully bad; it is sin. But if He is represented in the form of a chest, with two angels sitting on each side, and a cloud hanging over it, it is the holiest of the holy. If God comes in the form of a dove, it is holy. But if He comes in the form of a cow, it is heathen superstition; condemn it! That is how the world goes. That is why the poet says, "what fools we mortals be!" (Vol.3,P.218)

(c) And what then is Sri Ramakrishna’s final advice? --

1. While raising a building, the scaffolding is indispensable; but when the work is completed, no one feels the necessity of it. So also image-worship is necessary in the beginning but not afterwards.

2. A marksman learns to shoot by first having big objects to shoot at; and as he acquires more and more facility in shooting, he aims more and more easily at the smaller marks on the target. So when the mind has been trained to focus on images having forms, it is easy for it do so on things having no form.

3. As a toy fruit or a toy elephant reminds one of the real fruit and the living animal, so do the images that are worshipped remind one of God who is formless and eternal.

4. You were talking of images made of clay. There arises a necessity for them too. These various forms used for worship have been provided to suit the needs of different men at different stages of spiritual evolution.

5. Why call it an earthen image? The Divine image is made of spirit (consciousness) .

6. Why do these images rouse the idea of mud and clay, stone and straw, in your mind? Why can you not realise the presence of the eternal, blissful, all-conscious Mother (The Supreme Reality) even in these forms.?

7. If a worshipper is convinced that the images of the Deity in the shape of various gods and goddesses are verily divine, he reaches God through their worship. But if he holds them to be nothing better than mud and straw and clay, to him the worship of such images does no good.

8. If there is anything wrong in image-worship, does He not know that all worship is meant for Him? He will surely be pleased to accept that worship, knowing that it is meant for Him alone. Love God; that is the duty nearest to you.

9. When one sees God, one realises that everything, images and all, is a manifestation of the Spirit. To him the image is not made of clay but of spirit (consciousness). (Sayings of Sri Ramakrishna,P.100-101)

Q.15 What is the effect of Mantra (specially Gayatri Mantra) on our body and mind?

Answer : (a) Let us start with the meaning of Gayatri -- part by part.

Aum = God, the Absolute, Ultimate Reality.

[Bhuh = Earth; Bhuwah = Intermediate space; Svah = Skies]

Bhurbhuvah Svah = The Absolute Reality pervades the earth, intermediate space and the skies.

[Tat = It, Savituh = of the Sun]

Tat Savituh = It is like the luminousity of the Sun OR Sun is the symbol of its self-luminosity. But the sun is the source of physical light while the Reality is the source of awareness and knowledge.

Varenyam = Adorable -- because it is supremely wise.

Bhargo Devasya = The shine of the Self-luminous [as explained above]

Dheemahi = We meditate on It (as the Absolute and pervading Reality and as the source of awareness and knowledge).

Dhiyoyo = Intellects

Nah = ours

Prachodayat = May God, the source of our knowledge, kindle, awaken our intellectual faculty.

(b) In the Indian tradition this mantra was taught by the father to his son/daughter in presence of the teacher who was to take him/her for being educated under his guidance.

(c) If repeated in morning, mid-noon and evening, its effects are

(i) Freshness, vigour and poise of mind and intellect is maintained.

(ii) The feeling that God is my own innermost reality and source of my intelligence and power gives a hold on God, devotion, strength and confidence.

(iii) The repetition of Gayatri or any such mantra representing God increases the power of concentration and memory.

(iv) It checks the mind from becoming wayward.

(ii) It generates spiritual eminence.

Q.16 What are the benefits of meditation?

Answer : (a) Let us take an allegory to understand, first, as to what is ‘meditation’. During the British regime the administration used to appoint sergeants for night patrolling on the streets of big cities. These sergeants used to carry a lantern each which was shaded on their side. So, in the light of the lantern the sergeant could see all people and all that was happening, and also all people could see each other but could not see the sergeant.

Let us think of such a situtation, now. What could be the different responses of the people involved in it? Most of the people would neither bother to look at the light nor bother about the sergeant but remain satisfied in going about their own pursuits. A few people would feel that they could not have gone about their business without the light, and they would say "Thank you, O light!" and a fewer still would say "Thank you, O sergeant!" without even looking in that direction. Some rare people now and then would look at the light and bow down in that direction. Now, light cannot stand or move by itself, hence there has to be somebody holding it, and the fact that we are not seeing that person implies that there is shade on that side. This is the inference. It is also known from the newspapers that there is a sergeant holding the light -- seeing the people and helping them. So, some one -- different from others -- would be keen to ‘know’ and ‘see’ and ‘talk to’ the sergeant. Hence looking in that direction he would pray, "Sergeant, Sir, will you please turn the light towards your face, so that I can see you? And will you please talk to me!" The sergeant would oblige him if he felt the sincerity in the prayer.

Now, it is the light of God -- who is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss -- which reflects in our minds and in the world enabling us to have this interaction. One feels respectful grateful love called Bhakti for the Source of everything and prays and tries for turning the direction of the light reflected in our soul towards its source. This in short is the philosophical foundation of meditation.

(b) But, there are almost infinite variations in human temperaments, and hence the actual practice of meditation takes innumerable forms -- meditation suitable for each individual is to be learnt from expert guides only.

(d) The ‘benefits’ of meditation which can be enumerated as below -

(i) Everything positive in life grows, everything negative recedes.

(ii) There is a flow of supreme inner joy not dependent on anything in the world and hence

(iii) Mind has a positive outlook.

(iv) It is filled with vigour, strength and confidence.

(v) Is active with clarity of vision, but never restless or out of control.

(vi) Is controlled, steady and steadily active.

(vii) Is concentrated and properly focused.

(viii) Physical health is toned up.

(ix) Memory and power of retention increases.

(x) Potential divinity is manifested more and more

(xi) and, ultimately God is realised, the supreme Goal of life is achieved, man/woman himself/herself becomes divine.
on-the-goal-of-life:
## From where do we come and where do we go?

There is the following scene in the life of Bhagavan Buddha. His father, King Shuddhodan, had made such arrangements that no kind of unhappiness could cast its shadow on the life of the prince. One day he was seated in his royal chamber along with his beautiful and worthy wife Yashodhara and his charming infant son, Rahul. Music and dance surrounded them. At such a moment some angels appeared above him and floated from one side to the other (or were they forms taken by his own higher thoughts?). They were singing a song with the following refrain:

> From where we come—we do not know!
> To where we go from here—we do not know!
> Drifting, drifting, drifting—all the time
> We yearn for rest and peace—but we get neither!
> Drifting, drifting, drifting—we go.

And then he experienced the 'awakening' that unless one knows the truth—the meaning and the purpose of life—all pleasures only make one more and more blind. Hence before we can answer this let us turn to some more fundamental questions.

## Why is man born? Why do we live?

A few years back a girl student of first year. B.E.(Electronics) told me that she found absolutely no meaning in life. 'Life is certainly a vacuum' she said. 'Whatever meaning we try to find in life can be proved to be zero, a mere nothing.' On being asked the 'history of her thoughts' she stated: 'When I was in the 9th standard I thought only of one thing—my aim of becoming an electronic engineer. Mathematics and Science subjects were to my liking; I studied hard, secured good marks in the 12th class, got admitted into the Engineering College and the branch of my choice. I scored good marks in 1st year engineering examination also. So I thought my aim of becoming Electronic Engineer was almost fulfilled—as it was only a matter of time. It was at this point that it struck me that this "becoming an electronic engineer" is absolutely nothing and then I thought about everything that people find worthwhile and I realized that all of it was absolutely nothing. Hence I think that there is no meaning in this life—it is a vacuum.'

After a few days, another person, a lady aged about 35, came to the Ashrama and enquired whether we taught 'meditation'. On being asked what made her enquire about it, she said: 'I completed my studies, went into a job, got married and had children—all this happened like a flow. Then I faced struggle on all fronts. But now the job as well as the married life have become smooth and the children are growing up nicely. The necessary struggles brought about by the flow of life are thus over. And at this point I am struck with the feeling that life is a vacuum. I now realize that I don't know why I live. I have heard that meditation may help me to find out the "why" of living.'

Since then several people at different stages of life—boys studying in engineering colleges, even a girl studying in 8th standard—have been asking the same question over and over again: Why do we live? Has life any meaning or is all this just a vacuum? Some boys have even told their parents that the 'meaning' which they (the parents) find in life is nothing but a subjective projection of their own, while life itself does not appear to have any meaning.

I told all of them that (a) what they thought was correct to an extent; (b) this could be called an 'awakening'; (c) but there was another side to it also. The reason why we feel this futility etc. is that we are dealing with mere shadows. But shadows always indicate the 'thing' of which they are shadows. If we can get a hold over that 'thing', then alone will this feeling of emptiness vanish.

This 'thing' of which this world is a shadow is called God, the Absolute or Ultimate Reality which lies hidden in the deepest recesses of our own being.

## What is the goal of life?
## What is religion?

Swami Vivekananda tells us

> Each soul is potentially divine.
> The goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal.
> Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy—by one or more or all of these and be free.
> This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms are but secondary details.

When we try to understand these four aphorisms, we find that

(i) The truth applies to 'each' one of us without any exception whatsoever, irrespective of caste, creed, gender etc.

(ii) Each living being is called a 'soul' because it is basically of the nature of 'awareness' working in a particular body-mind set up which is like an external covering.

(iii) What we see now is not our real nature. Today our senses are continuously interacting with the objects outside and our mind is very restless and hence our real nature—the pure, perfect, blissful awareness—is hidden as it were. We will have to go very deep within ourselves to find out what we really are. And yet, that being our very nature, it is never really lost, and hence it is termed as 'potential'. It is really Infinite.

The great sages, whose vision is not obstructed by outside appearances, clearly see that One Infinite Universal Existence-Consciousness-Bliss Absolute with Infinite Power and Perfection is present in every individual hidden by the individual's limited thoughts, feelings, actions, etc.

Hence, just as the goal of each seed is to evolve into a fully grown tree—a mango-seed into a mango tree, an apple-seed into an apple tree—so also the 'goal' of each individual being is the manifestation of the Divine within in his/her own way. What obstructs this manifestation? The 'nature' of our body-mind set up. This has to be properly 'attuned' to our Reality—our divine potential within.

Each individual finds himself to be finite, limited, imperfect and has several wants and desires, and is acted upon by the outside world. He is pulled and dragged by his desires, wants and imperfections. All these are his bondages. Finally when the Infinite Divinity manifests itself in the individual, he finds himself free from all limitations, bondages, imperfection, drags and desires. This is called Freedom (Moksha) and is another way of looking at the goal. For this, we have to properly use whatever faculties we possess, after learning the secrets of work, worship, psychic control and philosophy.

Thus in the first aphorism Swami Vivekananda has revealed the fundamental Truth. In the second he has pointed out the goal as the natural corollary of this Truth. In the third he has shown us the various possible methods of achieving it and has also given us the impetus to do it. These three together constitute 'the whole of religion' says the Swami.

Of course the same Religion can be thought of in various other ways. 'Religion is realisation', says the great Swami over and over again. Let us try to understand what this means. When we analyse our lives and the world around us philosophically, we come to the conclusion that the Ultimate Truth is one universal Reality, which we generally call God. But when we consider our ordinary, superficial experience of the world we do not see 'God' at all. God is thus the ultimate Truth though it is not a fact of our experience today. But by proper spiritual practice and struggle this ultimate Truth has to be made a permanent fact of experience. Then only can we say that it has become 'real' to us. This is called 'real-isation' of Truth—and this is religion.

## How do we attain Moksha?

Suppose (figuratively speaking) God is sitting in a place and to reach Him there he has dropped several ropes which he is continuously pulling towards himself. When we catch one of these ropes and hold fast to it we are pulled by God to himself and we attain Moksha. If we catch several ropes and hold fast we may be more quickly pulled. What are these ropes? KarmaYoga, Bhakti Yoga, Raja Yoga, Jnana Yoga and all the paths of sadhana laid down by the different religions and sects of the world are the ropes held out by God himself for different temperaments. And practising them steadfastly is like holding fast to the ropes.

Moksha is not a place to be reached but the realisation of God, here, in this human life. Moksha means 'Freedom'. Freedom from what? From bondage.

## What is bondage?

(i) Our wrong identification with a particular body-mind set up which is changing continuously. (ii) As a result of this wrong identification, we have a feeling of limitedness, incompleteness. This is bondage. (iii) To remove these feelings we try to get something from outside—but anything added from outside, however big it may be, does not change our limitedness or incompleteness. Rather we tend to get lost under those outside accumulations, and that leads to further bondage. (iv) For us this body-mind alone is 'I' and everything else is 'not I' or 'you'. Behind everything is the same God who is hidden but His reflection makes everything appear real, animated and pleasurable. This apparent source of pleasure together with our limitedness gives rise to infinite desires which in turn generate other passions—anger, greed, delusion due to infatuation, intoxication, jealousy, competition and the like. These are all bondages. (v) Desires do not end when we try to satisfy them; they increase like fire fed with fuel. So bondage continues. (vi) The body collapses exhausted in the pursuit of desires but desires do not stop; hence we are born again and again and this rotation goes on. This is called the bondage of samsara.

In spite of all this we are potentially divine and if that divinity is fully manifested we no longer feel identified with any particular body-mind. Then there is no more feeling of limitedness or incompleteness, no craving for something from outside and no more getting lost under any outside thing, no more drags of desires, no more troubles from passions, no more burning of the fire of desires, no more compulsion to go through births and deaths again and again. Then we attain permanent and Absolute Perfection, permanent and Absolute Knowledge, permanent and Absolute Bliss—everything as in God. This is Moksha.

## How does one 'realise' that?

By steadfast and intense practice of everything which helps the manifestation of divinity and removal of the identification with a particular body-mind. This practice, according to individual temperaments forms the different yogas or different paths of sadhana laid down by different religions.

on-life-past-and-future:
## What happens after death?
## In the Gita it is written that when the soul leaves the body, it roams about for some time and then gets a new body. Is this true?

It is not written in the Gita that when the soul leaves the body, it roams about and then gets into a new body. In the Gita as well as in the Upanishads it is written that the soul gets a rebirth and a new body according to its karmas.

## What kind of life does the soul have after death?

We have a mind and a body which we obtained at birth. As we live our life, the body grows, evolves and decays, mostly according to the fixed potential which it has at birth. The mind, being much more changeable, has two forces working on it: (i) the starting potential and (ii) our relatively free will, thoughts and feelings, and the tendencies which are moulded by the training which we receive in the world and which we consciously cultivate.

Suppose, out of infinite tendencies playing in the human mind, a person cultivates the cat-like tendencies—moving about stealthily, stealing things, etc.—then by the time of death the mind of such a person would mostly become a 'cat-mind'. So when his present body would collapse, the 'cat-mind' would necessarily get a 'cat-body'.

Thus the following categories (types) of life after death have been described by the scriptures:

(i) Life in sub-human species like birds, animals, insects, trees and plants—even a tree or a stone.

(ii) Rebirth as a human being, with a human mind with all the tendencies or impressions gathered in this life.

These two types of births take place at the very point of death of the present body. The Chhandogya Upanishad explains the process by the example of a leech travelling from one leaf to the other by first getting its hold on the next leaf and then leaving the hold on the previous leaf.

(iii) If a person has done exceptionally good deeds and has accumulated exceptionally good tendencies, his mind is transformed into a god-mind. For the enjoyment of happiness resulting in such a mind, a body made of gross materials like that of man or animals is not enough, and hence he gets a refined divine body and lives in a different type of subtle abode. This is called Swarga (heaven). There are different categories of these heavens corresponding to the grades of refinement of the mind. Here he/she lives for a very long time since such a body does not decay so quickly.

(iv) The mind of the person who thinks of God, undergoes a different kind of change whereby he feels the nearness to and a tangible presence of God. Such a person goes to those spheres where he obtains a different type of bliss resulting from God-vision. The highest among these is called Vaikuntha by the devotees of Vishnu, Kailash by the devotees of Shiva, Sach-khand by the Sikhs and Satya-loka or Brahmaloka by philosophers.

(v) Those who get Illumination, full God-realisation, and identification with God, do not have to 'go' anywhere. Even while living in this life, they do not feel bound by body—they experience the infinitude even while living. This is called Jivanmukti or liberation while living. When the body drops, they permanently experience the identification with God, the Infinite. This is called videha mukti.

Except (v) none of the other states are permanent, and after exhausting the respective momenta one in these states is born again as a human being to get a chance to struggle for full God-realisation. It is important to note that the nearness to God achieved in (iv) is present in the next life also, and therefore the person gets a corresponding higher start.

## How can we perceive those lives from our frame of reference?

This can be done in three ways:

(i) To intellectually understand as explained above with the help of scriptures;

(ii) To study the descriptions of these lives given by mystics like Sri Ramakrishna, who perceived such beings and described them vividly.

(iii) To develop higher mystic consciousness which will enable us to directly perceive all these.

## Why do we forget after death the affectionate relationships which we have on this earth? Can they not be kept intact after death?

Compared to the innumerable lives an individual passes through one single human birth is too insignificant to make a permanent impact of 'affectionate attachments'.

## What are heaven and hell?
## It is said that if one does bad actions he/she goes to hell, and if one does good actions, he/she goes to heaven. Where are these heaven and hell?

What happens if we do good actions? The heart expands and becomes purer. The mind becomes less restless. God or Atman, the abiding indwelling Reality is Blissful by nature. This bliss of Atman reflects better in a mind which is not restless, but is broad and pure. This reflection is what we experience as the inner happiness. This persists even after the present body dies. The purified, expanded and steady mind remains with us even after this gross body falls off and we have our own inner bliss. This is called going to heaven.

What happens if we do bad deeds? The heart becomes contracted; it becomes impure; the mind becomes restless. The reflection of the Bliss of Atman gets distorted in our mind and we feel miserable. This continues even after death. Thus we remain miserable even when this body in which we did bad deeds is not there. This is called going to hell.

Jesus Christ calls God as 'father in heaven. He also tells us, 'The kingdom of heaven is within you', and again, 'Blessed are the pure in heart for they shall see God.' Combining these three utterances, we can conclude that heaven is nothing but a pure heart in which God is experienced.

## What are ghosts?
## Do ghosts and spirits really exist?

There are certain exceptions to the rules of rebirth mentioned above. A person has to exhaust a certain type and amount of karma or stored up momenta, in a specific life through a specific body. But if he/she dies of an unnatural death prematurely, through accident, suicide etc., without having worked out the momenta meant to be exhausted in that body, he/she does not get a body immediately. He/she has a mind and desires, but no body to work them out. Such beings are ghosts.

These ghosts and spirits do remember affections and associations of the previous incomplete lives and are sometimes helpful or hostile to their relations of the previous life because of their unfulfilled desires.

It is commonly believed and also verified that such beings get released from that state if someone prays for them or makes some devotional offerings to God for their sake.

As far as the truth of their existence is concerned, one should remember two things: (i) They do exist because they have been percieved by sages and mystics with an immaculate wider range of perceptions. (ii) And yet, ninety-nine percent of the cases reported by ordinary people are subjective imaginations.

## In the field of religion is there any place for astrology?
## How can we interpret the effect of planets in relation to religion?
## If the effects of planets are so powerful, what role should we give to God?

I would like to quote the great saint Tulasidas in this matter:

> Janakinath sahay kare jab
> Kaun bigar kare nara tero
> Suraja mangala soma bhrugusuta
> Budha aru guru varadayaka tero
> Rahu ketu ki nahi gamyata
> Sang sanichar hota uchero

Which means, 'When God becomes your helper, who can do any harm to you? Sun, Mars, Moon, Venus, Mercury and Jupiter will become bestowers of boons to you. Rahu and Ketu cannot reach you and Saturn will be on the ascent to help you.

## Is previous birth a fact? Do the actions of a previous birth influence the present life?

There is no doubt about the existence of previous births without which the samskaras present in this life cannot be explained. These samskaras represent the momentum acquired in the past lives. Their result determines largely our birth in a particular species, of a particular gender, in a particular family, and endowed with a certain life span and with the share of pleasure and pain to be experienced by us in this life. On the other hand, our experiences, progress and evolution in this life are the resultant of this past momentum plus the effort which we make in this life.

## Can we know about previous birth?

There are perhaps three ways of knowing about the previous birth:

(i) The great sage Patanjali tells us that if we are perfectly established in aparigraha, and absolutely refuse to accept any gift from anybody, we shall get the memory of past lives. Swami Vivekananda explains: 'When a man does not receive presents, he does not become beholden to others, but remains independent and free. His mind becomes pure. With every gift, he is likely to receive the evils of the giver. If he does not receive, the mind is purified, and the first power it gets is memory of past life.'

(ii) Again, in another chapter Patanjali says: By perceiving the impression, (comes) the knowledge of past life. As explained by Swami Vivekananda, 'Each experience that we have, comes in the form of a wave in the chitta, and this subsides and become finer and finer, but is never lost. It remains there in minute form, and if we bring this wave up again, it becomes memory. So if the Yogi can make a Samyama (perfectly steady concentration) on these past impressions in the mind, he will begin to remember all his past lives.

(iii) In Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master, Swami Saradananda tells of another method for the Jnana Yogi. When the consciousness of non-duality of Reality is cultivated to perfection the mind gets almost God-like purity. And in that mind all the past lives are seen like a cinematographic film.

Apart from these three methods which depend upon the tremendously evolved state of mind, we see in rare cases some people remembering their past lives without any effort. This happens only when the impressions of the past life are very strong. I know the case of a Sikh lady born in Chandigarh who remembers her past life as the daughter of a Kashmiri Pundit who used to worship Shiva in the temple of a particular village in Kashmir. Her husband took her to the village mentioned by her and she could easily identify the temple etc.
