on-the-philosophy-of-god:
## Is there a God or is it a supernatural power?

It is a wonderful question and let us first try to understand the mind of the questioner who asked it. Many people think God to be just a supernatural power while this question has put these in two separate categories.

When we look at this infinite world around us and try to think rationally about its origin and also about its actual running, our reason, with its sense of cause and effect will not allow us to feel satisfied with the idea that the world is functioning by itself or automatically. Either there must be a supernatural power which is the cause of all this or there is a Conscious Entity called God. Now, if the supernatural power is an unconscious force like electricity, how can it rule, govern, and direct this world? Not only has it to be a conscious entity, but It has to be the Infinite Consciousness having infinite power.

Of course, all our ideas of God are hazy in the beginning. However let us start with this basic logical necessity of an Infinite Consciousness with an infinite power ruling the universe and try to obtain clearer and clearer views of such a God.

## Is it really God who made us? How was the world made?
## How are we to believe that God exists?

The sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad relates an anecdote. Shvetaketu returned home after completing his education. He appeared conceited, proud of his learning and immodest. His father, a great sage, asked him, 'Did you ask for that instruction by which even the unknown becomes known?' On being asked by Shvetaketu to illustrate what he meant, the father said, 'By knowing a lump of clay in reality, everything made of clay is known, as the product is only a name and a form of the clay which alone is real. Similarly for things made of gold or iron. Such is the instruction about the Reality of this entire world.'

Shvetaketu then requested his father to give him that special instruction. His father said that in order to know who made us or how we were made or how the world was made, we must first of all try to think of the situation before the world was created and before we were created. All this that we see now, including ourselves, was absolutely non-existent then. But our reason will not allow us to think that anything can come out of 'nothing'. Hence we have to think of the starting point as the Infinite Absolute Existence—One, without a second. And again, for 'this' to come out of 'that', 'that' has to be not only Absolute Existence, but Absolute Consciousness also—One, without a second. This is the answer to the question: Why we believe in God?

## If we say that God is one, then why aren't people one?
## How did God come into the world?
## How does God spread his powers?

That Absolute Consciousness-Existence 'willed'—'I am one: I shall be many: Let me take the forms of separate individuals.' This is the answer of the question: Why, though God is one, we are many. From It (It is remarkable that God is not called 'He' or 'She' but 'It', by the Upanishads because such difference of gender cannot exist in the Infinite Absolute Ultimate Reality) then emerged space, air, light, water, solids and the different bodies, and in each body the absolute consciousness reflected itself as the individual consciousness. This is the answer to the question: How God spread His powers and came into this world?

Now let us try to understand God in relation to us—the living beings. A dark room gets illumined when we switch on an electric bulb. We conclude that the bulb is the source of light. Now look at the bulb. The whole bulb is not really the source of light nor is it self-luminous. The source of the light is the heated filament which becomes luminous due to heat. The bulb has a cover and shape which separates it from the room and air has been removed from the space enclosed by it, differentiating it from outside and hence it is filled with the glow of the light emanating from the filament. Now let us apply this illustration to ourselves.

We have our consciousness which illumines our mind and body and the entire universe for us, and this consciousness of ours is like the separated glow of the Consciousness-in-itself which we call God.

Swami Vivekananda gives an illustration: A gigantic engine is running on a track and a small worm sitting on the rails climbs down to save itself. What is the difference? The mighty engine is not aware of itself or of the worm, while the worm is aware of itself and also of the engine and hence tries to save itself from the engine. The difference between dull matter and living beings is therefore this awareness. We know ourselves and the world because of this awareness. We really are this awareness. This awareness is a reflection or a limited form (like the glow in the bulb) of THE Awareness-in-itself. This Absolute Awareness—One without a second is called God. (Like the electricity that heats the filament and makes it shine and thus expresses itself through the bulb).

That is why a girl, when asked for proof of God, replied, 'The very fact that "I" exist and I am aware of my existence has been possible only because God exists as the Absolute Ultimate Existence-Consciousness.'

Let us analytically understand one more vital fact pertaining to our knowledge. Swami Vivekananda explains:

> The mind must always travel between two extremes. You can think of limited space, but that very idea also gives you unlimited space. Close your eyes and think of a little space, at the same time you perceive the little circle, you have a circle round it of unlimited dimensions. It is the same with time. Try to think of a second, you will have, with the same act of perception, to think of time which is unlimited. So is it with knowledge. Knowledge is only a germ in man, but you will have to think of infinite knowledge around it, so that the very constitution of our mind shows us that there is unlimited knowledge, and the yogis call that unlimited knowledge God. In thinking of the limited, the mind must think of the unlimited, and if one part of that perception is true, so also must the other be, for the reason that their value as perceptions of the mind is equal. The very fact that man has a little knowledge shows that God has unlimited knowledge. If I am to take one, why not the other? Reason forces me to take both or reject both. If I believe that there is a man with a little knowledge, I must also admit that there is someone behind him with unlimited knowledge. (Raja Yoga P 139,140-41)

So on both sides—universal and individual—God is the basis of all existence, activity and awareness. Not to understand this is blindness, foolishness and shallowness of thought.

## How was God born? Who created God? From where has God come?

These questions which appear rational on the surface are found to be irrational and foolish with a little thought. 'Birth', 'coming', 'creation'—what do they mean? Our conception about this universe and the objects in it is that there was a time when all this was not there, and then it came into being. So we clearly assume the pre-existence of something which could be the cause of this. Now, God is to be understood as the ultimate cause, the eternally existing Reality. There was never a time when God was not there. Even when time itself was not there, God was there. So no question of 'coming', 'birth', 'creation' can apply or have any meaning in relation to God. Our experience of the finite cannot be projected onto the infinite God—who pre-exists everything that is born and continues to exist when all is gone. And so we call God as beginningless and endless—Absolute Existence—One, without a second.

## What is the Zeroness (shunyata) advocated by Indian Philosophers?

This has two aspects. One is about the Ultimate Reality and the other is about the transitory world of our experience.

Some of the non-vedic (heterodox) schools especially, Buddhists, talk of shunyata (zeroness) regarding the ultimate nature of Reality, but not the vedic schools. In Chhandogya Upanishad the teacher tells the disciple: 'In the beginning all this was only Absolute Existence—One, without a second. Some people say that in the beginning all this was non-existence alone—One, without a second. But, my dear one, how can existence come out of non-existence. Hence, my dear one, all this, in the beginning was Absolute Existence alone—One, without a second.' So this is the position regarding the Ultimate Reality.

But why refer to what others say? Because, all this as we see and feel today, was surely not there before it was created. Hence it is necessary to feel the 'zeroness' of the world as it appears to us today, in order to grasp the ultimate Reality behind and beyond all this.

There is a third context: the necessity to feel the 'zeroness' or hollowness of 'ego'—to really get at the Reality behind and beyond. Mahapurushji, a disciple of Sri Ramakrishna, used to say: 'If you want the poorna (the Infinite), you should become shunya (zero).' If 'you' become shunya, you will attain the poorna (Infinite).

## What is spiritual strength?

While we are climbing steps, we have to leave the lower step before we can put our foot on the next higher step. But a tendency of not leaving the previous step is present in us. In such a situation we require the courage to go ahead, the conviction of ultimate success and the strength to leave the previous step. This is called spiritual strength. There is a proverb in Hindi: Kuch paane ke liye kuch khona padata hai! i.e., to get something worthwhile we have to lose some trash. But we ask sometimes: Kya kuch khoye bina paa nahi sakte? 'Can we not get what we want without losing even the trash?' This is spiritual weakness.

## What is sin?

A very simple and universal answer is given by the great sage Vyasa in this pithy couplet:

> Shruti-smriti-puraneshu
> vyasasya vachanadwayam;
> Paropakarah punyaya
> papaya parapeedanam;

Doing good to others is holy action; while giving trouble to others is sin.

^^ These questions were asked by the students and teachers of Modi Institute of Education and Research, Lakshmangarh, Rajasthan during their interaction with Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh, on 22 and 23 January 1999. The Swami has rearranged these questions and their answers under specific themes.
on-god-and-man:
## What is there in God that we call him God?

This question asks us to define God. Let us try: God is Absolute, Infinite, Undivided, Eternal. Existence-Consciousness-Bliss (Sat-Chit-Ananda).

God is both the efficient and the material cause of creation (or projection or appearance), preservation (or sustenance or continuation) and dissolution (or disappearance) of the world. When a potter makes a pot from clay, he is said to be the efficient cause of the pot while clay is the material cause. In the case of the world, God is both the efficient and material cause, i.e. God projects the world from within himself by his own will.

God is the one Ruler of this universe. Nobody has the power to overrule him. He is Eternally pure, All-pervading, Ever-free, Almighty, All-knowing, All-merciful, Teacher of all teachers.

God is inexpressible Love and Bliss. He is Absolutely Perfect and is the repository of an infinite number of blessed qualities. God is our Father, Mother, Friend, Lover, Beloved, Support, Innermost Reality, the Life of our life, our All in all. Hence God is called God.

## Why do we respect God so much?

We respect anyone for his/her merits or noble qualities. But all merits and qualities in every respect are in God to an infinite degree.

We respect parents and other elders as they are 'older' and wiser and know more about the world and life than us. But God is the 'Oldest'—pre-existing before the world itself. God is the wisest and knows everything about the world and about life.

Parents are also respected because they are like 'causes' and we are 'effects'. God is the Ultimate Cause and everything and everybody is an effect coming out of God. That is why we respect God so much, though our respect is much less than what it should be.

God is also the source of all good found anywhere. Hence when we respect anyone we respect God reflected in that person. If we know this, we will love and respect God as well as all creatures.

## Where does God exist?

God exists everywhere, permeates every atom and yet is also beyond everything by his very nature. God is ever present concealed in the cave of the heart of every living being.

## How should we recognise God?
## It is said that an incarnation comes to the earth whenever there is a crisis. If such a thing happens in this age, how will we recognise it?

In the world we see egotism, selfishnessess, attachment, narrowness etc., born out of identification with a limited body-mind complex. But we also see egolessness, respect for others, broadmindedness, non-attachment to particulars, universal love, unselfishness, a spirit of service, dislike for enjoyment and a liking for tyaga and tapasya, etc. Wherefrom do these things come? From God, no doubt, for such is the nature of God—the Absolute Perfection—the repository of infinite blessed qualities. Hence whenever and wherever we see the play of these divine qualities, we should recognise the presence of God. If we see in any person these qualities in abundance, we should recognise him/her as vibhutimat, i.e. a very special manifestation of God. And if we see the full manifestation of these qualities we can recognise that person as God. This is the theory of divine incarnations like Sri Rama, Sri Krishna, the Buddha, Jesus Christ and Sri Ramakrishna.

God comes down in the form of these incarnations so that man may recognise God and feel sure that God can manifest in a human body and mind. So one must struggle hard to manifest his/her potential divinity fully in life.

## Are the tales about God true?

The tales of God can be divided into several categories: (a) Biographical and historical (b) Legendary and mythological (c) Allegorical (d) Mixed. Valmiki Ramayana and Mahabharata belong to the first category and are called itihasa, i.e., iti-ha-aasa—meaning 'like this-it is well known that-it happened.' The stories contained in the Puranas, on the other hand, fall mostly under (b), (c) and (d). The purpose of these Puranas is not to provide biographical or historical facts. According to Swami Vivekananda:

> Philosophy of course is the essence of every religion, mythology explains and illustrates it by means of the more or less legendary lives of great men, stories and fables of wonderful things, and so on; rituals give to that philosophy a still more concretised form, so that everyone may grasp it—ritual is in fact concretised philosophy. (CW.1,72)

> Some historical truth is the nucleus of every Purana. The object of the Puranas is to teach mankind the sublime truth in various forms; and even if they do not contain any historical truth, they form a great authority for us in respect of the highest truth which they inculcate. .. Hinduism stands independent of any man, and for the purpose of estimating the philosophical truth contained in any Purana, we need not consider the question whether the personages treated of therein were really material men or fictitious characters. The object of the Puranas was the education of mankind, and the sages who constructed them contrived to find some historical personages and to superimpose upon them all the best or worst qualities just as they wanted to, and laid down the rules of morals for the conduct of mankind. (C.W 5, 207-208)

## Are our prayers really heard by God?

A Christian saint, Brother Lawrence, says: 'When we talk and God listens, it is called prayer; and when God talks and we listen (i.e. we get responses from God within) then it is meditation.'

## If we pray to God for something do we really get it?

Ours is to pray, to give or not is God's discretion.

## Is it necessary to make offerings to God?

Offerings made to God should be called naivedya. It becomes prasad (sanctified food) only after God has accepted it.

God has created everything in the world including us. God has also created in us a capacity to do what we like. God has created food and has given us the capacity to eat food. Everything belongs to God. If we understand this thoroughly, should we not think and feel always that we owe God our food, our enjoyments in the world, our activities? If we do not, we will be thieves, and shall incur sin by eating without offering it to God, says the Gita.

If we really love anyone—do we not feel more happy by feeding him/her first and then eating what remains? If we do not feel that way, aren't we acting selfishly and loving our enjoyments more than anything else? Those who love God feel that way. And hence they offer everything to God or rather they try to make God eat before they do.

Similarly, if you have a high regard for someone, do you not feel like serving him/her? Those who have highest regard for God feel so. Offering food and other items becomes a part of those acts of service. All these actions help us to feel the living presence of God.

## How does God accept the food offered?

It is described in Sri Ramakrishna The Great Master that when Sri Ramakrishna used to offer cooked food to Mother Kali, he used to see a ray of light coming out from Her eyes, touching all the offered articles, taking their essence and withdrawing again into Her eyes.

This has been corroborated with some more explanation by the Holy Mother Sarada Devi. Once a disciple asked her whether the Master really partakes of the food that she offers him and if so, how does He do it? The Mother replied that a light comes out of his eyes and licks all the articles of food. His ambrosial touch replenishes them again. So there is no decrease. Although the Master does not require any food, He eats the food offering only for the gratification of the devotees. The sacred prasad purifies the heart. Mind becomes impure if one eats food without first offering to God. She further said that in the case of some offerings, He actually eats and in other cases he merely looks at them. Just as we don't like to eat all things at all times, nor do we relish the food offered by anyone and everyone, similar is the case with God.

## Can a person be a devotee of God without giving up worldly pleasures or will he have to leave his family and turn into a vairagi?

Please do not mix worldly 'pleasures' and 'family' life. There are many people who lead a family life and yet are very much devoted to God. If you read The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna you will find that from the first page to the last, Sri Ramakrishna is telling the householders how they can be devoted to God.

## Who is a friend? Why does the human heart yearn for a friend? Give us guidelines for being a good friend.

Really speaking, God alone is our best friend. The great sage Shankaracharya says in his commentary on the Gita, that usually a friend is a friend only so long as we are nice to him, but God is our friend always and ever.

This God, who is the Ultimate Reality—One only, without a second—manifests Himself in innumerable ways through the infinite variety of human beings. This leads to a situation where each individual finds himself/herself different from others and separate from others, limited, and hence, to complete himself/herself, he/she craves for a friend who is an expression of the same common Reality and yet is differently constituted. So much so that many of us feel totally at a loss to cope up with life without a proper friend or friends.

If we can be always aware that friendship is based on two factors— (a) variety outside, and (b) a common background and support of the single Universal Reality called God—we can be true friends always. In that case the third friend, God, will always be available in case we fall out with each other due to some reason.

The purpose of friendship is to complement, supplement and help each other to attain perfection. When perfection is reached we don't need help and then we can be real friends because we feel the same God in us and in others.

Friendship should be based on giving and not expecting. 'A friend in need is a friend indeed' is the old proverb. Friendship should lead to more and more improvement together. It should never be against anybody and never lead to common disaster by doing anything bad together. Friendship is destroyed by imposing and expecting. It is really built up in freedom.

Select your friends very carefully in such a way that your merits get a boost and not the demerits or evil passions. Friendship is sustained by each one struggling to be a better individual and by always helping each other.

^^ These questions were asked by the students and teachers of Modi Institute of Education and Research, Lakshmangarh, Rajasthan during their interaction with Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh on 22 and 23 January 1999.
on-japa-and-meditation:
## What is the effect of Mantra (specially Gayatri Mantra) on our body and mind?

Let us start with the meaning of Gayatri.

> Aum = God, the Absolute, Ultimate Reality.
> Bhuh = the Earth; Bhuwah = the Intermediate space; Svah = the skies. Aum Bhurbhuvah Svah = The Absolute Reality pervades the earth, intermediate space and the skies.
> Tat = It, Savituh = of the Sun. Tat Savituh = It is like the luminosity of the sun or sun is the symbol of Its self-luminosity. But the sun is the source of physical light while the Reality is the source of awareness and knowledge.
> Varenyam = Adorable, because it is supremely wise.
> Bhargo Devasya = The shine of the Self-luminous. Dheemahi = We meditate on It as the Absolute and pervading Reality and as the source of awareness and knowledge.
> Dhiyo = Intellects, yo = who, Nah = our
> Prachodayat = may kindle, awaken, guide.

Thus the full meaning of the Mantra would be: We meditate on the excellent glory of that Divine Being who permeates and ilumines the three worlds. May he awaken and guide our understanding.

In the Indian tradition this mantra was taught by the father to his son/daughter in presence of the teacher who was to take charge of the education of the youngster. If repeated in the morning, mid-noon and evening, it produces:

(i) Freshness, vigour and poise of mind and intellect; and (ii) the feeling that God is my innermost reality and source of my intelligence and power. It gives strength, confidence, and devotion.

The repetition of Gayatri or any such mantra representing God increases the power of concentration and memory. It checks the mind from becoming wayward and generates spiritual potency.

## What is meditation?

(a) Let us take an allegory. During the British regime sergeants used to patrol the streets of big cities at night. They used to carry a lantern which was shaded on their side. So, in the light of the lantern the sergeant could see everything and everybody. Also people could see each other, but could not see the sergeant.

Now, what could be the responses of the people to such a situation? Most of the people would neither bother about the light or the sergeant but would be satisfied going about their own pursuits. A few people would feel that they could not have gone about their business without the light, and they would say 'Thank you, O light!'. A fewer still would say 'Thank you, O sergeant!' without even looking in that direction. Rarely would someone look at the light and bow down in that direction. Now, light cannot stand or move by itself; there has to be somebody holding it. So, some one, different from the others, would be keen to 'know' and 'see' and 'talk to' the sergeant. Hence, looking in that direction he would pray, 'Sergeant, Sir, will you please turn the light towards your face, so that I can see you? And will you please talk to me?' The sergeant would oblige him if he felt that the prayer was sincere.

Now, it is the light of God—who is Existence-Consciousness-Bliss—which falls on our minds and on the world enabling us to have this interaction. One feels respectful and grateful towards such a God—the source of Light and knowledge and tries to discover that source. This in short is the philosophical basis of meditation. It is the attempt to turn the light towards its source within.

## What are the types of Meditations?

There are infinite variations in human temperaments, and hence the actual practice of meditation takes innumerable forms. Let us discuss a few broad categories:

(i) Karma Yogi's meditation: The predominantly active Karma yogi, before plunging into activities, sits quietly and tries to feel deeply that God is present in the heart as the source of consciousness and intelligence and imparts all the strength required for work. He/She is God's beloved servant who loves his/her Master very dearly and wishes to carry out God's will; or he/she is merely the instrument through whom God gets His work done.

Throughout the day, whenever units of work are complete, he/she tries to be with God for just a few moments before the next work.

In the evening or before going to bed, he/she tries to introspect, and becoming aware of his/her follies of ego, selfishness, haughtiness etc, prays to God from the depth of his heart and surrenders all actions, good and bad, and their fruits, to God and seeks God's help to do better the next day.

(ii) Bhakti Yogi's meditation: The devotee loves God both inside the depths of the heart and also outside through some image, photo, symbol, book etc. which are kept in a secluded place. He/She keeps that place clean, decorates it with flowers, burns incense, waves a light and reads a devotional text. He/She tries to feel through these acts, God as the dearest centre of his/her life. He/She steadily visualises the chosen form of God seated on a lotus in the heart, concentrates there lovingly and repeats a mantra for as long as he/she can. He/She does the same thing in the evening—may be with some other text—but using the same mantra.

(iii) Rajayogi's meditation: The introspective self-observant mind of the Raja Yogi is very harsh on himself/herself. The Raja Yogi tries to keep the mind absolutely still, observes what is going on on its surface as well as in the depth—crossing layer after layer—and checking the mind from within till he/she comes to have total control of mind. He/She tries to keep the mind absolutely still so that the innermost Reality may shine in Its true form.

(iv) Jnana Yogi's meditation: The mind of a Jnana yogi is aware that this world, including his body-mind etc., is merely an appearance and the Reality is one without a second—Undivided Existence-Consciousness-Bliss. He/She listens raptly to the experiences of the sages recorded in the scriptures, reflects upon this truth and always tries to remain deeply absorbed in such awareness.

These are very broad outlines. Since in the human mind there is usually an overlap of different types and has innumerable varieties, meditation suitable for each individual is to be learnt from expert guides only.

## What are the benefits of Meditation?

The benefits of meditation are:

(i) Everything positive in life grows, everything negative recedes. There is a flow of supreme inner joy not dependent on anything in the outer world.

(ii) Mind is filled with vigour, strength and confidence; gets clarity of vision, gets controlled, steady and active, concentrated and focused. Physical health also improves. Memory and power of retention are increased. In short one's potential divinity is manifested more and more and ultimately God is realised, the supreme goal of life is achieved; man woman himself/herself becomes divine.

Swami Vivekananda says:

> Meditate! The greatest thing is meditation. It is the nearest approach to spiritual life—the mind meditating. It is the one moment in our daily life that we are not at all material—the soul thinking of itself, free from all matter—this marvellous touch of the soul! (C.W.5, 253)

## What is Brahma Muhurta? Why is this time best for meditation? Does the effect of Mantra depend on time?

Precisely speaking, Brahma Muhurta is little more than three-quarters of an hour preceding sunrise—e.g. if the sunrise at a place on a particular day is at 6 a.m., then 5.12 a.m. to 6 a.m. would be the Brahma Muhurta for that place on that day. Brahma Muhurta means the time when Brahman, the all pervading Reality, is comparatively more manifest in nature and in human mind also.

The external nature as well as our body and mind have three cyclic functional phases called Sattva, Rajas and Tamas. Sattva is the quality of pure existence and is characterised by equipoise, serenity, balance of mind and a tendency for pure knowledge, devotion, unselfishness etc. Rajas is of the nature of colouring of the mind and is characterised by likes and dislikes, passions, restlessness, etc. Tamas is of the nature of darkness and is characterised by ignorance, dullness, inertia, delusion, inability to exert or improve oneself etc. All these three occur cyclically. In the external nature Rajas predominates during the day; Tamas pre-dominates at night; and Sattva dominates only for a short while in the four null points: (i) when night is over but the day has not set in, (ii) when the day is over but night has yet to set in, (iii) mid-noon and (iv) mid-night. Human life also follows this course. In the night Tamas covers our mind. Before the day breaks sattva dominates. Then follows Rajas. If we catch the periods when sattva-mode predominates, we are likely to succeed better in meditation, japa or in mental worship. Hence it is advised to meditate during these meeting points or sandhya-kalas.

^^ These questions were asked by the students and teachers of Modi Institute of Education and Research, Lakshmangarh, Rajasthan, during their interaction with Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh, on 22 and 23 January 1999.
womens-empowerment:
(submitted to Rev. Pr. Vivekaprana Mataji by Arpita Mitra, Prachi Singh and Soma Sen)

This questionnaire was re-submitted to Swami Pitambarananda who replied, in essence, as follows —

## 1. What is empowerment?

Reply : The literal meaning of ‘empower’ is ‘to give’; hence ‘empowerment’ is ‘the act or process of giving power’. The very idea, taken literally, is presumptuous. You can give power to someone only if you possess it and if he or she does not. In reality God alone has all the power or all the powers gives to both men and women some powers temporarily to use. But in the present world scenario some seemed to have usurped the power given to some others and that is why this so-called ‘empowerment’ has become necessary.

In the Vedantic view, is only a particularized manifestation of the One-without-a-second, Infinite Divine. Hence everyone has recourse to infinite power which belongs to the Infinite Being. Everyone needs to be made aware of this twofold Truth — (i) no one has power of his own — hence this trying to usurp the power is self-destructive; and (ii) everyone has recourse to Infinite power — hence let us make each other ‘aware’ of this truth, and that would be real ‘empowerment’.

## 2. Why do we talk about women’s empowerment and not of men’s empowerment? Is women’s empowerment different form men’s empowerment?

Reply : Brahman, the Ultimate, Universal Reality is Itself Atman, the real reality of every individual. It is beyond subject-object split. Everything in the manifested world, which is called ‘appearance’ or ‘apparently real’ or the creation of Maya is essentially endowed with subject-objectness. Russian philosopher Ouspensky calls this ‘subject-objectness’ as “ the irreducible minimum of human experiences”. (When the indescribable ‘fourth’ or Turiya is described as ‘Advaitam’ in the 7th mantra of the Mandukyopanishad, it refers to this subject-objectlessness of the Reality in contrast with the subject-object split in all our experiences in the states of waking, dream, and dreamless sleep.) In this context of the ‘creation’ ‘man’ has preponderance of subject-ness while ‘woman’ has preponderance of object-ness. Without this basic difference there would be no ‘creation’. This basic difference cannot be ignored, nor can it be obliterated except in the state of dissolution of the universe called Pralaya (or in Jnana-pralaya, i.e., the realization of one’s own Reality, which is beyond subject-object split.) This object-oriented consciousness gives rise to Tamas or inertia, dependence on man loke creeper on tree, tendency to receive or accept rather than be pro-active or take initiative, always prompting, persuading, provoking, seducing men to take initiative, be aggressive etc. The foolish women want to be bare-bodied to attract men to do something. (When they do not like what is done, they shout.) Naturally men have usurped all the powers which women have allowed them to usurp. Hence the need for empowerment of women and not of men.

The solution, of course, is neither in ignoring nor in trying to obliterate this basic difference, in but firmly asserting the potential divinity or the real reality — subject-objectless Infinity, the repository of all knowledge, wisdom, love, and power hidden behind this manifested subject-object split. This has to be done by the women themselves and helped by men for the ultimate welfare of the society as a whole.

## 3. In today’s day and age, what is the real definition of a “smart woman”?

Reply : Useless question.

## 4. What is Swamiji’s message for women?

Reply : Each soul is potentially divine; stand on your own legs.

## 5. What is the role of women in the framework of the nation?

Reply : Womanly wisdom; all-forbearing heart. The westerners believe that while men use their reason, women work by their intuition. It may or may not be true, but it shows that women have different type of wisdom than man.

## 6. Why do fewer women as compared to men come forward to embrace monasticism? Are there reasons both external and internal?

Reply : They are differently constituted and they can achieve their goal without formal monasticism.

## 7. Do women require any special qualities to embrace monasticism? [Holy Mother had once remarked that sannyasa is not possible in a woman’s body; again, in another context, she had said that women renunciates like Gouri Ma were basically very manly]

Reply : Instead of “very manly” make it “more than manly” and you have got your answer.

## 8. Is women’s nature different from that of men? Is the path to freedom and internal development different for women as compared to men given the combination of social and individual factors?

Reply : Yes, predominance of ‘object’-consciousness makes them have Tamas or inertia, and also being attached to their own bodies they become extremely attached to their own children which gives them a sort of blindness.

## 9. Why did Swamiji leave it entirely upto women to decide their own collective future, totally independent of any interference from men?

Reply : Because ‘man’ can never understand ‘women’ psyche; and also because if they depend on men, they lose their power.

## 10. From our experiences of collective living in hostels, we know that it is relatively easier for ten men to stay together, but difficult even for two women to stay together — frequent bickering and the flow of a lot of negative emotions. What is the root of this problem? What is the solution? Is the lack of feeling of oneness with other women an impediment to women’s empowerment?

Reply : Women’ due to their object-consciousness have a slavish mind-set which is the root of suspicion, jealousy and mistrust.

## 11. There was a change that occurred from Vedic times to the later times of Manusmriti. Education and life-long brabmacharya of women were in practice during Vedic times. Gradually, their education took a back seat and they were being married off early to protect their sexual chastity. Why did this happen? Was this the origin of the shift from soul-consciousness to body-consciousness of women? Logically, are not education and brabmacharya better ways of preserving women’s chastity?

Reply : Only due to Muslim invasion who saw women only as ‘object’ ( to the extent that they said that women have no souls).

## 12. How can women change their own mindset in today’s highly materialized age that they are not commodities and objects of enjoyment?

Reply : The only way under any time and circumstance is the Truth enunciated by Swami Vivekananda — “Each soul is potentially divine.”

## 13. What are the specific struggle points for women of today? How can they overcome them?

Reply : The women should themselves find out the struggle-points — then only a ‘man’ can make humble suggestions.

## 14. What are the special qualities that today’s women need to develop to take up Swamiji’s work of service to the nation?

Reply : This term “Swamiji’s work”, used mainly in Sarada Math, is strange. Swamiji himself always talked of Sri Thakur’s work’. Any way, the qualities to be developed are unselfishness, devotion, self-control and study of Swamiji’s Karma-Yoga and the Bhagavadgita.

## 15. When once asked whom he liked better — Indian or Western women — Swamiji said that he liked both, for both have their special qualities. Elsewhere he had written that each nation is a type, and the time has not yet come for the destruction of types, each nation has to nationalize ideas it assimilates from other nations. So, is the road to empowerment different for Indian and Western women — especially in this modern age, when a lot of differences have dissolved? If yes, do the two paths still converge somewhere?

Reply : Convergence of all paths is only in realization of Brahman and still the manifestations will differ — as between any two disciples of ShriRamakrishna. Otherwise the world will cease to exist when external sameness is achieved.

[[PAGE 3]]

## 16. In what ways can modern women take up Holy Mother as a model of empowered womanhood?

Reply : The foremost thing is her ‘universality’ — try to broaden yourself in your thoughts, feelings, unselfish action - along with supreme self-control.

## 17. I would also want to know at some point Mataji's opinion or advice to women regarding self-reflection and self-awareness and how they relate to empowerment. Often in society, it seems like if a woman is engaged in self-reflection and follows her heart in ways that makes the soul happy, it can be perceived as selfish.

Reply : There is ‘self’-ishness and ‘Self’-ishness, e.g., Swamiji says — “Faith in Self means faith in all, because the same Self is in all. To blind-like eyes, even this may appear as selfishness, but it can’t be helped. One’s self-reflection should lead to the awareness of ‘Self’ which is One-without-a-second’. One should discriminate to find whether the ‘happy soul’ refers to ‘oneself’ or The Self.

## 18. Another question I have is the role of the rational self and the role of emotional self in building empowerment. Typically in patriarchal societies men's way of thinking has been the hegemony. Women's way of relation based thinking may seem personal and not universal. Often this has been seen as a weaker or "less than" cognitive process. However, if I look around the world women seem to be the ones that hold a society together. So why do we feel so divided?

Reply : There is a ‘feeling’ self which is much deeper than the ‘rational’ self and far removed from the ‘emotional’ self. “Emotion is biological” — a great sage used to say. He said — “Genuine feeling proceeds from the absolutely tranquil heart. Of course he used to add in the same breath — “Genuine thinking proceeds from the absolutely tranquil heart; genuine will proceeds from the absolutely tranquil heart.” One has to separate ‘heart’ from the emotional mind, though in the beginning the two are mixed. The work of the rational self is to ‘analyse’ which may lead to ‘division’, but if wedded to genuine feeling, it would lead to ‘filtration’ of the pure from the biological. The emotion has a ‘trace’ of ‘feeling’, that is why it holds the society together, but unless it is filtered it leads to ‘war’ often. (Picture showing mind and heart attached.
