## Letter 1

From: Swami Pitambarananda
Ramakrishna Kutir,
Mayakund, Rishikesh — 249201
(India)

Dt/- January 18th 2012

To, Dr. Koenraad ELST, Ph.D.

Dear Dr. Konraad Elst,

Just now I happened to read your excellent article "Why 108", at the end of which you have invited suggestions about any additional significance of 108. Well, this is what I have heard —

Late Most Revered Swami Gahanananda, who was pesident of the Ramakrishna Mission for some years was once asked why are we asked to tell our beads 108 times. He replied —

The Indians did not divide the day into 24(hours)x60(minutes)x60(seconds) bits of time, but into 60(ghatikas) x 60(palas) x 60(Vipalas) = 216000 bits of time; and if we cannot remember GOD once every particle of time, we can atleast do so once in 1000 bits of time; hence we are asked to do so 108 times in the morning and 108 times in the evening = 216 times (or any multiples thereof).

Hope, this may be of some interest to you.

Yours in the service of the LORD
Swami Pitambarananda

## Letter 2

From: Swami Pitambarananda
Ramakrishna Kutir,
Mayakund, Rishikesh — 249201
(India)

Dt/- January 18th 2012

To, Dr. Koenraad ELST, Ph.D.

Dear Dr. Konraad Elst,

In your excellent article on 108, the idea about 'Big 1 small 8' is the most appropriate. But, as you do not think that the 'planets' give objectively rational explationations, you have tried geometrical explanations. But there are directly metaphysical explanations. E.g., in the Gita(Bhagvadgita) chapter 7 verses 4 & 5, we are told that the 'lower nature' is eightfold consisting of 5 elements of matter, mind, intellect and ego (which are all material — gross and subtle), while the 'higher nature' consists of the single principle — the 'Conscious Being'. This is based on the truth of experience that if a man contemplates only the material components of the universe, he gets more and more entangled in them, can't rise higher. But if he/she contemplates on the Conscious principle, he rises higher and higher and realises his inherent Divinity. This truth — this categorisation and enumeration — has pervaded Indian metaphysical thought. Your other observation about the intervening zeroes that 'an abyss of worshipful distance is created between the regal 1 and the servile 8' is very apt.

We need not discuss here the psychological relevence of 9 planets of ancient Indian astrology. The Earth may be a 'planet' in physical astronomy, but as we live on it, we can't psychologically take it as an object called 'planet'. Similarly, though Sun may be thought of relatively as that around which the other planets revolve (though even the Sun is known to be moving), yet so far as affecting our life is concerned, it is sometimes available and sometimes not, and thus gets the place of a planet, though the most important one, without which we can not live, while the other planets, including the mythological 2, affect our life in a smaller manner. ...

This is offered to 'a brother in the thought-world'.

Yours in brotherly thoght,
Swami Pitambarananda
guidelines-for-youth:
## What should be the basic guidelines of life?

1. Conviction in one's own and other's potential divinity should be the first principle.
2. Faith in oneself, which directly follows from the above conviction.
3. The four cardinal virtues : i. Unselfishness; ii. Devotion to God; iii. Self-control; iv. Rational understanding of the nature of things.
4. Devotion to duty
5. Regularity of spiritual practice.
6. Planned and disciplined life.
7. Zest for knowledge.
8. Following everything that makes oneself strong—physically, mentally, morally, spiritually—and avoiding everything which weakens.
9. If one is cent-per-cent sure about a thing being right, one must have the courage to follow it.

## Which yoga should students follow?

Let us remember Swami Vivekananda's aphorisms:

(i) Each soul is potentially divine;
(ii) The goal is to manifest this divinity within by controlling nature, external and internal;
(iii) Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy—by one, or more, or all of these and be free.
(iv) This is the whole of religion. Doctrines, or dogmas, or rituals, or books, or temples, or forms are but secondary details.

In another place Swami Vivekananda says:

> Our main problem is to be free. It is evident then that until we realise ourselves as the Absolute, we cannot attain deliverance (liberation). Yet there are various ways of attaining this realization. These methods have the generic name of yoga (to join, to join ourselves to our reality). These yogas, though divided into various groups, can principally be classed into four; and as each is only a method leading indirectly to the realisation of the Absolute, they are suited to different temperaments. (C.W.8, 152)

According to Western psychologists, the human mind has three functions, viz., 'thinking', 'feeling' and 'willing'. There is yet another one which can be thought of as a separate function of the mind: self-control or self-discipline. In each individual these four faculties are present in different degrees and in varying proportions. Add to these the variety within each of these functions, e.g., fatherly love, motherly love, brotherly love, etc. Thus, there is no limit to the variation in individual temperaments. This makes for an infinite number of approaches towards controlling nature, external and internal, so that the Divine within may manifest. Each person has to start from where he or she is and has to use whatever faculties he or she possesses in whatever degree.

Swami Vivekananda classified the paths by grouping them under four broad categories—Karma Yoga, Bhakti yoga, Raja Yoga and Jnana Yoga—dealing respectively with the faculties of will, feeling, self-control and thinking.

So we will have to analyse our own personalities with the help of wise people to find out what faculties and potentials we possess and how to harness them and how to improve them. Thus we can have a more active student, a more feeling student, a more disciplined student, a more intelligent student etc. We should always try to develop ourselves harmoniously with respect to all these four faculties. Education itself is not defined merely as studies but as physical, mental and moral training wherein mental training includes training of thinking, feeling, willing and self-control.

## What should the children do whose first and primary goal is to study?

I was once amidst students of the higher secondary (11th & 12th standard) classes who told me that their parents enjoyed watching T.V. but did not allow them to do so and told them: 'Now you should go on studying so that later on you may enjoy yourselves.'

They then asked me: 'Why should we not enjoy pleasures now itself? What would happen if we die tomorrow?'

I exclaimed: 'Alas! How wrong it is to motivate students towards study by telling them that it would show them the way (through money) to the enjoyment of pleasures (which even a pig can have without any education)! Why not tell them that education will make them better individuals and help them to express their respective potentials, fully and properly. Side by side, they should develop their physical skills, their feelings, in the right direction and learn to control passions and self-destructive emotions. Indulging in fleeting pleasures of the senses which titillate the nerves and fritter away their energy will hamper their capacity to improve. If we run after enjoyments, we shall not have the power to improve ourselves and those enjoyments will also slip away from us like shadows, but if we continually struggle for self-improvement, then happiness will follow. Of course, we must have some recreations which are an essential part of education. And we can derive abundant pleasures from creative cultural activities, along with games, sports and healthy hobbies.

## Is meditation and long prayers, the only way to reach God?

Some students engage in meditation and long prayers and come up very well in their studies. Some others use meditation and short prayers to improve their power of concentration and easily succeed in studies. It all depends on individual temperament, but the important point is to be aware of the goal of life which is to be a well-developed man or woman in whom all faculties are harmoniously developed, and to manifest the divinity within.

## What is the importance of good behaviour?
## Is culture to be shown to everyone or it is enough if we have it in us?

There is a subtle difference between character and conduct. Character is what we really are and conduct is how we appear to others.

If character is perfect, it reflects in good behaviour. Otherwise good behaviour can also be a mask. By good behaviour others are pleased. Its effect on ourselves varies. If it is an expression of good character, then good behaviour strengthens it. If behaviour is only a mask, then it may make us hypocrites.

Similarly, if we are cultured, it will find expression in our dealing with others. But if it is not being expressed, we should know that we have not fully developed it, and hence we must strive hard to develop it more and more within.

^^ These questions were asked by the students and teachers of Modi Institute of Education and Research, Lakshmangarh, Rajasthan, during their interaction with Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh on 22 and 23 January 1999.
youth-forum-1994-10:
Question: How do you define 'Youth'?

Answer: Children cannot think, while old people have lost the power of action. So youth, in contrast with childhood and old age, is defined as that phase of life when we can think and also act up to our thinking.

Question: Is it true of all young people?

Answer: Potentially, yes. They can think and also do as they think.

Question: Do you mean to say that in actual life it is not being carried out?

Answer: I am afraid not. We seldom think. And even when we think, there is no connection between our thoughts and our actions. We are more led by impulses than by any thinking. Swami Vivekananda said humorously: when a man walks, his stomach goes in front; only in old age, when he is bent, does his head go first. But then it is too late.

Question: Can it be remedied?

Answer: Yes, not only it can, but it has to be, and it must be remedied. i) Every young person should feel the importance of thinking. ii) This thinking should be, to use Swami Vivekananda's words, 'as broad as the sky and as deep as the ocean', and whatever is found, by this thinking, to be really beneficial to whole humanity should be acted upon wholeheartedly.

Question: Is it not true that, even if we think and want to act up to that thought, we are unable to carry it into practice?

Answer: Quite often, yes. But that is because we do not use two more faculties which we possess in our youth; the power of feeling and the power of resistance.

Question: But just now you said that we are often led by our impulses and now you are talking of the power of feeling?

Answer: Yes, they are quite different. Not only are feelings different from impulses, but feeling is different from so-called 'emotion' also. Emotion is mostly biological and leads to 'excitement', while genuine feeling proceeds from the most tranquil heart and leads to constructive steady action. Hence if we learn to feel deeply the conclusions of our thinking, and try to act accordingly, we will have much better chance of success.

Question: What is this power of resistance? And, why are you talking of 'chances'? Do you mean to say that even then there is no guarantee?

Answer: We shall take both these questions together. Swami Vivekananda says: 'A carriage with four horses may rush down a hill unrestrained, or the coachman may curb the horses. Which is the greater manifestation of power, to let them go or to hold them? ...All outgoing energy following a selfish motive is frittered away; but if restrained, it will result in development of power. This self-control will tend to produce a mighty will, a character which makes a Christ or a Buddha.'

So if we develop these four faculties in our youth—broad and deep thinking, genuine feeling that proceeds from a tranquil heart, action guided by and moulded by such thinking and feeling, and, last but not least, the power of self-control, so that the energies are not frittered away, we will surely succeed.

Question: What is the success you are talking of?

Answer: In the words of Swami Vivekananda, 'Each soul is potentially divine. The goal is to manifest this divinity within....

Question: How can we practise action and also restraint?

Answer: We have to restrain impulsive action and practise action guided by reason.

Question: Is it not true that the strongest urge in youth is for freedom? Should we curb that?

Answer: We must analyse and understand what is real freedom.

(to be continued)

^^ Questions by Youth, discussed by Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission, Chandigarh. (Prabuddha Bharata, October 1994)
youth-forum-1994-11:
(continued from the October issue)

Question: What is Brahmacharya?

Answer: 'Brahmacharya' has three meanings, or rather three levels of meaning.

Brahman is the Reality Ultimate, which is all-pervading and one without a second. When that is felt, experienced and realized, then one lives in Brahman, moves in Brahman, and has his being in Brahman. This life in Brahman, or living and moving in Brahman, is the primary meaning of 'Brahmacharya'.

In order to live a life anchored in the Ultimate all-pervading Reality, one has to be trained for such a life. This training usually consists of—living with a teacher who is an exemplar of such a life; learning from him the secrets of higher life; study of the scriptures which reveal the nature of the Ultimate Reality; regulating one's life to tone up the body, organs, mind, intellect, and heart; and imbibing moral virtues which enable one to lead a life anchored in Brahman. This training is the second meaning of 'Brahmacharya'.

The third meaning is control of lust.

Question: What is its part in spiritual life?

Answer: Brahman is the Ultimate Reality. On analyzing dream we find that our mind itself takes the form of the objects as well as the apparent subject, i.e. ourselves, who perceive objects in dream. Similarly, Reality is one, but through the mind it appears to be bipolarized into enjoyer-enjoyed. So long as we are engrossed in this enjoyer-enjoyed mode of thinking, feeling and action, we lose sight of the Reality. This bipolarity is acutest in the physical-mental awareness of the opposite sexes, and it covers the vision of Reality.

Question: Is it not natural to have this awareness of opposite sexes?

Answer: It appears natural today, and is common to man and animals. But one who has the capacity to think and discriminate finds that the nature of the Ultimate Reality, of which he or she is only a 'form', is beyond all sex and beyond all dualism, and that sex is a creation of the body-mind complex. As soon as we attain to the non-dual vision of our real nature, we rise beyond all bodily instincts and find true perfection and bliss. A universal love then flows from us, filling everyone around with bliss.

Question: But what can be done today?

Answer: Life should be planned and regulated with a proper awareness of what has been discussed above.

(concluded)
youth-forum-1995-09:
Q. 1: Everyone says, 'You are very emotional and immature.' But what are the exact meanings of the words 'emotional' and 'immature', and how to overcome these bad qualities?

Answer: Let me first mention the meanings of 'emotion' and 'emotional' as given in various dictionaries.

## EMOTION:

1. Strong mental or instinctive feeling such as love or fear. (Pocket Oxford)
2. Strong feeling of any kind; excitement or disturbance of the mind or the feelings. (Oxford Advanced)
3. Mental agitation, excited state of feeling as joy, fear, etc. (Collins)
4. Strong feeling, e.g. fear, wonder, love, sorrow, shame—often accompanied by a physical reaction, e.g. blushing or trembling. (Webster)

## EMOTIONAL:

1. Liable to excessive emotion.
2. Having emotions that are easily excited
3. Given to emotion.
4. Ruled by emotion rather than by reason.

This is what the dictionaries tell. Now let me tell you what I have heard from the wise people: The human mind has three distinct functions— (a) thinking, (b) feeling, and (c) willing. If thinking does not proceed from an absolutely tranquil brain, it is vitiated by our likes and dislikes and a lot of subjective imagination. Similarly, if the feeling does not proceed from an absolutely tranquil heart, it biologically excites the person, and this biological part of feeling is called 'emotion'. In ordinary human beings like us, all the feelings are emotions.

It is only when we attain sufficient tranquility that we are able to remain calm always, and then only emotions are gradually replaced by genuine feelings. Till then we have to apply two forces to avoid emotionalism. On the one hand, we have to practise calmness of mind and self-control, and on the other, we must always temper our emotions by 'reason' based on philosophical understanding of the true nature of things; and also by 'practical reason' based on the experience of the elders. As far as the word 'immature' is concerned, again I am giving the dictionary meanings along with the meanings of 'mature':

## MATURE:

1. Fully developed, ripe, adult.
2. Fully grown or developed mentally or physically; having achieved one's own potential.
3. Ripe, completely developed, grown up.
4. Having reached a state of full natural development; when development is complete; having reached a state of maximum development.

## IMMATURE:

1. Not mature.
2. Not sensible in behaviour or in controlling one's feelings.
3. Less mature than one would expect.
4. Not yet fully developed or grown.

From this it is clear that we cannot 'do' anything to become mature except to try to develop the faculties of thinking, feeling and willing (—will power is developed by selfless work on one side and self-observation and self-control on the other—) and wait for the process to complete itself slowly and gradually.

Q. 2: I always hear that girls are emotional and boys are not. Why is it so?

Answer: About girls being more emotional than boys—well, it is a very general statement and not worth paying much attention to.

Q. 3: Over the last few days I was busy preparing for my half-yearly exams, held in the Bachelor of Education course. Yesterday, when the exam was to be conducted, the students went on a strike—simply on the plea that they did not want to take exams. They had put up a petition earlier that the exams should not be conducted, because once our principal had said that on the basis of the marks obtained in these exams we would be given marks in our practicals in our finals, to be held in April–May. Thus the students did not want to be graded now in these exams. Yesterday, when the bell rang for the exams to start, out of 180 students only 5 went in to take the exams. Somehow I could not gather sufficient strength to be the 6th student. Even though I was very well prepared, I somehow could not leave the majority of 175 students.

I do not know if I am behaving like a coward or if I should have taken the exam, thereby pleasing the teachers and betraying the people with whom I have to stay for another 6 months. It was not even the betrayal, but in fact I was so scared to stand against those 'goondas' of my class.

Answer: Once, when I was in college, the boys declared a strike. I did not resist on the first day. But next day they said that it would continue indefinitely. I did not pay heed to that and went to the college. Just near the college, two or three of them blocked my way and started pleading, arguing, threatening. I did not budge. Finally when they left, I entered the college. One more boy entered unnoticed. The two of us went up to the staff-room and reported ourselves to the teacher concerned, who then came to the classroom and taught us.

The thing snowballed. 'Students' unity' was raised as an argument; we challenged the authority of the 'few' to take decisions and try to force it on all by the slogan of 'unity'. A General Meeting of all the students was called and it was seen that 70% were against the strike, and it had to be withdrawn.

I am not asking you to do what I did, but you should never join a strike unless you are yourself convinced of its propriety and absolute necessity. Where is the question of betraying the students? Did they consult you before taking the decision? Have you not betrayed the wishes of your parents who rightly expected you to appear for the examination legitimately announced by the principal? And have you not betrayed the principal and teachers who were not wrong in holding the examinations?

Considering all the things mentioned by you in your letter, I think you must appear in the remaining part of the examination. Not to do so would be cowardice before what you have termed the 'goonda' element of your class, and a betrayal of the teachers who have helped you all along to learn the subjects. It would also be a disappointment to your parents who have allowed you to join the B. Ed. course as per your wish, though they had other things in their minds. The students who are your companions for the next six months are not going to be of any help to you in your future life, while what the teachers have helped you to learn will be your asset throughout life. And your first duty is to them.

Please take the examination in all seriousness.

Q. 4: Am I a coward, always uncertain of myself and depending on someone to clear my thought, my vision?

Answer: Depending on anyone whom you think to be a wise person for clearing your thoughts, your vision, does not make you cowardly. It rather makes you wiser and wiser.

Q. 5: How to give myself up to HER, the Divine Mother?

Answer: If you force yourself to do what you think to be righteous and side by side be guided by the wise regarding what is really right and proper,—you would reach a stage where you directly feel that you are under 'Divine protection'.

And you have to love HER—the Infinite. Do you have the book, Sarada Devi, the Great Wonder? In case you do not, you should get it from the Ashrama on your next visit.

^^ Questions by youth discussed by Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission, Chandigarh. (Prabuddha Bharata, September 1995, pages 788–789 and 800)
mandukya-introduction:
## MANDUKYA UPANISHAD

An introduction and a Short Study

Swami Pitambarananda

The three states and their witness

Let us consider our daily experiences of the three states of waking, dream and dreamless sleep. The waking world, comprising all its factors – the apparent experiencer, his experiences and the various objects experienced by him – is completely obliterated when we go to sleep; a new world of dream – with its own experiencer, experiences and objects of experience – arises and then vanishes when the sleep becomes profound; now only the experience of happiness remains, and the one experiencing it experiences ‘nothing else’. This is again followed by the waking experience; the bliss and the ‘nothing else’ also vanish when we wake up. What a wonderful phenomenon! And yet there is in us a memory of all the three states. There must have been an unchanging witness separate from all these three apparent experiencers and their experiences. He must have seen all of them and revealed all of them to make all the three types of experiences possible. Had he not been someone different from them, he also would have been lost along with them; had he not permeated all of them he could not have made them possible. This the ultimately Real, sometimes called the ‘fourth’, is distinct from the other three and yet is pervading in all the three! This ‘fourth’ is the Absolute Reality and who else can be our Real SELF? It is not He, but we ourselves in our real nature that is the transcendent-immanent Reality Absolute. Should we not know who we really are? Should we not find it out by direct perception?

Who are we?

Can we perceive ourselves? When we try to perceive ourselves, we at once realize that our eyes cannot help us at all. The problem is not solved by taking the aid of the most powerful telescopes or microscopes or the like. Moreover, unless we free ourselves of that functioning we cannot fix our gaze on ourselves. Naturally, then, we dissociate ourselves from all the external organs of perception, e.g., ears, skin, eyes, tongue and nose. We then become aware of something called the mind or the internal organ. What is this mind and what are its functions. It is a subtle substance, not perceived by the organs, being itself involved in all their functions. Its own function seems to be to project thoughts and ideas and objects in the form of images at one end of a wave and simultaneously to generate the sense of agentship or perceivership or enjoyership, or the sense of ‘subject’ called ego, at the other end. We see these mental waves being tossed up and down in succession and we realize that if we don’t dissociate ourselves from them, they make us oblivious of our real nature by covering us and involving us, as it were in their own flow. Thus we find that, in order to perceive our real nature, we have not only to dissociate ourselves from, and almost stop the functioning of, the external organs, but also to firmly stand aside without involvement in the mental waves and see that they almost die out, leaving a comparatively higher degree of clarity in self-perception. What is behind the mind? When we try to penetrate through the tranquil and serene mind stuff with the transcendental gaze fixed on ourselves, we become aware of ourselves as the self-luminous Being, the Consciousness-in-Itself. And yet, what is the fundamental nature of this being of ours in itself and in its own glory is not fully known to us. We seem to know about so many things outside but we do not know ourselves.

What a pity! Through centuries and eons we have been vegetating without knowing anything about our own selves, our real nature, the luminous Being that we are! Life cannot have a meaning, let alone any value, till this question of all questions is solved – what is the full and real nature of this Being that we are? Mandukya Upanishad

At this point let us remember that from time immemorial there have been people-men and women like ourselves – who were able to know their real being and as a result achieved perfection and fulfillment in life. Out of their overflowing mercy they have communicated their experiences to those other seekers who were ready to receive the instructions. These revelations and transcendental communications are collectively called the Upanishads. They form a vital part of the Vedic literature, which is the most ancient record of man’s spiritual endeavors and successes. All the Upanishads have this one end in view to enable one to reach the summum bonum of life. Life becomes meaningful only when what we really are is known fully, realized truly and manifested spontaneously. Various allied approaches to this problem are dealt with in the Upanishads. The Mandukya Upanishad, which occurs in the Arharva Veda, proposes to lead the aspirant there by the shortest possible route, consisting of three/four spiritual ‘hops’ as it were 1 That is why it is the smallest among all the Upanishads, consisting of just twelve mantras or spiritual revelations. According to another Upanishads called the Muktikopanishad : Mandukyam ekam eva alam mumukshunam vimuktaye, ‘The (knowledge revealed in the) Mandukya Upanishad is alone sufficient for the final liberation of the aspirants.’ Such is its greatness!

The prerequisites

But before we begin the study of any Upanishad, we must fulfill certain preliminary conditions. Unless the following pre-requisites are present in the student of Vedanta his study of the Upanishads would be futile: (1) Capacity or aptitude to distinguish and separate i.e., to discriminate between, the unchanging and the changeful, the real and the apparent. (2) An attitude of dispassion or distaste about all that is found to be temporary, not ultimately real, that which titillates the nerves and is detrimental to transcendental steadfastness in the path of self-realization. (3) Self-control – mental and physical capacity to withdraw, to bear and to forbear; contentment and a continuous struggle to fix the gaze ‘inside’ and readiness to absorb the instructions given by those who have already succeeded in reaching the Goal. (4) An intense longing for perfection and freedom from the bondage of matter, a burning passion to know the truth. The initial instructions

When a person endowed with the above qualities opens the Mandukya Upanishad, he finds the following revelation:

Om, the Word, is all this. A clear explanation of it is as follows: All that is past, present and future is verily Om. That which is beyond the triple conception of time is also truly Om.2

A frog hops to its desired place. In Sanskrit a frog is called manduka. The Upanishad which leads man to his goal through the fewest possible hops is therefore called mandukya, meaning ‘spiritually akin to a frog’s hopping.’

– Mandukya Upanishad, 1.

That is to say – Whatever is perceived is but a projection not real. Whatever we remember, experience or hope for is but a projection not real. Whatever we remember, experience or hope for is but a projection, not real. That which is supposed to be the stable background of all this, is itself the seed of projection.’ When we assimilate this communication from the Rishi, the second instruction follows: Are we in a position to feel the Reality? The Rishi says: All this is verily Brahman. This Atman is Brahman.3

That is to say – It is the Reality that is being projected and perceived as all this. This, the Real in you, is the pervasive, self-same Reality.’

The corrective vision

This is the formula, the medicine, the corrective vision, to be applied to, or to be assimilated by, our consciousness, mind, determinative faculty, mode of thinking, feeling and willing:

Whatever is perceived is but a projection, not real; it is the Reality that is being projected and perceived; it is our own Real nature, which is the ultimate Reality, being projected and Perceived.

This formula has three parts: the first two can be understood with the help of the classical analogies of rope- snake’ and ‘mirage-water’; and the third part, with the help of the dream analysis.

In semi- darkness, rope is mistaken for a snake. When the room is lighted we see that the snake was but a projection, and it was the rope which was being projected as the snake. When we behold water in a desert it appears to be so real from a distance But when we go neat it vanishes and we realize that the water which we perceived was but a projection, a mere appearance, and it was the sand which was being projected or which was appearing as the water.

Similarly, when we analyze our dream experience we understand that the space time, objects, and the person experiencing all these and inter-acting with them were all these and interacting with them were all but projections, not real, and we ourselves, though sleeping, were projecting all these The Reality of the entire subject object universe of our dream world, including the Rishi of the Mandukya Upanishad, through his revelations, to be assimilated by those aspiring to realize the ultimate Truth. The first step of evolution

What happens when this truth is realized? We are freed to a great extent from the shackles of this limited individuality and the temptations and weaknesses associated with it, and we are able to experience our cosmic personality. The totality of this manifold universe is then experienced to be our own self or individuality. The totality of this manifold universe is then experienced to be our own self or individuality. This realization is described in the Mandukya Upanishad thus:

The first quarter is Vaisvanara... who has seven limbs and nineteen mouths and whose experience consists of gross objects.4

– Ibid, 2.

– ibid, 3.

Or – ‘The first step in the ladder of evolution of consciousness is the realization or the experience that my being is infilled in this entire universe – the sky is my head, the sun is my organ of vision, all the air is my own vital breath, the space is the middle part of my body, the water in all the oceans is my kidney, the earth is my feet and the fire everywhere is my own mouth through which I devour food … and I myself comprise all beings.’

Consider the greatness of this Being!

And yet it is described to be only the first step in the evolution of consciousness, because the grossness still persists, the enjoyment causing impurity is present, the enjoyment causing impurity is present, and the awareness is not from matter, though we have grown from tiny individuals facing the vast universe into immensely big individuals covering the entire cosmos.

Again the Rishi asks us to apply and ponder over the same formula, the same corrective vision:

Whatever is perceived is but a projection, not real; it is the Reality that is being projected and perceived; it is our own Real nature, which is the ultimate Reality, being projected and perceived.

The second step of evolution

Now the scene changes. The world, which was perceived to be in our body, is now to be perceived to be in our mind. The absence of grossness makes the experiences more refined, more pure and more luminous because of their proximity to our own self. Divine visions are also seen. This is the subtle cosmic individuality. The Mandukya Upanishad says:

The second quarter is luminous ... who experiences subtle objects.5 Though the physical body and gross objects are transcended, the mind itself functions as the body, desires become the objects, and the cosmic consciousness now pertains to a subtler universe thus: ‘My being is infilled in this luminous universe, and ethereal and more luminous sun is my beautiful organ of vision, luminous air is my breath ... luminous earth is my feet. ...’

And yet the sense of enjoyment, the consciousness of variety, the subtle titillation of nerves does not leave us fully. We strongly feel the need for further evolution, more purposeful transcendence over even the subtle universe. Our longing for freedom, our yearning to realize the truth and be our own ‘real’ selves increases. We remember the correction of the Rishi and find that it is still valid and applicable: Whatever is perceived is but a projection, not real; it is the Reality that is being projected and perceived; it is our own real nature that is the ultimate Reality. We make effort again to assimilate it more deeply, more firmly. The subtle universe begins to melt away.

The Third Step of Evolution

The entire manifestation is now withdrawn, as it were. The Rishi of the Mandukya Upanishad describes:

– Ibid, 4

(Like) in the deep sleep the sleeper does not desire any objects nor does he see any dream.6

Then what is the nature of experience in this state? The Mandukya continues : The third quarter is the knower par excellence in that state... where all experiences become unified or undifferentiated, who is verily a mass of consciousness entire, who is full of bliss and who experiences bliss and who is the path leading to the knowledge of the other two states.7

Have all the projections really vanished? No, they have only become unified in the vision. It is something like what happens when the darkness of the night covers all objects; you cannot differentiate between things; the vision becomes, so they say, unified. Here, of course, in this high state of evolution, the objects or the experiences are unified. Here, the vision becomes, so to say, unified. Here, of course, in this high state of evolution, the objects or the experiences are unified by an extremely powerful though reflected, luminosity. The perception takes the form of unification of all objects with the subject, the ego the differences remain suspended and an overpowering bliss is felt. This is the ‘lower Samadhi’ not the real, ultimate one. This is called the third step because the ‘bondage of enjoyment’ still continues and, if not transcended, sends the aspirant back in the reverse gear. giving rise first to the subtle projection and then to the gross one as well. The aspirant is then compelled, as it were, to perceive the manifold and be a part of it. Hence the Guru, the spiritual guide, the mastermind of the Rishi of the Mandukya Upanishad, calls this also a mere stage’, though a very high one, in the evolution of consciousness. He calls upon the aspirant to proceed further by transcending even this causal or seed state. Here also, he cautions, there is a projection and a perception of unified bliss. But remember, he says,

Whatever is perceived is a projection, not ultimately real; it is the Reality which is projected and then perceived; it is our own real nature that is the ultimately Reality. This Corrective vision is to be carried to its ultimate conclusion, beyond even this unification or an apparent all knowingness of a godlike consciousness. The ‘Fourth’ is not a stage...

Once that is done, the mind becomes free from not only ideation but also the suspension of ideation. Then – and only then – we become clearly aware of our real innate nature, the Atman, the Absolute, the non-dual Brahman, transcendent and (at the same time) immanent Reality, the one-without-a-second What we really are and what we have been always- the fullest knowledge of this dawns The Self, our reality, shines is Its own glory This awareness is neither a stage nor a state but the unchanging Reality, which was manifesting more or less through all the states and stages we have transcended. It removes forever the darkness of ignorance and remains ever shining by Its own effulgence throughout one’s life in all its states and even beyond This is called the ‘fourth’ figuratively only as we have to through and transcend the three stages of evolution to attain this awareness. It is the eternally existing, unchanging witness of all life through all the states.

It is the Eternal FREE SELF

– Ibid, 5

– Ibid, 5

The Rishi of the Mandukya Upanishad declares in what can undoubtedly be called the rarest gem of spiritual communication between man and man:

The wise consider that to be the ‘fourth’ (turiya) which ; is not internally conscious (as in dream), nor externally conscious (as in waking state), nor conscious both ways (as in a state intermediary between waking and dream); which is not a mass of consciousness (dormant state of the conscious process as in profound sleep), nor all-consciousness nor unconsciousness; which is imperceptible (by the organs of action); unrelated (or imperceptible to any empirical dealing), and ungraspable (by the organs of action); which is uninferable, inconceivable, indefinable, which is the cessation of the manifold; which is non-dual, calm and blissful. This is the Self. This is to be realized.8 We shall find that we (our real nature) are distinct from the ‘subject’ of the dream experience. We are equally distinct from the so called experiencer of our normal waking state. The experiencer in the waking state is as much a projection as the one in the dream state. This is equally true of the ‘subject’ of any state intermediary to the waking and dream state of the ‘subject’ of deep sleep whose do rmancy or temporary suspension of projection into the causal seed state is the object from the subject which knows all objects simultaneously in any Yogic supervision, as that subject related to all objects is also a projection. We are, of course, quite distinct from anything which is inert or unconscious. We cannot be seen by the organs as we are the innermost reality. We cannot be approached by any empirical means as we are absolutely transcendent by nature. We cannot be grasped by any outgoing organs of action as we are always inside. We are not matters of inference, as all inferences are drawn in the projected world, but we are drawn in the projected world, but we are immediately aware of ourselves. We cannot be conceived by the mind as we can conceive only those ideas which are projected in the mind by the mind. We are beyond all definitions, for to define is to compare. Realization dawns in the heart that we are the very essence of Self-consciousness; we are the essence of the feeling of ultimate oneness of this projected universe of subjects and objects; Pure Awareness is the very essence of ourselves, our real Being. When our real nature manifests, all multiplicity ceases. We are the non-dual i.e., subject-objectless Reality Absolute Good, Purity, Auspiciousness. And this is our realization of this is the summum bonum of life.

Conclusion

The supreme truth that, when our real nature is manifested, the manifold ceases to be was verified and declared by the Lord Buddha (prapanca-upasamam); that we are the subject-objectless transcendent Reality was verified and emphasized by Sri Adi Sankaracharya (advaitam); and that we are in our real nature the very essence of the feeling of oneness in this universe was verified and expressed by Saint Jnanesvara (ekatma-pratyaya-saram). In our own times Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna and his disciples have demonstrated that these three are but aspects of the realization of our own real nature called Brahman or Atman or the Supreme Lord.

– Ibid, 7.

## GIST OF MANDUKYA

This dual world of our experience appears to be real only because all the momentary forms in it are denoted by ‘names’ which are mere sounds. There is the Existence- Consciousness-Bliss at the back which is One-without-a-second; and this ‘appears’ as the dual world. This is our own ultimately real nature.

When we try to realise this, It manifests in our consciousness in 4 steps. First is the realisation that there is no separate individual even in the gross world. Then this Cosmic gross Virat consciousness loses its grossness and appears subtle – more full of light called ‘Taijas’. Then it loses its manifoldness and even the duality present goes into hiding. Then this ‘seed’ present in ‘Prajna’ or ‘Isvara’ is also detected and we are freed from the trappings of all the three states and find ourselves to be Jivanmuktas.

This Reality free from the trappings of three states can be contemplated in several ways:–

(i) As the cause of the constancy factor during the three changing states OR amidst all the momentary waves of consciousness. (Ekatma-pratyaya-saram)

(ii) As the cause of the Unity felt in the manifold world of subjects and objects. (Ekatma-pratyaya-saram – Jnasesvara.)

(iii) As the source of My existence and My awareness. (Eka-atmapratyaya-saram)

(iv) As the Reality behind and beyond the manifold. (Prapanchopasamam)

(v) By not allowing any agitation of the personality even amidst all sorts of temptations and provocations. (Santam) [Example : Sw.Saradananda]

(vi) As the Absolote beyond all the relativities of the universe. (Sivam)

(vii) As the subject-object-less Reality free from subject-object-ness (Advaitam)

Steps in Vaitathyaprakarana

01. Dream perceptions are unreal because space inside is not sufficient

Shankar’s introduction to the Upanishad (as a whole)

Section 4

1. Atma – A single unit; the Self of all; Unit existence-consciousness.

2. Eva – alone; nothing else or apart from it.

4. Agre – When this was not there; nothing of this was there, nor I, nor thou, nor he, she it.

concept-of-body:
## CONCEPT OF BODY IN VEDANTA

--Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh

[Paper read at an Interreligious & Interdisciplinary seminar on "The Concept of Body" held at Gurudwara Gurugianprakash, Jawaddi Kala, Ludhiana on April 8, 1994.]

1. First of all let us know what is `Vedanta'

`Vid' is `to know'. But today what we think we know is only the external view of things. When we develop the inner vision, we then have the `Vedas'. When this inner vision reaches its culmination, it is then called `Vedanta' -- the culmination of transcendental knowledge. In the known history of mankind, this culmination was first reached in the `Upanishads'. These Upanishads are said to be 108 in number and are included in the four collections called Rigveda, Samaveda, Yajurveda and Atharvaveda. How many centuries old are these Vedas? -- nobody really knows. These upanishads are neither dogmatic nor doctrinal. They are the revelations of the sages, the spiritual truths discovered by the courageous wise men called the Rishis which means `seers'. They do not ask us to "believe", but they goad us to think, understand, feel, and raise ourselves to perceive and realise those truths for ourselves. So the process of valid knowledge of ultimate nature of things called Vedanta has always been -- listening to the direct transcendental experiences of the seers, understanding and assimilating the truths and their implications and practical applications etc. through reason and feeing in a tranquil mind, and then to rediscover them in our own being by raising our consciousness to the required level and thus achieve absolute perfection in life by the culmination of this ultimate wisdom.

2. The Bhagavadgita also is an `Upanishad'

The Bhagavadgita is also called Upanishad though it does not form part of the Vedas and comes much later in point of time. But it is an authoritative source of Vedanta as, according to Swami Vivekananda, it is `its divine commentary',(C.W. of Sw.V. Vol 4,P.335) and, according to tradition, it is `the milk taken out by Bhagavan Sri Krishna from all the cows in the form of Upanishads'.(Gita Dhyana 4)

3. The Vedanta-aphorisms of Vyasa

Another equally authoritative source of Vedanta are the aphorisms of Shri Vyasa. In these the great sage Vyasa has presented the revelations of all the Upanishads in a combined and harmonious presentation, and he has been so much successful that anyone trying to understand Vedanta takes recourse to these aphorisms and they themselves came to be called the ` Vedantic View' (Vedanta Darshana). They are also known as `Vyasa-Sutras', `Vedanta-Sutras', `Brahma- Sutras', or `Uttara-Meemansa' -- but the remarkable thing is that Vyasa himself calls them as `Shariraka-Meemansa' -- or the analytical search for the real nature of the Being who lives in the body. One must here point out the difference between `Sharirika' and `Shariraka'. `Sharirika' means `bodily' or connected with or belonging to body. Vyasa does not think that the Being of man belongs to the body though to the non-discriminating it appears to be so and so he calls it `Shariraka' -- the real Being in the body.

4. The final proof of Vedanta is in our own life and experience

It should again be pointed out here that other than these three sources of Vedanta accepted by all there is a vast mass of literature known as Vedanta Darshana which consists of Commentaries on these or independent writings of philosophers and scholars. These may be personal views and interpretations and we should not confuse or identify Vedanta with any of these particular schools, though we can take help from all of them for gradually comprehending the import of Vedanta. But the final proof or comprehension

comes by our own direct experience, as pointed out by Swami Vivekananda -- " This Rishihood, this power of supersensuous perception of Vedas, is real religion. And as long as this does not develop in the life of an initiate, religion is a mere empty word to him, and it is to be understood that he has not yet taken the first step in religion. "(C.W. of Sw.V. Vol 6, P.181)

Hence,

5. Let us have a bright example of a Rishi of our own times.

Mahapurush Swami Shivananda (A.D. 1855-1934), a direct disciple of Shri Ramakrishna and the second president of the Ramkrishna Order was a model of Vedanta. In his old age, even when the body was suffering from various ailments, he was always at rest with himself and disseminating knowledge and radiating joy all around. Once when the health was very bad and there was no sleep at night, some one, while paying respect to him in the morning, asked " How are you, Maharaj ? " Mahapurushji (spontaneously) -- Very fine, there is full joy.

The enquirer (surprised) -- But Maharaj, I heard that you could not sleep whole night?

Mahapurushji (with an effort, as if coming down from a higher plane) -- Oh ! You were talking about the body ? Yes it's correct that the body is not well. But when you asked how am I, naturally I said I am fine, having great joy.(Swami Shivananda, P.155-156) On another occasion he said -- " I am not the body; I am the eternal Supreme being -- ever pure, perfect and free. The Master has granted me knowledge of this in the fullest measure. That is why it makes no difference whether the body is well, sick or old. The body will certainly follow its own course. "(Saga of a Great Soul, P.235) And on another oaccasion -- " You know this body is old. That is why there is always some complaint or the other. The body is subject to six-fold change (birth, existence, growth, transformation, decay and death). That is the nature of the body. Now it is proceeding towards the last change, death. Of course these changes pertain to body only; the Self which dwells within remains eternally the same. These changes do not affect it at all. The Self which dwells within the body is alright. The body cannot be the Self. The Master out of compassion has given me that knowledge. Now it does not matter whether the body lives or goes. " After keeping his eyes closed for a while, the Swami burst out laughing and said -- " Yes the Master has given me full knowldge within. ... "(For Seekers of God, P.57-58)

And on still another occasion,

An old monk came to salute Mahapurushji and inquired about his health. Mahapurushji smiled at his inquiry, pointed to the attendant nearby, and said : " Put your questiuon about this body to him. I care very little about that. Often enough, I have little consciousness of having a body at all. This is the real truth. But when people ask such questions, I answer them just as it occurs to my mind. What I know is that I have dedicated my body, mind, life, and everything at the feet of the Master -- all these are his. Now, he will do with these just as it pleases him. ... But that does not mean that I neglect this body. I try to keep it going, just as you all and the doctors desire . ... Do you know why I do all this? . ... God-realisation has been attained in and through this body; this body has touched Divinity, lived with it and served it. The Master has made this body a vehicle for the propagation of his message for this age. That is why I bestow all this care. Otherwise, this body is nothing but a bundle of flesh and blood. "(For Seekers of God,P.222-223)

This, then, in a nutshell, is the Vedantic concept of body. One will understand the full significance of these utterances when it will be remembered that this comes not from a person living alone in a cave but from the president of a world-wide organisation, one who was " supremely unconcerned, and intensely concerned, about the world. Inclined to be indrawn and withdrawn, he was yet anxious for all and at the service of all. "(For Seekers of God, preface to the III edition)

It is about such sages that the Bhagvadgita declares -- " But those also, who worship the Imperishable, the Indefinable, the Unmanifested, the Omnipresent, the Unthinkable, the Unchangeable, the Immovable, the Eternal -- having subdued all the senses, even-minded

everywhere, engaged in the welfare of all beings -- verily they reach only Myself. "(Gita 12 - 3,4)

6. Let us also understand the purpose of discussion about the Vedantic concept of body

It is not that Vedanta gives any great importance to the body, but it is we -- ordinary un-evolved human beings who give supreme importance to it and suffer endless agonies for it. Let us compare animals with men and then ordinary men with those who have achieved real greatness. We find that animals have their whole life in the body alone, while we, though tremendously attached to the body, do have a mental, moral, intellectual, artistic, feelingful existence. When we observe really great men, we see that they are hardly aware of their bodies ! That is why we are approaching Vedanta to find out the secrets of real greatness through proper concept of body.

This can be nicely illustrated by an anecdote from the Chhandogya Upanishad. Prajapati, the creator of gods and demons said that if you know yourself, you will be free from sin, old age, death, grief, hunger and thirst, and all your desires and thoughts will come true. Indra, the king of gods, and Virochana, the king of demons, approached Prajapati as students, lived a life of discipline with him for 32 years, and then he told them that the `self' is of the nature of `seer' (and not that of `seen'). Both of them initially thought the body to be the seer self. Virochana went back to the demons and proclaimed that the creator had told him that the body-self alone has to be worshipped and served. Indra, on the other hand, became thoughtful and found out that the body, being subject to birth, changes, defects, decay and death, cannot be the `self' knowing which one becomes free from sin and hunger etc. He then went back to Prajapati and stayed with him for another 32 years. He then thought that the mind could be the self but soon found out that the mind also is subject to pain, defects and limitations. After living another 32 years, he felt that when the mind is withdrawn into `I', that could be the real nature meant by Prajapati. But again he found out that such a state is sleepy and neither permanent nor permanently desirable. After another 5 years with the teacher he finally realised that the Self is entirely incorporeal and transcendent though present in all the three states mentioned above, and it is this `Self' which is free, perfect and immortal.(See Chhandogya Upanishad, 8-7-1 to 8-12-6)

Vedanta will thus teach us how to look upon the body, how best to utilise it and how to come out of its clutches and realise our real blissful divine and perfect nature even while apparently living in the body. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says -- " If a man knows the Self as `I am this', then desiring what and for whose sake will he suffer in the wake of the body? " " He who has realised and intimately known the Self that has entered this perilous and perplexing place (the body) beset with numerous dangers, is the maker of the universe, for he is the maker of all, (all is) his Self, and he again is indeed the Self (of all). Dwelling in this very body, we have somehow realised Brahman; otherwise we should have remained ignorant, and great destruction would have overtaken us. Those who know Brahman, become immortal, while others (the ignorant who regard the body as the Self) only suffer misery. "(Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4-4-12,13,14)

In the light of the foregoing introductory observation, let us now discuss the following points:-

7. `I am not body'

While introducing Vyasa's `Analytical search for the real nature of the embodied Reality', the great commentator Shri Shankaracharya points out -- It is an established fact that the object and the subject which are the contents of `you' and `I' respectively, and are of as contradictory nature as darkness and light cannot logically have any identity ... and yet what do we see? The `natural' human behaviour, evidently based on non-discrimination or wrong identification, is in the form of `I am this' (body) or `these (bodily attributes) are mine'.(Shankara's commentary on Shariraka-Meemansa – Introduction)

Thus we find that to feel body or bodily functions as `I and mine' is illogical though natural to an unillumined person due to his non-discriminating mind. All the perfected sages including the example quoted above have realised the non-relation with the body and declare that the aim of perfection in human life is reached only when all of us realise this truth of our own Being. The Chhandogya describes this thus : " He who is aware of the thought, `let me smell this', he is the Self; the nose is only the instrument of smelling. Similarly, he who is aware of the thoughts `let me speak', `let me hear', `let me think' etc. is the Self; the tongue, the ear, the mind are but the instruments. "(Chhandogya Upanishad 8- 12-4,5)

The next point to be considered is --

8. `Why do we live in this body?'

This question has distinct answers in the Vedanta for the unillumined and for those who know themselves. For us it is `desires' which make us live in the body and then this wrong identification, desires, and works done though desires make us assume body after body in a beginningless endless chain until we know ourselves.

The Mundaka Upanishad says -- " He who longs for objects of desires, making much of them, is born along with those desires in bodies in which he tries to fulfil them. "(Mundaka Upanishad 3-2-2)

The Brihadaranyaka says -- " The self is identified with desires alone. What it desires, it resolves; what it resolves, it works out; what it works out, it attains. "(Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4-4-5)

But for a man of true knowledge?

Swami Turiyananda, another disciple of Shri Ramakrishna and a blazing example of Vedanta, used to wonder in his young age why he was associated with a body when he had no desires at all. One day he came across a stanza which set him at rest -- -- The ever-free Atman takes up a body to verify that it is free and blissful even while seemingly associated with the body, and not for any desires pertaining to the world. This is called `Jivanmukti'.

But so long as this is not achieved, we must also know --

9. How to use this body?

The Katha Upanishad compares body with a chariot and draws a graphic picture of its proper use for reaching the summum bonum of life --

" Know the individual self as the master of the chariot, and the body as the chariot. Know the intellect as the charioteer, and the mind as verily the bridle. " They call the organs the horses; the organs having been imagined as horses, (know) the objects as roads. The discriminating people call that Self the enjoyer when It is associated with body, organs, and mind.

" But the organs of that intellect, which, being ever associated with an uncontrolled mind, becomes devoid of discrimination, are unruly like the vicious horses of the charioteer. " But of that (intellect), which, being ever associated with a restrained mind, is endowed with discrimination, the organs are controllable like the good horses of the charioteer.

" But he, (the master of the chariot), does not attain that goal (through that intellect), who, being associated with a non-discriminating intellect and an uncontrollable mind, is ever impure; and he attains worldly existence.

" That (master of the chariot), however, who is associated with a discriminating intellect, and being endowed with a controlled mind, is ever pure, attains that goal from which he is not born again.

" The man, however, who has as his charioteer a discriminating intellect, and who has under control the reins of the mind, attains the end of the road; and that is the highest place of Vishnu. "(Katha Upanishad 1-3-3 to 1-3-9)

For this reason the sages ask us to pray --

" May my limbs, speech, vital force, eyes, ears as also strength and all the organs, become well developed. ... "(Kena Upanishad - Peace Chant)

And

" May we hear auspicious words with the ears; while engaged in sacrifices, may we see auspicious things with the eyes; while praising the gods with steady limbs, may we enjoy a life that is beneficial to the gods. "(Mundaka Upanishad - Peace Chant)

10. How to distinguish the Self from the body?

The Vedanta compares body with the most external sheath and says man wrongly identifies the soul with the sheath.

One couplet from Saint Kabir is worth mentioning here --

" Do not ask a sage the family of his birth, better ask him for wisdom only. Evaluate the sword; do not weigh the sheath. "

But the Taittiriya Upanishad speaks of 5 such sheaths consisting of the body, the vital airs, the mind, the knowledge or self-consciousness, and bliss. When our consciousness is fully or completely externalised, (then only) we feel the body itself as our `self'. With a slightly inward vision and sense of detachment from the body, we feel we are the dynamic vitality permeating in the body and working through it. When our consciousness is little more evolved and we are little more detached from the body, (then only) we really feel the `mind' and then simultaneously we feel that mind to be ourselves pervading the vital and physical personalities through which we are functioning and working. When the tossing of the waves of the mind subsides and we are calm and peaceful, (then only) we are able to feel `self-consciousness', and then we feel we are that self-consciousness which is functioning through the mental, vital, and physical sheaths. When the ego in that self-consiciousness subsides, (then only) we can feel the natural bliss of being or existence which functions through the self-conscious, the mental, the vital and the physical personalities. But this blissful self-consciousness also has an unperceived `I' which is submerged in that bliss which fills it. So when this hidden or suspended `blissful I' is also transcended, then only we realise what we really are -- Existence-Knowledge-Bliss Absolute, transcendent over all sheaths and yet immanent in all of them. It is then not `I' filled with bliss, but the Existence which is Bliss itself. It is this real Self, universal which appeared to be embodied in all these bodies. It cannot be described in words but it is that which we really are and can be realised without any shadow of doubt.(See Taittiriya Upanishad 2-1-1 to 2-5-1)

In the next chapter of this Upanishad we find that this was discovered by the sages through meditation and that it is open to verification by the same method.(See Taittiriya Upanishad 3-1-1 to 3-6-1)

In recent times this has been verified through the realisations of Shri Ramakrishna - -

" The Master began to describe the death of Akshay (his dearest nephew) as an example. He said -- `Akshay died. I felt nothing at the time. I was standing and was witnessing how man dies. I saw there was, as it were, a sword in a sheath and the sword was brought out of it. The sword was not at all affected. It remained as it was and the sheath lay there. I felt great joy to see it. "(Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master, P.340)

Another sage describes :-

" The sense-objects are higher than the senses, and the mind is higher than the sense-objects; but the intellect is higher than the mind, and the Great Soul is higher than the intellect. "(Katha Upanishad 1-3-10)

" Of the unborn One, whose consciousness is unflickering, there is a city with eleven gates. Meditating (on Him), one does not grieve and, becoming freed, one becomes emancipated. This indeed is that.

" When this dweller in the body becomes detached, when He is freed from this body, what else remains here (in this body)? This indeed is that.

" Well, O Gautama, I shall tell you of this secret eternal Brahman; and also how the Self fares after death.

" Some souls enter the womb for acquiring bodies and others follow the motionless, in accordance with their work and in conformity with their knowledge. "(Katha Upanishad 2-2- 1,4,6,7)

" If one succeeds in realising here before the falling of the body, (one becomes freed); (else) because of that failure one becomes fit for embodiment in the worlds of creatures. " " One should unerringly separate Him from one's body like a stalk from the Munja grass. "(Katha Upanishad 2-3-4,17)

11. The Gross, the Subtle and the Causal bodies :-

By another method of analysis, the Vedanta tells us that we have three bodies, i.e., three levels of identification with non-self. The first, the gross body, consists of " seven limbs and nineteen mouths to enjoy gross things."(Mandukya Up.-3)

The head, the mouth, the eyes, the vital force, the middle part, the bladder and the feet are the seven limbs, while the five organs of perception, five of action, the five vital forces, and the four internal organs are counted as nineteen mouths through which we interact with the gross objects. The second, the subtle body, also has seven limbs and nineteen mouths by which it enjoys the objects projected in the dream state from the impressions gathered in the waking state. It is again due to desires and actions done with desires that we identify with this subtle body in the dream state. The third, called causal body, is found in the deep sleep. The mind which projects the differences does not function there nor the gross sense and motor organs, yet `I' am a subject enjoying undifferentiated bliss as the `object' and this `I' contains the seeds of all desires and actions. The Real Self has to be separated from all these three bodies as the unchanging witness which is present in all these three states without actually getting affected by these in the least.

12. Finally let us now see what the Gita has to say about the body

(a) In the Second chapter --

" Of this indwelling self -- the ever-changeless, the indestructible, the illimitable -- these bodies are said to have an end. " " It is not killed when the body is killed. " " Even as a man casts off worn-out clothes, and puts on others which are new. " " This, the indweller in the bodies of all, is ever indestructible. "(Bhagvadgita 2 - 18,20,22,30)

(b) Then in the thirteenth chapter we get a complete summary of the Vedantic concept of body. Bhagavan Shri Krishna says --

" This body, O son of Kunti, is called, Kshetra, i.e., Field [the body is so called because the fruits of action are reaped in it as in a field], and he who knows it is called Kshetrajna, i.e., knower of the field, by those who know of them.

" Know Me also, O descendant of Bharata, to be Kshetrajna in all Kshetras. The knowledge of Kshetra and kshetrajna is considered by me to be the real knowledge. " What the Kshetra is, what its properties are, what its modifications are, what effects arise from what causes, and also who He is and what His powers are, that hear from Me in brief.

" (This truth) has been sung by Rishis in many ways, in various distinctive chants (in the Vedas), in passages indicative of Brahman, full of reasoning and convincing. " The great Elements, Egoism, Intellect, as also the Unmanifested, the ten senses and the one (mind), and the five objects of the senses; desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, intelligence, fortitude -- the Kshetra has been thus briefly described with its modifications.

" Humility, unpretentiousness, non-injury, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-control; the renunciation of sense-objects, and also absence of egoism; reflection on the evils of birth, death, old age, sickness, and pain; non-attachment, non-identification of self with son, wife, home, and the rest, and constant even-mindedness in the occurrence of the desirable and undesirable; constant application to

spiritual knowledge, understanding of the end of true knowledge; -- this is declared to be `Knowledge', and what is opposed to it is ignorance.

" I shall describe that which has to be known (by this true knowledge), knowing which one attains to immortality, the beginningless Supreme Brahman. It is called neither being nor non-being.

" With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and mouths everywhere, with ears everywhere in the universe -- That exists pervading all.

" Shining by the functions of all the senses, yet without the senses; Absolute, yet sustaining all; devoid of Gunas, yet their experiencer.

" Without and within all beings; the unmoving and also moving; incomprehensible because of its subtlety; It is far and near.

" It cannot be divided into parts, yet It exists as if divided in beings. It is to be known as sustaining beings; and devouring, as well as generating (them).

" The Light even of lights, It is said to be beyond darkness; knowledge, and the One thing to be known, the Goal of knowledge, dwelling in the hearts of all. " Thus Kshetra, Knowledge, and that which has to known, have been breifly stated. Knowing this, My devotee is fitted for My state. ...

" The Being identifying itself with nature, experiences pleasure, pain and delusion born of nature; the reason of his birth in good and evil wombs is his attachment to manifestations of nature.

" And the Supreme Being in this body is also called the looker-on, the Permitter, the Supporter, the Experiencer, the Great Lord, and the Highest Self.

" He who thus knows the Being and the nature together with its modifications, whatever his life, is not born again. ...

" Whatever being is born, the moving or the unmoving, ... know it to be from the union of Kshetra and Kshetrajna.

[The union of Kshetra and Kshetrajna, of the object and the subject, is of the nature of mutual superimposition owing to the absence of discrimination of their real nature. This false knowldge vanishes when one is able to separate kshetra from kshetrajna.] " He, who sees the Supreme Lord, existing equally in all beings, deathless in the dying, he alone sees truly.

" Since seeing the Lord equally existent everywhere, he injures not Self by self, and so goes to the Highest Goal.

" He truly sees, who sees that all actions are done by nature alone and that the Self is actionless.

" When he sees the seperate existence of all beings inherent in the One, and their expansion from That (One) alone, he then becomes Brahman.

" Being without beginning and devoid of Gunas, this Supreme Self, immutable, O son of Kunti, though existing in the body neither acts nor is affected. " As the all pervading Akasha, because of its subtlety, is not tainted, so the Self Existent everywhere in the body, is not tainted.

" As the one Sun illumines all this world, so does He who abides in the Kshetra, O descendent of Bharata, illumine the whole kshetra.

" They, who thus, with the eye of knowledge, perceive the distinction between the Kshetra and Kshetrajna, and also the emancipation of being from nature, they go to the supreme. "(Bhagvadgita Chapter 13)
