individual-and-universal-being:
Individual Being and the Universal Being

While reading Sri Shankaracharya’s commentary on the Mandukya Upanishad, we come across the following observation :

“… Otherwise, the indwelling Self, as circumscribed by one’s own body, will alone be perceived, as It is by Sankhyas and others; and in that case the specific statement made by the Upanishads that It is non-dual will remain unestablished for there will be no difference from the philosophies of the Sankhyas and others. But as a matter of fact, it is desirable to find all the Upanishads propounding the unity of all the selves. …”

On reading this, a Sadhaka who had no pre-knowledge of what this Sankhya is asked for elaboration on this point in simple, spiritual terminology. This resulted in the following attempt :

The question you have asked is very fundamental and it requires big, elaborate answer. We shall discuss it from various angles under three headings.

1. Sankhya attitude. 2. Vedantic Rishis and their realization and

3. Necessary corresponding attitude of the true sadhaka.

## 1. SANKHYA PHILOSOPHY:

There are persons who are individualistic, who have experienced the life in the world to be full of miseries and who believe in rational intelligence and follow the methods of observation and generalization like that of science. The difference is that science does not go beyond data collected by five organs and verification also by five organs; while these Sankhya philosophers follow all the subtler and subtler generalizations by perceiving those subtler truths by yogic methods of concentration. Their ultimate conclusions are

(i) There are two eternal categories – consciousness and matter.

(ii) There are infinite or innumerable consciousnesses called purushas

(iii) All matter gross and subtle is unified in an indiscreet matrix called prakriti.

(iv) This indiscreet prakriti functions in the presence of Purushas and evolves into the world. Its purposes to give experiences (enjoyments) to purushas and then to release them into a state of Moksha.

(v) Moksha means conscious dissociation from prakriti.

(vi) Man is miserable because of his wrong identification with elements or evolutes of prakriti from gross matter up to intelligence (Buddhi).

(vii) So moksha consists in conscious dissociation from prakriti – leaving it to work for others.

(viii) This man is free from possibility of misery (they do not know whether there is anything called ananda or Bliss apart from release from the possibility of duhkha)

(ix) There is no Real God in their philosophy. They say, “if God is perfect why should he create this universe; if God is imperfect he cannot create the universe.”

(x) They accept a temporary ruler god – that person, who, instead of enjoying his separation from prakriti identifies with whole entire prakriti instead of with individualized evolutes of prakriti. So he gets the power to direct the affairs of the world.

(xi) They do not get stuck-up in the five organs, like the scientist but get stuck-up in buddhi which ends in this purusha-prakriti separation.

(xii) They say, “Purusha has no sukha-duhkha” and yet they say that as different people have different sukha-duhkhas, so there are different (infinite) purushas! It means that they are not able to remove ‘my’ factor from consciousness.

## 2. VEDANTIC RISHIS AND THEIR REALISATION :

They have neither individualism nor are afraid of misery as they well know that Bliss is their very nature. They find :

(i) Ultimate Reality is One without a second.

(ii) It is of the nature of unbroken Existence-Consciousness-Bliss.

(iii) It itself appears in infinite forms.

(iv) These forms hide the absolute Existence-Consciousness-Bliss nature of the Reality and then only we call these forms as “matter”.

(v) While appearing in manifold forms it creates or projects or rather appears as an instrument called mind including buddhi – which has the property of illusorily splitting all the forms into subjective and objective categories. And the “souls” appear different only because of consciousness being wrongly identified with individualized subjective parts of matter which identification has no basis in reality. If I am searching for “my reality”, I cannot reach the Ultimate Reality unless everything which is ‘my’ is dropped.

(vi) Bliss is our nature. It is identical with Consciousness which has nothing to do with any form. As soon as it appears to be identified with particularized form, the bliss is covered and the unreal apparent subject-object split produces permanent tension. Because whether we posses an object or dissociate from it, we and the object are separate and this separation between apparent subjects and apparent objects eternally produces a tension. There is no tension only when there is no split. This cannot be achieved by denying objects or embracing them because this does not remove the split.

(vii) Moksha or perfection consists in the realization that :

(a) There is no ‘matter’, but everything is continually changing forms of the Reality One without a second.

(b) The split between subject and object is not real, hence there is no split in Consciousness. Even the split in matter (forms of consciousness) is caused by mind – which itself is a form of appearance of Reality.

(c) Same God – Sat-Chit-Ananda appears as I, you, he, she, it – objects and subjects in this world. All appearances are illusory as God has not changed at all and in reality God is beyond all forms and hence no split is possible in Existence-Consciousness-Bliss.

(d) Such God was appearing as ‘I’ and the ‘world’ – but in moksha It shows itself as without split, without form as in Sri Ramakrishna’s nirvikalpa samadhi. This is infinite Existence, infinite Consciousness, infinite Bliss – One without a second. This itself is the source of the feeling of an unchanging atman in us, this is beyond manifoldness, this is real and absolute tranquility – all other tranquilities are reflections of this on different levels, this is all good and all bliss, this is non-dual.

(viii) There is The God. He (or She) is perfect. He has no motive or purpose in creating the world (due to which we can think that he has some imperfections). It is His (or Her) nature to appear in myriad forms. Really it is the Reality Absolute denoted by “It”, which, without any change, without any split appears as all this and then we say there is “power of appearance” and we identify this power as feminine and hence when “It” appears as having a power then “It” appears as ‘He’ and the power as ‘She’. Saint Jnaneshwar declares; “IT is the essence of all zeros (i.e. when everything is reduced to zero you really get at the Reality-at-the-back which is It); but this ‘power’ (to appear as the manifold) is like a woman who makes this “It” appear as ‘He’ and who herself appears as power due to his mere presence.

(ix) We are all one or rather non-different in this God.

## 3. NECESSARY CORRESPONDING ATTITUDE OF A TRUE SADHAKA :

In the beginning the sadhaka feels as follows –

(i) I am imperfect. I am incomplete like a fraction. I have a subject-object polarity. God is perfect. He is partless whole. He or rather ‘It’ is beyond all polarity, beyond all split. Such a God or Brahman is my Atman. Unless I realize It fully in my being – in my consciousness and in my life, I can never be at peace.

(ii) God, who is Sat-Chit-Ananda is all pervading. The ‘all’ as such is continually changing, evanescent forms – this includes all the parts and phases of my personality; the feeling of something real, something continuous is only due to His all-pervasiveness. How to realize this God who is my own reality and also the One Reality of the entire ever-changing universe?

(iii) All the problems of my life will be automatically solved when I realize God who is my Self and also the Reality of all phenomena and who is ever beyond any manifoldness or differences, beyond any subject-object split.

(iv) I do not want anything of this world; I do not want to be attached to any part or phase of my so called personality. I want my Reality; I want only the Reality One without a second.

(v) For such a sadhaka, any hindrances due to Maya in the form of hidden wrong attitudes etc are removed by the force of love for the Absolute Reality whose real nature is revealed in the Rishi-vakyas (Scriptures) and which Itself is God, Ishta, and Guru, because they are much more powerful by the power of Truth than the combined power of all forms of Maya internal or through objects of the world.

(vi) The true sadhaka is taught to think and feel “This body etc. are not mine, the experiencer in me is not ‘I’, but everything belongs to the Reality, the Reality is the experiencer, experienced and experience.

(vii) In the light of the Vedantic truth described above as revealed by the Rishis, it is abundantly clear that It is the Absolute Reality Itself which is appearing as sadhaka in one of the illusory forms. As the form is illusory and as the Reality is covered, the sadhaka feels all the parts and phases of his personality to be real and belonging to himself, and also the objects of the world of innumerable types

– animate, inanimate, men, women etc. – all to be separately real, and the subject-object split created by the mind also to be real. But by the mysterious leela of the Reality the sadhaka comes across a person or persons in actual life or he comes across such a person or persons and their teachings through (living) books and at once recognizes them as representing the Truth, their life as the True perfect life and also feels drawn to them. He feels either as ‘He or It is my only support, I am supported by It alone and so is the whole world’; or as ‘I belong to Him and so does the world and He belongs to me’ or as ‘there is neither world nor “I”, it is all He and He alone’. This starts a process of transcendental illumination of all parts and phases of personality, transcendental illumination of the entire phenomena called the world, and transcendental illumination of the illusory subject-object split. But the sadhaka is a sadhaka; the Reality is not yet manifested in him. The covering or the hiding power called Maya functions in him in different ways. (One of the ways of this functioning of Maya is called the Sankhya tendency of perpetuating individualism and dependence on buddhi. There are various other ways in which Maya shows itself in Sadhaka’s mind and they are called by various names.)

(viii) But in the true sadhaka’s life the ultimate authority is the Rishi-vakyas (as explained by the great Acharyas), the incarnations and the Guru. Through love for these authorities and detachment from everything else including all objects and persons and all parts and phases of his own personality with the knowledge that they are all illusory appearances of the Reality – the sadhaka rises higher and higher, crossing all hindrances in his mind and outside. Depending on the power of these authorities which is constantly pulling the sadhaka higher and higher, and on their words of advice, the sadhaka goes on revising his own thinking, feeling and will and absorbing the illumination playing in the form of these authorities till he himself finally comes to the full realization of Brahman – one without a second.

This, in a nutshell, is the elaboration you had asked for.

practical-vedanta-gita-13:
Practical Vedanta as depicted in the 13th Chapter of Bhagavadgita

--Sw.Pitambarananda, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh.

What is "Vedanta"

Let us first try a little to understand what is meant by "Vedanta". `Vid' is to know. But the knowledge which we generally have of the world and of ourselves is very little and superficial. Really we do not know the real nature or the inner content of anything. We only know the stimulus it gives to or the sensation it induces in the organs of hearing, touch, seeing, taste and smell. So, we know nothing really, though we may theorise endlessly.

However if we transcend these stimuli by keeping the mind unaffected and fully concentrated, we start knowing things from inside. The direct knowledge thus gained is called the `Vedas'. And when this transcendental knowledge reaches its culmination, we reach `Vedanta', i.e., the ultimate knowledge.

What shall we know of the world then ?

That the common content or the real nature of all the things in this world is Homogeneous Existence-Consciousness-Bliss Absolute, One - without-a-second (called Brahman), and it assumes endless names and forms which have no realism of their own but appear real on account of this Existence-Consciousness-Bliss Absolute, One - without-a-second or Brahman.

And what about ourselves ?

Evidently, in our our real nature we can not be anything but the same Brahman – Indivisible, Absolute, One-Without-a-second.

What is Practical Vedanta ?

What is, then, `Practical' Vedanta ?

(i) It should mean that we should be able to translate this Vedantic Knowledge in our behaviour and actions;

(ii) it should mean that when Vedantic knowledge is assimilated - our thinking, our feelings, our actions should be metamorphosed; our consciousness totally transformed and our entire personality transfigured, as it were.

(iii) But, it could also mean that we will have to undertake certain `practices' to really assimilate or directly experience or realise Vedantic Truths. And these practices again should not be divorced from Vedantic Knowledge, rather they should be the natural corollary of the Truth discovered by the seers of Vedanta.

Bhagavadgita : 13th Chapter

This is how Bhagavan Sri Krishna has -- rationally and authoritatively -- dealt with the subject in the 13th chapter of the Gita.

He tells us that there are two phases in the realisation of the highest truth of Vedanta.

The first phase is to know what we are not ! We have an assumed identity with our ever-changing body-mind complex. Hence it is absolutely necessary, first, to know that all this is `not I'. It means that, first, we have to separate our consciousness -- which is what we really are -- from its trappings.

The second phase would be to know the real, exact nature of this consciousness. We shall see that it is One Without-a-second, or that the Supreme Reality called God itself is THE Consciousness in all the `forms' called `I' and `you' and `he,she,it' etc.

This whole process can be called `Vedanta', - Sri Krishna calls it `Knowledge'.

What we are not ?

Let us first see little more critically what we are not - rather what is `not I'.

Elements of matter (Constituting the body), egotism, intellect, the mind in the sleeping state (they are all functions of the apparatus called the mind-stuff) -- these are not `I';

The five organs of perception, five organs of action and mind the co-ordinator of all these, - they, again, are mere `instruments' and not `I'.

Similarly the five types of sensations carried in by the organs, desire, hatred, pleasure, pain, the body-mind complex that reflects the Consciousness and appears to be a unit, the reflection of Consciousness in the intellect, our tenacity - these are all non-self. (Gita 13, 5-6)

Krishna tells us that that it is so has been repeatedly seen by the "seers" and expressed through Vedanta which is fully supported by rational thinking.

God, the Absolute is the only Reality in all beings

The second phase, as said above is to know that God or the Supreme Consciousness itself is the reality everywhere.

But can we realise or experience this ? Or should we be satisfied with mere theories, howsoever noble they may be ?

The `PRACTICAL' Vedanta ?

Well, our present apparatus is evidently inadequate to experience these higher truths, as our mind, at present, knows only the five-fold stimulus received through the senses of hearing, touch, vision, taste and smell, and co-ordinates them and theorises on that basis. If we really want to experience anything higher,- we require a corresponding apparatus.

This necessary orientation is naturally achieved when we, on the basis of the knowledge of what is `not I', filter out ourselves from this body-mind complex. This involves a complete overhauling of our personality and total transformation of character.

Then only we shall be in a position to know the real nature of the Supreme Reality.

Thus it is here that Sri Krishna introduces the interlinking phase which can very properly be called `Practical Vedanta'.

The essential points of this character transformation which are the natural corollary of the separation of `I' from `non I' on the one hand and are to be fully cultivated to enable us to really comprehend, assimilate, experience and realise the Supreme Reality on the other hand have been authoritatively narrated in stanzas 7 to 11 of the 13th chapter of the Bhagavadgita.

Sri Krishna asks us thus to cultivate - humility, unpretentiousness, non-injury, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-control, renunciation of sense-objects, absence of egoism, reflection on the evils of birth-death-old age-sickness and pain, non-attachment and non-identification of self with wife, home etc., constant even-mindedness in desirable and undesirable occurrences, unswerving devotion to God by the yoga of non-seperation, resort to

sequestered places, distaste for the society of men, constant application of one's mind to spiritual knowledge, and understanding of the end of true knowledge. (13, 7-11)

Let us deliberate a little on each of these.

1. Humility (Amanitva) - To praise oneself and expect to be honoured by others is called Manitva. The absence of such a tendency is to be cultivated.

This Manitva is a direct outcome of our identification with a particular body-mind complex. As soon as or as much as we are able to separate ourselves from this assumed personality, there will be absence of such a harmful tendency. Let us see an example. Contemporary with Sri Ramakrishna, there lived a great saint called Pavahari Baba at Gazipur in Uttar Pradesh. A devotee having visited this sage who was widely honoured and reverenced was narrating his experiences to Sri Ramakrishna. He said that Sri Pavahari Baba keeps a photo of Sri Ramakrishna in his room. To this, Sri Ramakrishna spontaneously replied that it is only about the shell (the body), and didn't feel much elated about it.

2. Unpretentiousness (Adambhitvam) – To `show off' one's religiosity is dambha. We have to cultivate the absence of this attitude which again is due to this wrong identification with the outside personality. That is why a great teacher used to constantly remind his disciples that the purpose is not to `appear' as great and good but to strive hardest to become great and good more and more. If we are keen on showing we cannot be really sincere in actually improving !

3. Non-injury (Ahimsa) – To be a source of trouble to others or to harbour ill-will against anyone is Himsa. Such a tendency has to be weeded out.

4. Forbearance (Kshanti) – Forbearance is absolutely necessary for being in a position to realise the Ultimate Truth.

5. Uprightness (Arjavam) – Straightforwardness, simplicity, absence of crookedness, not using unfair means to gain our ends – this uprightness has to be a part and parcel of our personality.

6. Service to the teacher (Acharyopasanam) – To serve the teacher - to be of whatever use to him - who leads us onwards in spiritual progress should be our natural tendency.

7. Purity (Shaucham) – Purity of thought, word and deed - cleanliness has to be cultivated.

8. Steadiness (Sthairyam) – Without steadiness no real knowledge can be gained. The Supreme Reality is absolutely unchanging; to be able to experience It we have to be fully steady in every limb and organ -- external and internal. We shall find that our unsteadiness stems from our identification with the body-mind complex which alone gets affected by the interaction with the world. The more we filter ourselves, the more shall we be steady and fit to experience the real nature of Truth.

9. Self-control (Atmavinigrahah) – And for this, we require self-control.

10. Renunciation of sense-objects (Indriyartheshu Vairagyam) – When the objects attract us, we, through our identification with our body-mind complex, go into a subject-object mode of relationship with the objects. This is totally against the nature of the Supreme Reality which is the common reality of both the objects and the apparent subject, and which in its own nature is devoid of any such polarity. Hence to experience God -- the Absolute Reality -- we have, necessarily, to come out of this polar mode. Hence a distaste for the very idea of deriving pleasure from the organ-object contact has to be cultivated. This is natural when we filter ourselves from the body-mind complex, because, the filtered `consciousness' is non-polar and of the nature of Bliss-in-itself and hence anyone who has filtered his consciousness is so happy with himself that he finds that the so-called enjoyment is nothing but debasing oneself.

11. Absence of egoism (Anahankar) – If `enjoyment' through contact with objects is one side of the polarity, `egotism' is the corresponding other side. Hence an attitude of `not I' is to be cultivated. And, when we separate ourselves from the body-mind personality, we don't find any

distinctive mark to separate ourselves from others, and hence feeling of egotism seems to be impossible. Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna has explained this by saying - " If one goes on peeling the onion, nothing remains as the kernel apart from the peels."

12. Reflection on the evils of birth-death-old age-sickness and pain (Janma-mrityu-jara-vyadhi-duhkha-doshanudarshanam) – But old habits do not die so easily. And hence the pull-back exerted by them retards our progress. A philosophy of compromise or false satisfaction ensues. Hence it is necessary to see through this deceptive game of appearances.

Discussing Sri Ramakrishna's constitutional temperament even from his boyhood, Swami Saradananda has this to say -

" It was also found that before the Master undertook anything, he would always discriminate and arrive at a definite conclusion by deep thinking as to why a thing should be done, where the relation with a particular person would ultimately lead him, and where it had led others under similar conditions. So false appearances could never deceive him by their glittering show and deflect him from the right course. The reader may argue, `But this kind of discriminating intellect will bring first of all the defects of all things before the eyes and paralyse all urge for activity and make all undertakings impossible.' It is exactly so. If the intellect were not purified before and freed from desires, and if it were not turned to the high ideal of of the realisation of God, the attitude of extreme caution and calculation would undoubtedly render man aimless and inactive and sometimes self-willed and reckless even. If, on the contrary, the intellect has attained to the required degree of refinement in outlook and aspiration, it can do this probing and assessment of defects without any detriment to its capacity for energetic action and quick progress along the path to realisation of God. Therefore Sri Krishna in the Gita (13,9) has asked only men of such faith and devotion to find out the painful evils inherent in birth, death, decrepitude and disease, and thereby attain dispassion." [Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master, P. 477]

13. Non-attachment and non-identification of self with wife, home etc. (Asaktih Anabhiswangah putra-dar-grihadishu) – It is due to our identification with the body that certain persons or things become `mine' for us, and when this `mine' grows in its intensity, it is unconsciously replaced by `I'. Thus `my wife' and `my house' grows into the feeling that `I, as if, live in my wife' and `I am part of the house' or that `I can not live without the house' -- which means, in plain language, that `the house has become a part-and-parcel of my life'. Once the identification with the body-mind is gone all these chain-reactions vanish, -- they can never raise their heads again in our life; and then only we shall be free to realise the Supreme Reality.

14. Constant even-mindedness in desirable and undesirable occurrences (Nityancha Samachittatvam Ishtanishtopapattishu) – Another obstruction which does not allow the mind to have a proper glimpse of the Reality is its tendency to be tossed up and down by the inevitable throng of pairs of opposites in this world. The personality which has evenness as an asset -- with the knowledge that this passing show of the world has its own waves and curves -- is able to look beyond and see the Same Reality appearing through both the `desirable' and the `undesirable'.

15. Unswerving devotion to God by the yoga of non-seperation (Mayi chananyayogen bhaktiravyabhicharini) – Love is a potent force. But any particularisation in it vitiates it and makes our whole life full of poison. The whole force of love is to be directed to the source of Love itself - which is another name of the Supreme Reality. Sat-Chit-Anand, Existence- Consciousness-Bliss Absolute, One-without-a-second is the source of the force of love; That Itself is the Reality of our being; and That is the only satisfactory object of love. It will take us beyond all subject-object relationships.

16. Resort to sequestered places (Viviktadesha-sevitvam) – To cultivate all these habits of thinking, feeling and action, we have to be away from the influences contrary to them. We have to be with ourselves.

17. Distaste for the society of men (Aratih janasansadi) – The worldly company has a peculiar effect like drug-intoxication which makes us forget ourselves totally and our Goal is pushed to the background.

18. Constant application of one's mind to spiritual knowledge (Adhyatma-jnana-nityatvam) – Constancy of spiritual pursuit makes the separation between our being and the body-mind complex complete and makes us really fit for the realisation of the Ultimate Reality.

19. Understanding of the end of true knowledge (Tattvajnanartha-darshanam) – Last but not the least, is the remembrance that the very aim of the knowledge of the real nature of things is to gain freedom for our Being - freedom from the bondages of imperfection and the resultant polarity. This remembrance will not allow the practices to lose their direction or become mechanical. It will keep the orientation of all the faculties attuned to life's Ideal.

These, then, are the salient features of `Practical Vedanta'.

Nature of the Supreme Reality

And then what is the nature of the Supreme Reality which is to be realised ? It is the beginningless Supreme Brahman, different from the appearing and the disappearing things. (Gita.13,12)

With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads and faces everywhere, It rests pervading everything in this world. (13)

It is manifest (as consciousness) in the functions of the various sense-organs, yet bereft of all sense-organs; unattached, yet sustaining everything; without attributes, yet the protector of the qualities. (14)

It is without and within all beings; It is moving and unmoving; being subtle, It is incomprehensible; It is far, yet near. (15)

It is undivided in beings, yet remains as if divided. The Supreme Reality is the sustainer of beings as also the destroyer and creator. (16)

It is the light of lights and is said to be beyond all darkness. It itself is knowledge, the knowable and accessible through knowledge, and is implanted in the heart of all beings. (17)

The Man of realisation

And what happens finally ?

The man who realises the Supreme Being, always clearly sees the Supreme Lord abiding equally in all beings, the imperishable amidst the perishable. Seeing the Lord thus, he does not injure the Self by the self. Therefore he attains the Supreme Goal of life. (13, 27-28)

yaksha-anuroopo-balih:
“An offering should be in accordance with the nature of the demigod.”

[[ORIG]]

An individual soul is merely a reflection of the Deity. It arises from (Its) contact with the subtle elements in the form of intellect etc. It is like a reflection of a person, seeming to have entered into a mirror, and like (the reflection of) the sun etc. in water etc. The contact of the Deity possessed of inscrutable and infinite power, with the intellect etc. is (in the form of) a reflection of consciousness. This becomes the cause of multifarious and conflicting ideas such as, ‘I am happy’, ‘I am sorrowful’, ‘I am ignorant’, etc. owing to the non-realisation of the true nature of the Deity. Since the Deity has entered merely as a reflection in the form of an individual soul, therefore It does not Itself become connected with physical happiness, sorrow, etc. As a person, the sun, and others entering into a mirror, water etc. merely through their reflections, are not touched by the defects of the mirror, water, etc. so also the Deity is not. It is also stated in the Kathopanisad: “Just as the sun which is the eye of the whole world, is not tainted by the ocular and external defects, similarly the Self that is but one in all beings, is not tainted by the sorrows of the world, It being transcendental”(Ka. II.2.11); “All-pervasive”, “Eternal”, “like space” (Cf. Ka.); and in Brihadaranyaka Upanisad it is said: “He meditates as it were, He runs as it were” (Br.IV.3.7).

[[ORIG]]

Objection: If the individual soul be a mere reflection, then, it becomes reduced to unreality, and so also are its attainment of other world, this world, etc.

[[ORIG]]

Reply: There is no such defect, since it is admitted to be true in its real nature as Existence. And all modifications such as names, forms, etc, are true only in their nature as Existence. But by themselves they are unreal because it has been said: “All transformation has speech as its basis” (VI.4.1). So also is an individual soul. There is the well-known proverb that “An offering should be in accordance with the nature of the demigod.” Therefore all phenomenal dealings and all modifications are true in their nature as Existence, but unreal as different from Existence. Hence, in this matter no such objection can be raised by the logicians that, being different from Existence, (the souls) are false, though this criticism can be asserted against the dualistic standpoints which are contradictory to one another, that they are mere fancies of their own minds, and are rooted in unreality. … commentary on Chhandogyopanisad (Translation by Swami Gambhirananda)

[[ORIG]]

“So also is an individual soul” – As it is said that the manifested world is real as Brahman and yet is unreal in itself, even so it has to be accepted that that which is the direct meaning of the word ‘Jeeva’ is real as Brahman and yet is unreal in itself. Now let the ‘experiencer’ be real in himself also and let us take only the ‘experienced world’ to be unreal – to remove such a doubt it is said “An offering should be in accordance with the nature of the demigod.” According to this worldly proverb the experiencer is also proved to be unreal when the world of experience is unreal. Therefore the understanding is that though that which is the direct meaning of the word ‘Jeeva’ is unreal, yet the indicated meaning of that word is real as Existence itself. … (Translation by Swami Pitambarananda)

> रुचीनां वैचित्र्यादृजुकुटिल नाना पथजुषाम्
> नृणामेको गम्यस्त्वमसि पयसामर्णव इव ॥” शिवमहिम्नस्तोत्र ॥

> “जतो मत ततो पथ ।” श्रीरामकृष्ण ॥

“The three Vedas, Sankhya, yoga, Pashupata doctrine, or the Vaishnava one – out of these different scriptures ‘this is supreme’, ‘this is suitable’ – in this way according to the variety of tastes – those who travel by different paths, You are the One final goal, as the rivers taking straight or curved paths the Goal is ocean.” (Shivamahimnastotra)

“As many faiths, so many paths.” – SriRamakrishna.

Bhagavan Sriramakrishna, the latest incarnation has asked us to give up the unripe ego – ‘I am so-and-so’s father, son etc etc’ and to substitute it with the ripe ego – ‘I am God’s son or servamt or part etc etc’, but God’s ‘what’? – that he has not told, as he knows that ‘as any minds, so many views’.

“The three Vedas” – This is a reference to Karma, “Sankhya” – Jnana, “yoga” – yoga, “Pashupata doctrine” – Jnanamishra Bhakti, or the “Vaishnava one” – Bhakti. Swamiji’s lectures on Universal Religion give these tendencies. And new Webster Dictionary says – “Mind is the seat of consciousness, thinking, feeling and will”. And ‘will’ we know has positive and negative aspects – “I shall do” and “I shall not do” which is yoga. “Consciousness” is a reflection of Parabrahman. “Kshetrajnam capi Maam viddhi” etc.

Now, in feeling we have naturally so many relations – “Shanta, daasya, sakhya, vaatsalya, madhura, motherhood of God, fatherhood etc. – “Ruchivaichitrya” infinite.

Similarly in Karma. How many types of karma we do? “Ruchivaichitrya”.

In knowledge also every “Upanishad” is different, though they all bring us to the same point in the end. “Ruchivaichitrya”. Yajnyavalkya teaches Maitreyee in a different way, Kahol in a different way, Gargi different and Janaka very differently.

Even Patanjali speaks of so many methods of Concentrating the mind – “Ruchivaichitrya” indeed!

So various paths are necessary and valid

## 11. Under the Banyan tree

> वटविटपसमीपे भूमिभागे निषण्णं सकलमुनिजनानां ज्ञानदातारमारात्।

I bow down to God in his benign aspect, who is seated on the ground near the Banyan tree, who gives knowledge to all thoughtful people sitting near him, who is the teacher of the three worlds, who is ever alert in removing the misery of birth and death.

## 12. The Wonder

> चित्रं वटतरोर्मूले वृद्धाः शिष्या गुरुर्युवा।
> गुरोस्तु मौनं व्याख्यानं शिष्यास्तु छिन्नसंशयाः॥ १२॥

The Wonder – near the root of the Banyan tree are the aged disciples and the young teacher; but the teacher’s exposition is through silence and the yet the disciples’ doubts have been removed!

## 13. Salutation

> ॐ नमः प्रणवार्थाय शुद्धज्ञानैकमूर्तये।
> निर्मलाय प्रशान्ताय दक्षिणामूर्तये नमः॥ १३॥

I bow down to God in his benign aspect, who is the purport of the syllable ‘Aum’, who is one embodiment of pure knowledge, who is beyond impurity and whose peace cannot be disturbed.

## 14. The Teacher of all

> निधये सर्वविद्यानां भिषजे भवरोगिणाम्।
> गुरवे सर्वलोकानां दक्षिणामूर्तये नमः॥ १४॥

I bow down to God in his benign aspect, the storehouse of all knowledges, the doctor for all those who are afflicted with the decease of worldly existence, the teacher of all the worlds.

## 15. Praise be unto Him

> मौनव्याख्याप्रकटितपरब्रह्मतत्त्वं युवानं
> वर्षिष्ठान्तेवसदृषिगणैरावृतं ब्रह्मनिष्ठैः।
> आचार्येन्द्रं करकलितचिन्मुद्रमानन्दरूपं
> स्वात्मारामं मुदितवदनं दक्षिणामूर्तिमीडे॥ १५॥

I praise God in his benign aspect, the Youth disclosing the nature of the Absolute Reality, surrounded by disciples – old sages dedicated to the Reality, the King of teachers, whose hands are showing the knowledge-posture, the embodiment of Bliss, resting in the Self, and possessing blissful countenance.

place-of-scriptures:
The Place of Scriptures in Spirital Life

## SWAMI PITAMBARANANDA

Necessity of Scriptures

(a) In the 7th chapter of the Gita the Lord says :

Among thousands of men, one perhaps struggles for perfection. Amongst these blessed ones who struggle, perhaps only one knows Me in reality.1

We cannot say that God is partial or that spiritual Knowledge is a matter of chance. Then why is perfection so rare? The answer is that ‘wish’ is not sufficient, even ‘struggle’ is not sufficient (even though ‘wish’ and ‘struggle’ are absolutely necessary) for success in spiritual life. The truth is, there is a science of success, and without knowing this science, success is not possible. This science is enshrined in scripures. The case of divine incarnations like Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna is different. They attained succees without taking the help of scriptures. But this exception itself proves the rule, because they were born perfect and they came to revalidate the scriptures and reestablish the truth of religion. But we, ordinary folks, are in ignorance and are subject to the delusive power of Maya. So for us, the science given in the scriptures is absolutely necessary.

(b) Then, again, at the end of the 16th chapter of the Gita, Sri Krishna says more directly:

He who, setting aside the ordinance of the scriptures, acts under impulses of desire, attains neither perfection nor happiness nor the supreme goal. So let the scriptures be your authority in ascertaining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done. Having known what has been prescribed by the scriptures, you should act in this matter.2 Even then Arjuna is not satisfied and, as if representiong many of us, he asks ( in the opening of the 17th chapter):

Those, who setting aside the ordinance of the scriptures, perform sacrifices with faith – what is their status, O Krishna? Is it Sattva, or Rajas, or Tamas ?3

Arjuna is, as it were, challenging Krishna to give an objective answer and perhaps also expecting it to be Faith = Sattva. But unfortunately, in this realm of Maya, nothing is simple and straight, for even the apparent Sattvaguna has in it elements of Rajas and Tamas. So the Lord replies:

Threefold is the faith arising from the different constitutions of embodied beings – Sattvika, Rajasika and Tamasika. Hear about it. The faith of each person is according to his natural disposition...4

[[ORIG]]

(c) Therefore, scriptures are necessary to reveal to us (i) who we are, (ii) where we have to go, (iii) how many ways to the Goal there are and which, among them, is the particular way suitable to us, (iv) what is ‘lower’ and what is ‘higher’ and what ‘the highest’ in spiritual life is, and (v) the graded course of spiritual discipline to be followed stepwise. In this connection we must never forget that life is a continuous struggle. Life which is static can never be spiritual. Only when one reaches the supreme goal of life does he become free from struggle. As Swami Vivekananda has said, ‘Man is man so long as he struggles to rise above nature, and this nature is both external and internal’. And the scriptures are the essential guides for success in this struggle. What the scriptures are

Basically, scriptures are the records of higher experiences, or rather they are the attempts of illumined souls to communicate their experiences to us. Hence Swami Vivekananda says in his lectures on ‘Practical Vedanta’ that Vedanta has been practiced first and theorized afterwards. In his thought-provoking article ‘Hinduism and Sri Ramakrishna’ he says:

‘Truth’ is of two kinds: (1) that which is perceivable by the five senses of human beings and is deducible therefrom by inference, and (2) That which is perceivable by the subtle powers arising from yoga.

The knowledge acquired by the first means is called [physical] science and that acquired by the second method is the Veda [scriptures].... The person in whom that power of intuition

[higher, direct experience] is manifested is called a Rishi, and the infinite knowledge that he comprehends through that power is called the ‘Veda’

The attainment of this Rishi-hood or seer-ship, consisting in the immediate knowledge of the Veda, is the true realization of religion. Until the aspirant’s life opens out to it, religion for him is a ‘mere meaningless word, and he cannot be said to have set his foot on the threshold of religion.5

Hence scriptures are not philosophical treatises, nor are philosophical treatises scriptures. Scriptural study thus is not an inellectual pursuit, though intellect plays an important part in assimilating the scriptural knowledge. A great teacher used to say, ‘the spiritual seeker should makes it a rule of his life to study the Rishivakyas (the experiences of the perfected seers) He should study these scriptures "critically” and “devotionally”. He should analytically study the ideals presented in the scripture and compare them with his own life and experiences. Then he should try to bridge the gap between the two

Types of scriptures

We have already seen that scriptures are the attempts of Rishis to communicate their higher experiences to spiritual seekers. In the subject-matter and form of presentation; however, there is a wide divergence amongst the many scriptures available in different religious traditions. It is necessary to classify the scriptures, so that we can utilize them properly and understand their message in the proper context.

Quoted in Swami Saradananda, Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master (Madras: Sri Ramakrishna Math, 1983) pp.367-68

First, there are the Vedas (‘Sruti’). Swami Vivekananda writes:

Although a little of the infinite knowledge is to be found in the Itihasas, puranas etc of our country and in the religious books of other countries, yet as the first complete and unaltered collection of the entire body of the eternal knowledge, this mass of word, compiled into four books called the Veda and well- known to the Aryans, is worthy of occupying the highest place in all respects, of being adored by the whole world and of being the ultimate proof of the truth of all scriptures, indigenous or foreign….

This mass of words is divided into two parts, namely, that relating to [the highest] knowledge and that relating to ‘work’ [i.e. knowledge which is lower than ‘the highest’ though higher than physical sciences]

The ‘knowledge’ [portion pf the Vedas, otherwise known as Vedanta, is eternally guiding men across the ocean of Maya, to the Other shore of liberation with the help of selfless action, concentration of mind, devotion and self-knowledge.6

These are called Srutis or direct revelations. The height of consciousness from which the Rishis speak necessitates tremendous transcendental struggle on our part to gain access there. Hence an abundant literature called the ‘commentaries’ has grown to help us, and we can also assimilate this knowledge with the help of competent teachers. The very attempt to assimilate and realize this highest knowledge raises the level of our consciousness.

Then come the ‘Smritis’ In this class of scriptures deep thinkers (Munis), basing upon the truth realized by them or by other seers, try to guide us in the conduct of our daily life. The Smritis are relatively easier to understand but, in following them, if we are unable to separate the ‘kernel’ from the shell’ our practices may degenerate into a blind, regimented observance of external, outdated forms. Swamiji writes : It is on the basis of ‘work’ portion of the Veda that books on the social system like those of Manu and others have taught, in addition to other matters, those actions that are conducive to social welfare, varying with time, place and agency... As the rituals of the Veda and their results described in the ‘work’ portion exist for all time in the domain of Maya they are subject to transformation according to the law of change with reference to time, place, person, circumstances etc. Yes, they have been and will be changed. As social manners and customs depend on this ‘work’ portion, they also do and will undergo change. Similarly, popular customs and manners too have been and will be accepted from time to time, only in so far as they are not contrary to the scriptures and the conduct of the downfall of the Aryans is their subjection to such popular customs and manners as are contrary to the Veda, to the conduct of the wise and to the scripture conformable to the Veda.7

This itself shows the paramount importance of the study of scriptures by the spiritual seeker and of the assimilation of their spirit in order to be freed from blind observances.

But the most popular of the scriptures are the Puranas and the Itihasas. … Books like the puranas have taken up the truths hidden in the Vedanta and have explained them in detail in their descriptions of the achievements and excellences of divine incarnations and other manifestations of one or other of the numerous aspects of the divine.

Ibid pp. 368-369

Ibid

These puranas... teach those different divine aspects and preach the subtle truths of Vedanta in gross and concrete forms for the consumption of weak humanity.8

When we remember this, we shall not confuse Puranas with books of political history. We shall understand that histories such as the Ramayana and the Mahabharata have also become somewhat mythological, because the purpose of their authors and subsequent editors has been to depict the different Vedantic ideas and ideals in gross forms through stories historical or otherwise. But the impression they produce on the mind of the spiritual seeker is extremely beneficial for the growth of the spiritual personality.

Special Scriptures

(1) The Bhagavad-Gita. The great commentator Sri Shankaracharya says concluding his introduction to the Gita:

The science of the Gita, thus elucidating especially the twofold way of the Vedas, is aimed at emancipation; it also sets forth the ultimate Truth that goes here with the name of Vasudeva which contains the Being which is usually denoted as the supreme Brahman.. To realize the meaning conveyed by it yields all values of life...

(2) Sri Ramakrishna, the Great Master. In this book the Supreme Being as Sri Ramakrishna is revealed in all his spiritual glory by a Rishi, Swami Saradananda. Once when Saradananda ji was pestered to narrate his own spiritual experiences; he remarked, “I have not written there (in the Great Master) anything which I have not realized.” One great teacher said that this is the Scripture of scriptures, the greatest scripture where we see the highest spiritual ideals in flesh and blood.

These two and other allied scriptures require much elaborate depiction and hence only a mention of their specific features has been made here.

How scriptural study functions in spiritual life

(a) Illumination. By trying to assimilate the experience of the Rishis we get clear illumination regarding the nature of the ultimate Reality or Para Brahman, the relation between the individual and God, and the science of spiritual progress with all its steps. We are no longer required to march blindly. We walk on an illumined path.

(b) Inspiration. Scriptures inspire us in many ways to go ahead. When we come across people who have realized the supreme goal of life and have thereby become a blessing unto themselves and unto humanity at large, we are also goaded to go that way. And the words of inspiration they utter are nonpareil:

Hear, ye children of immortal bliss! Ye, even those who reside in higher spheres, hearken! I Have known this universal Being, Luminous, lustrous, beyond the darkness of ignorance. Knowing Him alone ye shall conquer death. There is no other way to emancipation.

(c) Impressions. If we study the scriptures in depth, critically and devotionally, they create stable and strong spiritual impressions in us which enable us to withstand the force of worldly impressions that gather in our life. Actually a devoted, critical study is not only helpful to the spiritual seeker to maintain his Quality of life, but also to rise to higher and higher levels of thought, feeling and action.

Ibid

(d) Insight. Scriptures do not talk about God alone. They are primarily concerned with man, and with the deeper and deeper layers of his mind and its functions. We get such a power of insight into our minds and also of our fellow brothers that we are no longer deceived by the hidden antagonistic forces in our mind.

If meditation is taken as the principal means of spiritual progress, scriptural study is undoubtedly an important accessory. For it makes the contents of meditation clearer provides inspiration to meditate, keeps up the continuity of the spiritual currents released in meditation, and also teaches us how to conduct all our other activities so that they become helpful and not hindrance to our meditative life.

Those who walk on the path of devotion sometimes feel that they do not require any scriptural study. But Narada the great teacher of devotion says in his Bhakti Sutras: One must ponder over and assimilate the Scriptures dealing with devotion. Scriptural study saves us from the dangers of self-deception and blunders committed due to ignorance.

A word of caution

One should never forget that scriptural study is meant to help us achieve the supreme goal of life. Scriptural study is meant neither to derive intellectual pleasure nor to bathe in the glory of scholarship. If scriptures are not studied with the aim of realizing one’s real nature in the depths of one’s consciousness, they are reduced to a mere accumulation of words. Not only do they, in that case, cease to be aids, but also become positive stumbling blocks.

master-and-mother:
The Master and the Mother

Swami Pitambarananda

Question: Why did Sri Ramakrishna marry?

Answer: Swami Saradananda, in his ‘Sri Ramakrishna – the Great Master’, has analyzed and discussed this Question in great detail, and from various perspectives, and has come to the unambiguous conclusion that it was for the purpose of setting up a perfect ideal for conjugal life before humanity at large and not for anything less than that.

Question: What is this ‘ideal’ that you speak of?

Answer: The husband and wife are wedded for spiritual comradeship and not for the satisfaction of animal propensities.

Question: How did they – Sri Ramakrishna and his spiritual consort Sri Sarada Devi – set up this ideal in a perfect example?

Answer: (a) One day, while the Holy Mother Sarada Devi was gently massaging his lotus feet, Sri Ramakrishna suddenly asked her, ‘‘Have you come to drag me down to the life of this world?” Out came the reply: “Why should it be so? I have come to help you in my own way in attaining the aim of your life.”

(b) It was her turn one day to ask him all of a sudden, “How do you look upon me?” He replied without hesitation: “The Mother Who is in the temple is the same as the one who gave birth to this body and the same Mother in the temple in another (your) form is massaging my feet.”

Question: What is the significance of this last statement?

Answer: It means that throughout he had maintained the ‘mother-consciousness’ towards all women.

Question: How did the Holy Mother help him in her own way?

Answer: By serving him wholeheartedly without expecting anything whatsoever from him.

Question: How could she do so?

Answer: She says, “From the time of my first meeting with him (when she was about 13 years of age) at Kamarpukur, I felt, and I continuously feel since then, that a pitcher full of Bliss has been kept in my Heart.” ‘Pitcher full of Bliss in the Heart’ symbolically means ‘the Heart overflowing with spontaneity of nectarial bliss’. In such a state why will she ‘expect’ anything? She would rather serve him with her whole soul, not as a ‘duty’ but as a natural outcome of this joy which has come due to his mere presence as it were.

Question: Did everyone who come near him feel like that?

Answer: Yes and no. According to the purity of each one’s heart he or she would feel this spiritual bliss to that degree or extent.

Question: Does it mean that the Holy Mother Sarada was pre-eminently suited to receive the spirituality and pure bliss overflowing from Sri Ramakrishna?

Answer: Certainly so. It was during Sri Ramakrishna’s stay in his native place Kamarpukur. He had already accepted the position of a worshipper in the Kali temple at Dakshineswar near Calcutta. Through that worship, he had fully merged himself in the divinity of Mother Kali- the source of the entire creation. His behavior was becoming unintelligible to ordinary mortals who are mad after some worldly pursuit or other. It is these ‘normal’ people maddened by their worldly pursuits who think that a superconscious person is ‘abnormal’ or insane. This is why he was taken to his native village where his mother and elder brother watched him with attention and care. When his supernormal consciousness became digested as it were, they thought that he had come down to normalcy. They wanted to chain him down to this normalcy by arranging his marriage so that he might not be able to soar high again! But they were doing it secretly as they thought that he might oppose the idea. They were not aware of the mission for which he was born on earth. It was during these days that he gave out the ecstatic utterance: “It is futile to search here and there, for, the bride has been earmarked and you will find her in Sri Ramachandra Mukherji’s house in the village of Jayrambati.’’ Jayrambati is just two miles away from Kamarpukur and it was here that they actually found her – our Holy Mother Sarada!

Question: Did the Holy Mother herself know about the divine mission to be fulfilled by her marriage with Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna?

Answer: The villagers do say such a thing. Once in the village of Sihar, which is near Kamarpukur and Jayrambati, There was a festive gathering. Sarada was just an infant girl then and sitting on the lap of a lady. They asked her in jest whom she would like to marry and she pointed her small hands to wards Gadadhar, as Sri Ramakrishna was then known, sitting in the men’s wing!

Question: Can we not have any human, non-mystic indication of the supreme fitness of their union?

Answer: Let us try to analyze their respective mental make-up or innermost constitution. Superconscious wisdom, absolute and palpable renunciation, purity – this is what Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna represents to us. And Mother? Once when she found some of the girls taking on vain matters, she immediately changed the drift of their talk by posing a question: “Yes, dear ones, tell me – what should one pray for from God?” The girls, who thought much of their intelligence, started declaring: “Why? One should pray for all the good things of life”, “One should ask for merits of character”, “and intelligence”; “and devotion” etc. etc. A little while afterwards, they discovered that having given a new drift to their talks and thoughts she was keeping quiet and to herself as it were. “But Auntie.” asked some of them, “You have not told us your opinion of what one should ask for from God!” Then she spoke out her innermost thoughts; her very being was expressed in words when she said, “To me the only thing one should pray for is desirelessness” This is Sarada – unerring judgment, most natural noncovetousness and crystal purity. And what sort of purity?

Question: Yes, please tell us something about her purity.

Answer: Looking at the full moon on a bright night she would pray: “Lord, even this divine moon has spots on it; may not my mind have even the least spot of impurity in it.” What an Idea! And the fantastic purity and originality of the mind of Sarada which conceived this idea! Nothing, even a small fraction, less than full cent-per-cent purity, is acceptable to such a personality. This is what makes her pre-eminently fit to share the divine mission of Sri Ramakrishna – The blazing fire of pure renunciation. Swami Abhedananda pays homage to Sarada Devi in the blessed verse:

Pavitram caritam yasyah Pavitram jivanam tatha

Pavitrata svarupinyai tasyai kurmo namo namah

“We bow down again and again to her whose character is pure, whose life is pure and who is the very embodiment of purity.”

Question: Would you narrate some incidents where the words and actions of Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna and his consort Sarada Devi have been complementary to each other?

Answer: Beautiful question indeed! Smt Aghormani Devi, Who was known as ‘Gopala’s mother’ on account of her constant realization and various experiences of God in the form of the child Gopalakrishna, was highly praised for her devotion by Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna himself and was equally respected by all the devotees and Sadhakas who knew her. Once, when Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna was on a visit to the house of a great devotee Sriyut Balaram Basu, during festivities, he had her invited there for participating in the spiritual joy so that the members of that family and others might derive inspiration from her holy company. Balaram Basu’s devout wife and others loaded her with presents on account of their high respect for her and a bundle of these articles was kept in the boat which Sri Ramakrishna and others including ‘Gopala’s mother’ boarded for their return journey. On enquiry, Sri Ramakrishna came to know of the presents offered and accepted and then being carried away to her own house by ‘Gopala’s mother’. The Emperor of the empire of total renunciation that he was, it was too much for him to bear and, though he did not say a word to her, he went on looking at that bundle in such a way as if it were the most loathsome object in the world. He also started talking of renunciation and utter dependence on God and said ,”One who can come away empty-handed from the place visited by him can sit reclining with God Himself as his supporting pillow,” and so on and so forth. ‘Gopala’s mother’ understood it all and somehow controlled her own reaction all along, though she felt like throwing away the entire bundle into the Ganges. However, on reaching Dakshineswar temple, she went straight to the room where the Holy Mother lived and plaintively said to her: “Oh Daughter-in-law, (since she had realized Sri Ramakrishna himself as her child Krishna, naturally his consort was her daughter-in-law towards whom she had a unique love and for whose judgment great regard) Gopala is upset to see this bundle; shall I throw it away?” The holy Mother, the embodiment of compassion, replied: “Why, mother, have you not accepted these things only because you needed them? And who else is there to give you things so necessary for life?“

Question: Is this advice not contrary to Sri Ramakrishna’s attitude?

Answer: Not at all.

Question: Why

Answer: Judging from the results. ‘Gpala’s mother’, being thus consoled and advised by the supremely revered Holy Mother, took only one or two articles which were really essential and distributed the rest on the spot to others and then, cooking a dish or two with her own hands, offered the food to Sri Ramakrishna who also accepted it with satisfaction and was highly pleased to see the result of the whole episode. Thus we see that the actions and advices of Sri Ramakrishna and Sri Sarada Devi are harmonius and complementary to each other.

Question: How best to describe the relation ship of the Holy Mother with the Master?

Answer: In the words of Swami Saradananda, the seer of Truth, the Holy Mother is descried as:

Yathagner dahika saktih Ramakrsne sthita hi ya

Sarva-vidya-svarupam tam, Saradam pranamamyaham

“As the burning power of the fire , which is not different from the fire, ever lives in the fire, so is this Sarada, the Sakti of Bhagavan Sri Ramakrishna, non-different from him, and living and moving and having her being always in him.”

Question: Can their relation be descried in any other way?

Answer: Yes! Here is an incident. Miss Josephine MacLeod, the American disciple of Swami Vivekananda, was then living in the Guest House attached to Belur Math, the Head-quarters of the Ramakrishna Mission. Swami Shivananda, one of the foremost among the direct disciples of Sri Ramakrishna, was then the Abbot there. The Holy Mother was living in Baghbazar across the Ganges. One day, when Miss MacLeod entered Swami Shivanandaji’s room and was about to salute him, he asked her, “MacLeod, have you saluted Sri Ramakrishna?” “Yes, Swami,” she replied. “I am just coming from the shrine.” Swami Shivanandaji then exclaimed in a solemn tone, “I tell you MacLeod, salute salute Sri Ramakrishna again; take a boat, cross the Ganges and salute Sri Ramakrishna once more! She was charged with a divine fervor and immediately left Belur Math to visit the Holy Mother. Thus the one who is Sri Ramakrishna is also the Holy Mother, and the one who is the Mother is also the Master (Sri Ramakrishna)!

Question: Do our ancient scriptures say something about this relationship?

Answer: There is the famous conversation between the seer Yajnavalkya and his worthy consort Maitreyi in the Brihadaranyanka Upanishad.

[[ORIG]]

– “Not for the sake of the husband does the husband become dear, but he becomes dear on account of the indwelling Reality which is common to both and is One without a second; not for the sake of the wife does the wife become dear but she becomes dear on account of the indwelling Reality which is common to both and is One without a second....’’

Question: What is the highest point reached in this spiritual commingling of souls?

Answer: Let us see. It is a new moon day – Amavasya. This special day is meant for the

special worship of Mother Kali; it is called Phalaharini Kali Puja – the worship in which all the fruits of actions done are offered to the Mother. Sri Ramakrishna, the ‘Great Master’ as we call him is getting ready for a very special type of worship in his own room at Dakshineswar. A decorated seat for the Goddess has been kept to the right of the seat meant for the worshipper. The Sun has set in the west. Gradually the intense darkness of the new moon night has settled itself. As Sir Ramakrishna’s nephew Hridayaram has to perform special worship in the temple, he has taken leave of his uncle after helping him to some extent in the preparations. Meanwhile, Deenanath, the priest of the Radhakanta temple, has come to help the Master after finishing his temple duties. It is nine o’ clock in the night when the arrangements for this private worship have been completed. Word has already been sent to the Holy Mother to be present for the worship. She has come and the Master sits on the worshipper’s seat.

The articles of worship have been purified and the preliminary rites have been completed. At this time the Master, by signs, asks the Holy Mother to sit on the decorated seat. By this time, the Holy Mother, while looking at the preliminaries of worship, has already entered into a semi-indrawn state of consciousness. Hence, without full external awareness, she takes the seat indicated and sits facing north to the right of the Master who in sitting facing the east. He sprinkles her again and again with the water from the jar along with the appropriate Mantras. Now, after the incantations, he recites the hymns of prayer: “Oh maiden, supremely beautiful Mother of the universe, overlording all powers, open the gates of success and perfection; sanctify this (Holy Mother’s body) and manifesting Yourself in it accomplish everything that is auspicious and good.” Then systematically offering all the hymns and Mantras to the person of the Holy Mother he worshiped her with the prescribed sixteen articles with the direct consciousness of her divinity. Offering food to her, he places in her mouth a bit from each of the food offerings. Becoming bereft of all external consciousness, the Holy Mother enters into the deepest superconscious state of the One-without-a second Reality. The Master also, having chanted the hymns in a semi-divine state, loses himself completely in the superconscious state of Samadhi. Thus, through their respective merging in the self-same consciousness of the Absolute Reality, the worshipper and the worshipped realize their complete oneness and identity.

Let us bow down to this Supreme Reality, One without a second, manifesting Itself through the Master and the Mother – Sri Bhagavan Ramakrishna and the Mother Sri Sarada Devi, for the redemption of mankind.
