golden-person:
The Golden Person

Swami Pitambarananda

“Look at these bickerings, Golap; that Golden Person has disappeared and they are quarrelling about the ashes.”

– Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi

Introduction

There are various ways of looking at the phenomenon called Sri Ramakrishna, and, each way reveals the Divine most gloriously. One way is to look at Him through all the spiritual scriptures, Indian and alien, and another way is to look at Him through the eyes of the totality of the modern world represented by the great Swami Vivekananda. Both of these have been handled in a masterly way in the monumental hagiographical work ‘Sri Ramakrishna-Lilaprasanga’ (Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master) by Srimat Swami Saradanandaji. However, the most remarkable person one meets with in ‘Lilaprasanga’ – one who is incapable of misunderstanding Sri Ramakrishna through any event or utterance of his even once – is none else but the counterpart of Ramakrishna, the Holy Mother Sarada Devi. We find that the modern mind represented by Swami Vivekananda falters in the beginning to fathom the infinite ocean of Sri Ramakrishna; and it is only after the most sincere and intense struggle that it is enabled to understand him. On the other hand he has himself declared that his own experiences have gone beyond the Vedas and the Vedantas! Turning our attention, once more to the Holy Mother, as seen through the Lilaprasanga as well as through her biographies and conversations, we do not find even a single incident where she has not hit it right in understanding him in a flash as it were. And this is as it should be. Kenopanisad tells a story wherein Indra, the king of Gods, fails to understand the manifestation of the Supreme Brahman, and, in answer to his sincere attempt to investigate the Truth, there descends on the scene the power of the Lord, the Mother of the Universe, Brahmavidya or the Divine Intelligence embodied as a person, and reveals to Indra the meaning and content of the manifestation of Brahman. Has not Sri Ramakrishna said about the Holy Mother – “She is my power; she is Sarada who has come to give knowledge”? Is it a wonder, then, that she reveals Sri Ramakrishna’s divinity in an effortless way through her own words and reflections! Let us, then, ponder over the phenomenon called Sri Ramakrishna as revealed through her – the Goddess of right knowledge – his own power in the form of our Holy Mother Sarada Devi.

The Spontaneous Utterances of the Holy Mother

While in the temple garden at Dakshineswar, one day Sri Ramakrishna was in the temple of Kali, the Mother of the Universe. Taking advantage of his absence from his room Sri Sarada Devi busied herself in sweeping and dusting his room. While she was still at work, with her back to the door, he returned. He was swaying and shaking, staggering, unable to place his steps properly. In such a state, he gave her a nudge from behind and suddenly asked, “Have I drunk wine?” Without feeling the least hesitation she

replied, “Why should you take wine?” Sri Ramakrishna (falteringly), “Then why am I swaying? Why am I not able to walk properly?” Holy Mother (coolly): “You are drunk of the nectar of the love of Mother Kali.” He (very much pleased) – “Right, you have said it!” This must have been one of the innumerable occasions when she was ‘right’, without exception, in her spontaneous judgments.

It was the midnight of 15th -16th August 1886 The Holy Mother was living in a small room on the ground floor of the Cossipore garden-house. Sri Ramakrishna entered the final Samadhi and left his mortal coil in the room on the first floor, surrounded by his disciples. They worried themselves as to how to break this sad news to her. Lo! She by herself became aware of the happenings on the first floor and, before anybody could go to her room; herself rushed to the room of the sad happenings and threw herself on the ground with a wail – “Oh Mother Kali! Where have you gone leaving me behind?” Remarkable utterance indeed! And coming at such an agonizing moment when the innermost consciousness expresses itself unveiled and unguarded! So he was to her Mother Kali Herself!

Yet there was to be another sad scene and still another uncovered and deeper expression from her regarding him. It was a few days after the demise that they started quarrelling about his ashes, the holy relics. What was her response? She merely exclaimed to her companion Golap-ma: “Look at these bickerings Golap! That Golden Person (Sonar Manush) has disappeared, and they are quarrelling about his ashes!” It is impossible to translate what she spoke in those two Bengali words – “Sonar Manush” in any other human language and the whole scope and purpose of this article is to try to understand what she meant when she said that he was a ‘Golden person.’ What did the Holy Mother Mean?

We sometimes talk of ‘a man worth his weight in gold’ or ‘a man made of gold’ or ‘a man of gold’ etc. These idioms were coined before platinum and other more precious metals were discovered, and even after their discovery the idioms have retained their currency. So the use of the word ‘gold’ in these idioms cannot just refer to the mere conventional metal called ‘gold’ but it connotes a metal, pure, shining and of the highest value. When the Holy Mother herself uses a similar expression, it should primarily and necessarily mean ‘the only thing worthwhile in human life, the only value in life, the supreme value in this world’, in the context in which she spoke of him as the Golden Person. What is it then which is the only value in life, the Supreme Value, of which metal he was made, in the eyes of the Holy Mother?

The story of a Sadhu explains this beautifully. Once upon a time a king came and prostrated himself before a monk in veneration and respect at which, the monk, showing surprise, asked, “Why is it, O King, that a prostration is being made to me?” The king replied, “To whom else, Sir, shall we show respect and reverence if not to a man of renunciation?” At this reply the monk exclaimed, “In that case, I should roll down before you in supreme reverence as you are a man of superior renunciation!” “How can it be so, sir?” “Why? What have I renounced? The world, which is a mere trash and of no value whatsoever. Giving it up I cling to God who alone is the supreme Jewel. While you have given up that Supreme Jewel itself! Are you not a person of far superior renunciation?”

The lesson brought home through this amusing story is clear. To the discriminating intellect God alone has ‘value’.

Sri Ramakrishna himself once told his nephew Hridayaram who was always craving for more and more money – “Oh Hriday! I would have transformed the whole Kamarpukur (his own native village) into gold, had there been any reality about this world; but the Mother (of the universe) has clearly shown me that there is no reality whatsoever about this world.” It shows very clearly that the so called gold itself is a mere trash. Hence the ‘GOLD’ which the Holy Mother saw in Sri Ramakrishna is nothing but “the fullest manifestation of Divinity – unalloyed and impeccably pure” – in which she saw the infinity of existence or the Existence itself, the infinity of unerring knowledge or the Consciousness itself, and the infinity of bliss or the BLISS itself, unalloyed and untainted. About the time when she could first have his company at Kamarpukur for a few days she used to say in later days – “Since that time I feel that a pitcher full of BLISS has been kept in my heart.” It can be called the radiation of pure Bliss. And as for himself, she has repeatedly said, “I have never seen another ever-blissful person like him”, and also, “I have never seen him devoid of bliss.” When we hear all this in the face of the description of all forms of utmost human sufferings his life is apparently beset with, we have to pause and think: “What is the nature of this unalloyed and untainted Bliss which radiates so powerfully from this Golden Person?” She thus finds in him the fullest manifested Divinity which is the Supreme purity and Purity itself embodied. Ideals Embodied

Let us look at it from a slightly human angle. Once it so happened that whenever Narendranath (Swami Vivekananda) went to Sri Ramakrishna the latter would avoid talking with him. It went on for about a month or so, after which period Sri Ramakrishna asked Narendranath – “How is it that you continue to come here even though I have not talked to you for such a long time?” He replied, “I do not come to listen to you; I love you and I like to see you; that is why I come.” What was it that Swami Vivekananda loved to see? Srimat Swami Saradanandaji has explained it in his appendix to the monumental work ‘Lilaprasanga.’ He says that when we look at him without selfish motive in our hearts we are dazzled by the glorious and fullest manifestation of all the human ideals in him and we become captivated by him forever. Self-control, purity, unselfish love, simplicity, humility, respectfulness towards all forms of greatness, cleanliness, steadiness of wisdom, dispassion, aversion to worldly pursuits, equanimity in praise and blame and other pairs of opposites, unfailing concern for the welfare and well-being of others – the list can be unending – for, he shines supreme from any human excellence point of view. That is why the Holy Mother in her own unselfish purity finds him to be the Golden Person. Whatever is really covetable in human life is ever present in him and to such a degree which cannot even be imagined let alone hoped to be seen elsewhere. He comes as the perfect embodiment of Ideals.

Let us see him on a few occasions as mentioned in ‘Lilaprasanga’:– ‘Jealousy broke the heart of Haldar, the Kalighat Priest of Mathur Babu, when he saw the latter’s firm devotion to the Master (Sri Ramakrishna). He thought that this man (the Master) must have charmed the Babu by means of incantations and demurred: “Ah! Is this rogue of a fellow going to spoil my long attempt at getting the Babu under my

control? He again feigns that mood of a simple child! If he were so simple, let him tell me the incantation for ‘putting a man under a spell’. I had exhausted all my spells on this Babu and he was almost on the point of succumbing to my influence; but now this fellow of an interloper has come between us.’’

‘Now with the increase in his devotion and reverence, Mathur began to have a strong desire for keeping the Master’s company constantly and for serving him more and more. Therefore by extending pressing invitations, he often brought him to his house at Janbazar in Calcutta and enjoyed his company from time to time. In the afternoon he would take him for a drive to the Eden Garden and other places of interest in Calcutta. He thought, “Can any and every plate, cup, etc., be considered fit for Father (Sri Ramakrishna was addressed thus by Mathur Babu) to eat and drink from?” Thinking so, he had a new set of gold and silver vessels made in which he offered him food and drink. He dressed him in excellent clothes and said, “It is you, Father, Who are the owner of all these. I am nothing but the steward. ...”

‘Although he was living at Janbazar in Mathur Babu’s house abounding in all kinds of luxuries and worldly enjoyments, the Master was the same Master, unattached, devoid of egoism and beside himself night and day with his own divine mood. ‘One day, just before dust, the Master was lying in a divine semiconscious state in Mathur’s Janbazar house. There was no one near him. The master’s ecstasy was coming to an end and he was gradually having a little consciousness of the outer world, when Haldar happened to come in. When he saw the Master alone in that state, he thought it to be just the opportunity he was looking for. He approached him, looked around and said again and again while pushing his holy person about, “O man! Tell me how you have made the Babu subservient to you? Why do you keep mum, feigning ignorance? How did you captivate him? Speak out.” Although he repeated the questions again and again, the Master did not or could not say anything; for he had not then the power to speak at all. Haldar became very angry, kicked him violently, saying, “Damn you, rascal! You want to hide your secret from me!” and went away. Devoid of egoism, the Master made no mention of the incident, since he knew that Mathur Babu was sure to be furiously angry and inflict very severe punishment on the priest, should he come to know of it.’ Golden Person!

Supreme Renunciation – His natural asset

Let us once more turn our attention to the special estimations and readings of the Holy Mother about Sri Ramakrishna which are unique in character. Everyone knows Sri Ramakrishna to be the prophet of harmony; the very specialty of his life and teachings is seen to be the emphasis on religious harmony. Once a disciple asked the Holy mother about this remarkable specialty of his. What she said in reply is an object lesson in spiritual understanding. The conversation was as follows:

Disciple: Mother, did Sri Ramakrishna come this time only with the purpose of giving a new ideal to the world – is that why he harmonized all religions? Holy Mother: “Look here, my child, it did not occur to me that he undertook the practices of all religious creeds with the willful purpose or motivation of preaching the idea of harmony. But he was always filled with and full of divine modes of consciousness.

Christians, Mohammedans, Vaishnavas – all these worship God in different ways and realize the Ultimate Truth; Sri Ramakrishna used to practice all those modes of worship and taste the bliss of various divine sports of manifestation and in the divine moods he had no awareness of days and nights rolling by. But, one thing you should know, my child, that in this age his remarkable specialty was renunciation. Has anybody seen such a natural renunciation elsewhere? The ideal of harmony of all sects which you spoke of is also right. On the other occasions the respective particular ideas were specially manifested as a result of which the other ideas were suppressed.” On analysis we get the following steps:

(1) The specialty remarkable in sri Ramakrishna is renunciation; (2) His renunciation is supremely natural, i.e. without the specified consciousness of ‘I the renouncer’; (3) The corollary of such supremely natural renunciation was the complete absorption in the divine without specification of any sort; (4) The result of such divinity without specified “I” was the manifestation of divinity in all possible modes of expression without any contraction or exceptions; (5) Harmony of religions established and propagated not as a doctrine or policy but as the spontaneous and natural outcome of the unrestricted and not-contracted manifestation of the Divine; hence (6) TRUTH is harmonious and harmony is the spontaneous manifestation of Truth. This is not manifested fully because of attachments to specifications of ego, specifications of forms of worship, specified likes and dislikes etc. But the total, unprecedented, most natural and supreme renunciation embodying itself as Sri Ramakrishna – THE GOLDEN PERSON – caused the absence of any such obstructions and the spontaneous result that followed was Harmony as the natural manifestation of TRUTH in religious life.

Conclusion

In conclusion, let us remember that we have taken the Holy Mother’s judgments of Sri Ramakrishna as we find her to be His own Sakti – the purest mind and heart revealing His glory to us very directly. We bow down to both of them in words of Saint Jnaneswara which he has used to invoke the supreme Reality:

Sārdham kena ca kasyārdham Śivayoh samarūpinoh;

Jñātum na śakyate lagnam iti dvaitachhalān muhuh

Advaitam ātmanastattvam darśayantau mithastarām;

Tau vande jagatām ādyau tayostattvābhipattaye.

-- “I bow down to Siva and Sivā, the causes of the world, for clearly knowing and realizing their innate nature; their mutual union is incomprehensible because we cannot know who is complementary or supplementary to whom and whose half is who; we find that this duality is only an appearance, for to the persevering and tranquil enquirer they themselves reveal their real nature which is non-duality.”

glory-of-sarada-devi-1:
The Glory of Sri Sarada Devi

As Seen by Sister Nivedita

A Chronological Study – (1)

## SWAMI PITAMBARANANDA

In a letter to Sri Sarada Devi, dated 11 December 1910, written from Cambridge, Mass. U.S.A. Sister Nivedita exclaims :

“Dearest Mother, I wish we could send you a wonderful hymn, or a prayer. But somehow even that would seem too loud, too full of noise! Surely you are the most wonderful thing of God – Sri Ramakrishna’s own chalice of His Love for the world – a token left with his children, in these lonely days, and we should be very still and quiet before you except indeed for a little fun! Surely the wonderful things of God are all quiet – stealing unnoticed into our lives – the air and sunlight and the sweetness of gardens and of the Ganges, these are the silent things that are like you! …”

What would happen if we try to understand this ‘Mother’ who spreads her sweetness unnoticed? What would happen if we really try to fathom her infinitude? Swami Saradananda, the author of ‘Sri Ramakrishna the great Master’, says with reference to Incarnations of God, the embodiments of infinity :

“On reflection one is amazed to find such profundity of meaning in the ordinary daily conduct of the Master and his teachings. This is true of every one of the incarnations of God. ... The more we study them the more we find deeper and deeper meanings; and the more we muse over them, the more does the mind renounce the transient, inauspicious realm of the world and ascend to higher and higher regions. And the farther one proceeds towards the realization of the Supreme goal, ... the more does one comprehend in one’s heart of hearts the deep significance of those simple words.”

Some such process seems to have taken place in Sister Nivedita’s mind due to her effort to understand the Holy Mother. On one hand, Sri Sarada Devi’s infinite sweetness went on spreading its influence over Nivedita’s life with or without her knowledge and, on the other hand, this foreigner, endowed with a sharp intellect, analytical mind, tendency for comparative study, and a desire to unaffectedly understand such a divine personality, was trying to assess and estimate the Holy Mother in various ways. To study this process chronologically is an exercise that promises to be highly beneficial to all. For reference, we shall try to fully utilize (1) mainly – the two volumes of letters of Sister Nivedita, edited by Prof. Sankari Prasad Basu, (2) important extracts from the unpublished third volume and other material used by him in his article ‘Nivedita Dhruvamandire’ included in the Bengali book Shatarupe Sarada, (3) Some other articles from the same book, and (4) Complete Works of Sister Nivedita, published by the Advaita Ashrama, Calcutta.

Nivedita’s first visit to Sri Sarada Devi took place on March 17, 1898. What happened that day? When Swami Vivekananda sent Nivedita along with Mrs. Ole Bull and Miss MacLeod to the Holy Mother, he was extremely worried whether the Mother with her village background would keep Nivedita at a distance considering her a ‘mleccha’. Again, the Mother couldn’t follow English and Nivedita did not know Bengali. So he sent his disciple Swami Swarupananda to be the interpreter. The latter escorted the ladies and introduced the Sister, and the Mother was very happy. When the Mother asked for her name, she replied, “My name is Elizabeth Margaret Noble.” The Mother remarked, “My child, I shall not to able

to remember such a big name, I shall call you just ‘Baby’”. When Swarupananda translated this in English, Nivedita was delighted and exclaimed, “Yes, Yes, I am Mother’s baby.” Thus went off the introduction! Nivedita herself noted in her diary : “A day of days.” These are the first words used by Nivedita regarding her visit to the Mother. Why ‘day of days’? It was because of what happened that day and, as we shall see, Mother went on spreading sweetness in Nivedita’s life as stated by her in the letter partly quoted in the beginning.

The first clear reference to the Holy Mother in Nivedita’s letters occurs in her letter to Swam Akhandananda written at Easter in April 1898. She says, ‘Now I am going to tell you what I have been doing. I took your advice and went straight to Sarada on Thursday morning. It was so lovely. Gopal’s Mother was there and Swami Brahmananda and Swami Saradananda and some others. It was warm and beautiful and like home.’ The pen-picture she has drawn in her letter dated May 22, 1898 to Mrs. Eric Hammond shows the change undergone by her mind in two months and the assessment made by her intellect. She writes :

“I have often thought that I ought to tell you about the lady who was the wife of Sri Ramakrishna, Sarada as her name is. To begin with, she is dressed in a white cotton cloth like any other Hindu widow under 50. This cloth goes round the waist and forms a skirt, then it passes round the body and over the head like a nun’s veil. When a man speaks to her, he stands behind her, and she pulls this white veil very far forward over her face. Nor does she answer him directly. She speaks to another older woman in almost a whisper and this woman repeats her words to the man. In this way it comes about that the Master [Vivekananda] has never seen the face of Sarada! Added to this, you must try to imagine her always seated on floor, on a small piece of bamboo matting. All this does not sound very sensible perhaps, yet this woman, when you know her well, is said to be the very soul of practicality and common sense, as she certainly gives every token of being, to those who know her slightly. Sri Ramakrishna always consulted her before undertaking anything and her advice is always acted upon by his disciples. She is the very soul of sweetness – so gentle and loving and as merry as a girl. You should have heard her laugh the other day when I insisted that the Swami must come up and see us at once or we would go home. The monk who had brought the message that the Master would delay seeing us was quite alarmed at my moving towards my shoes, and departed post haste to bring him up, and then you should have heard Sarada’s laughter! It just pealed out. And she is so tender – ‘my daughter’ she calls me. She has always been terribly orthodox, but all this melted away the instant she saw the first two Westerners – Mrs. Bull and Miss MacLeod, and she tasted food with them!2 Fruit is always presented to us immediately, and this was naturally offered to her, and she to the surprise of everyone accepted. This gave us all a dignity and made my future work possible in a way nothing else could possibly have done. Isn’t it funny? The best proof I can give you of her greatness is that she is always attended when in Calcutta by 14 or 15 high caste ladies, who would be rebellious and quarrelsome and give infinite trouble to everyone if she by her wonderful tact and winsomeness did not keep perpetual peace. There is no foundation for this statement in character of these ladies. It is only my inference about women in general. “Then you should see the chivalrous feeling that the monks have for her. They always call her ‘Mother’ and speak of her as ‘The Holy Mother’ and she is literally their first thought in every emergency. There are always one or two in attendance on her, and whatever her wish is, it is their command. It is a wonderful relationship to watch. I should love to give her a

Translation of a passage from Swami Gauriswarananda’s article in Shatarupe Sarada [Bengali], 258. Nivedita herself was present during this first visit, yet refers to ‘two Westerners’ in an attempt to keep herself as a witness.

message from you, if you care to send her one. A monk read the magnificat in Bengali to her one day for me, and you should have seen how she enjoyed it. She really is, under the simplest, most unassuming guise, one of the strongest and greatest of women.”3 After this, Nivedita left for Kashmir with Swami Vivekananda. When she returned to Calcutta on November 1, 1898, she insisted on staying near the Holy Mother and this did come about through Swamiji’s mediation. After staying for a week in the Mother’s house, a separate house was found for her close by, but even after shifting there she used to spend the afternoons with the Mother and be filled with her overwhelming affection. Nivedita began her life’s work on the 13th of November : a girls’ school was started at her residence. The Holy Mother was the chief guest on the occasion. Giving her blessings, Mother said : “I pray that this school may be recipient of the grace of God and that the girls going out from here may prove to be ideal women.” Nivedita was overwhelmed with joy and exclaimed, ‘I cannot imagine anything more auspicious than the Mother’s blessings for the educated Hindu women of the future.’4 Nivedita’s experiences in the Mother’s household pertaining to the period November 1898 to June 1899 and some other significant facts narrated by her in her book The Master as I saw him, written during 1906-1907, reflect her vision developed by that time and so it will be better to consider them along with her other writings of that period. The next important event is Nivedita’s cooperation in getting the Holy Mother photographed for the first time. This first set of 3 photos was taken in November 1898 at Nivedita’s residence. Mrs. Ole Bull had somehow made the Mother agree to it as she wanted to take her photo to America for worship. She and Nivedita seated the Mother properly arranging her sari etc. The Mother was unwilling to look at the photographer; she sat inclined to one side and with her eyes cast below without facing the photographer and in that very posture became still in a divine mood. The posture was not satisfactory for a photo and yet the photographer had to take a shot. Mrs. Bull noticed that Mother’s toes were covered and hence she rearranged the sari slightly to expose the toes. That touch made the mother feel that the photographer’s work must have been over and hence she looked up. The photographer did not miss this opportunity and clicked again and the resultant photo is the one which is worshipped throughout the world today. Then Nivedita sat facing the Mother and the third photo was taken when the Mother was looking at her ‘baby’ with tender affection.5 Nivedita writes with reference to these photos :

16 Bosepara Lane, Bagh Bazar, Calcutta

Jan. 4, 99

My darling ‘Nell’ [Mrs. Eric Hammond],

... Swami has not started for Europe – but Mrs. Bull and Miss MacLeod have. ... They will bring photographs also of Sri Ramakrishna’s widow – who looks upon all of us as her ‘children’ and sends her blessings, but this photograph is not for general distribution. So don’t refer to it first! It is her birthday today. ...

Nivedita

And again, the very next day she writes :

Thurs., Jan.5, 1899

My darling Joy and Saint Sara [Joe MacLeod and Mrs. Ole Bull],

... The Mother tells me that Swami has his mother, sister and cousin with him at Baidyanath. She is quite sure that he will go West afterwards. He has much more to do she says. It was her birthday yesterday, as you I hope gathered from our telegram.

Emphasis added. Throughout this article, italicization in the quoted texts is done by the present writer. Pravrajika Muktiprana, Bhagini Nivedita [Bengali ], 135.

Shatarupe Sarada, 144 & 795 -96.

She suddenly without warning said last night that if I went to Allahabad she would go too. She intends to be with me always! ...

By next week’s post I send to London 10 photographs to her [Mrs. Bull ]. The two negatives are to be 40 rupees and expenses 3.4 - total 43.4 and my proof and negative cost nothing. So unless you write to the contrary we shall keep the 3 negatives here. Margot

Long before this, on 11th July 1898, Mrs. Bull had written a letter to the famous scholar Prof. Max Muller, giving some information regarding Sri Sarada Devi, and he utilized it in his book Ramakrishna : His Life and Savings. Referring to this, Nivedita writes to Miss J. MacLeod, on 11 January 1899:

... The Mother is as usual. She often talks of you. Hasn’t M.M. (Max Muller) made a lovely use of S.Sara’s letter? ...

Margot

The reference is to pp.64-65 of Max Muller’s book, where he wrote : I received not many days ago a letter from an American lady. ... She writes from Srinagar in Kashmir : “We were the first foreigners who were allowed to see Sarada Devi, the widow of Ramakrishna. She called us her children, and saying that our visit to her was of the Lord, she felt no strangeness in being with us. When asked to define the obedience to a Guru, who in her case was her husband, she replied to the effect that when one had chosen a Guru or teacher, one should listen to and obey all his directions for spiritual advancement, but in things temporal one could most truly serve a Guru by using one’s own best discernment, even if at times it were not in agreement with suggestions given.

“When she gladly gave her husband, to whom she had been united by child-marriage, her assent that he should lead a Sannyasin’s life, she gained his intimate friendship, and became his disciple, receiving daily instruction. During the years of her life with him she was his adviser, praying earnestly for such purity of motive that she might never fail him. She had also taken the vow of poverty and chastity, and in renouncing the natural joys of a mother, she became with him the spiritual parent of many children.” Continuing the same letter next day, Nivedita again refers to the photographs on Thurs., 12 January 1899 :

... A parcel has just come from Harringtons. Beautifully packed for transmission. I think I had better retain till next post. Consult Sw. Saradananda about sending negatives if inside – as once open we cannot repack – and must take to the city. The Mother wants 2 photographs herself and I am sure you would like her to have them.

Margot

References to the Holy Mother in Nivedita’s next few letters to Miss J. MacLeod are as follows :

Wednesday [8th Feb. 99]

... In meditation tonight the Mother said she saw Sara on her left and Joy in front all the time. Looking so well and happy. ...

Margot

March 5 [1899]

Sunday Night

... Went in and saw the Mother and her ladies and translated Mrs. Hammond’s letter straight through twice – and came here and went straight to bed. ... Margot

And then again we get a pen-picture :

16 Bosepara Lane, Bagh Bazar, Calcutta

Mar. 9, 1899

My own dear Nell [ Mrs. Eric Hammond ]

...... You do write the most wonderful letters. Please [say] where could I learn how to do it? Would a little journalism teach me? But no – for it’s the thoughts that are still lovelier than the style.

Well, I took it in to the Holy Mother and translated it straight through to her and her ladies one hot evening and every now and then they would say ‘Ah!’ and turn and kiss their right shoulders in token of their delight. I can’t tell you how deep all this touches them. Now how much you do in simply writing a letter like that. ...

Then I asked the Holy Mother for a message – and she sent you her love and blessings

– she regards you indeed as a daughter. But having got that you must not expect more. For in thought, outside the range of practicality and experience, these ladies have no range; it is in feeling that they are so strong. You see, they have never had the education that would enable to frame a thought that would appeal to a stranger.6

But in feeling she is perfect. You know that photograph meant the first time she had ever looked straight at a grown up man outside her own family, or been seen by one. ... Neither Swami nor Sri Ramakrishna himself ever saw her unveiled – after her marriage that is, when she was a little girl of 5! Men come up to the zenana door and sometimes inside, to worship her – but her long white veil is immediately dropped over her face, though sometimes she closes it with long point so that she can look down it with one eye. I have teased her so much about it that now she shakes with laughter the whole time if the man remains outside. But that is very interesting – a servant or a monk comes to the head of the stairs and in a loud voice announces that so and so is coming to prostrate before the Mother. And then a sort of tense air comes over the whole room. All chattering stops. Even fanning ceases, veils are quietly dropped, saris drawn up to cover the whole person – a back is turned to the door, if the lady sits in the middle of the floor and all this so quietly! The man comes, remains outside, and touches the threshold with his forehead or comes in and touches the Mother’s feet, and tells her what he is going to do.

He has just come to Calcutta – and brings presents or he is just going and begs her blessings etc. Then she whispers kind inquiries to the lady who sits next to her, and these are repeated in a louder tone to the man, and presently he prostrates for the last time, and she clasps her hands and is understood to bless him, and he goes. Then the tension relaxes. Old attitudes are resumed – chatter begins again and fans move – veils drop – and the rest. But fancy worshipping a man as she worshipped her husband, and never giving him even a glimpse of your face to make sure that he sometimes thought of you again! There is a deep self-abnegation about it all that fills me with amazement. ... Nivedita

It was Miss MacLeod who taught Nivedita to address Sri Sarada Devi as ‘Mother’, and this Nivedita acknowledged in her next letter.

March 12th Sunday morning

7.20 a.m. [1899]

My dear Yum [Miss J.MacLeod ] ,

... and I feel that if you can get our dear Mother (Yum darling - you have made be able to call Her that – I always had the possible claims of my own little mother at home tugging at my heart before) to make a special worship for the bairns. That will be better than any amount of religious dissipation for myself. ...

Margot

The memory of the ‘Day of days’ is expressed in the next letter to Miss J. MacLeod,

[March 1899]

We shall see later how Nivedita changed her opinion expressed in these two sentences.

... Tomorrow will be S.Patrick’s Day. This time last year – Belur – tomorrow a year since we all saw the Mother, and you took me practically into the family. Margot

Another beautiful picture we see in a letter to Mrs. Ole Bull :

Mar. 15, [1899]

Wednesday evening

... It was Sri R.K.’s [Ramakrishna’s] real Birthday on Monday last, and the Mother came and made a special puja before his image in the prayer room. And then her ladies made the fruits ready and 30 children and myself sat there and ate the Prasad. I wish you had seen their lovely little prostrations before eating, and heard the chatter! It was a lovely little Holy Eucharist with something of the Xmas Feast about it too. In the afternoon the Mother, the ladies, and the children and I drove in 7 gharis to see the orchids in Chatterji’s Nurseries – where it was a zenana day. And you must not think that all this meant wild extravagance. It ... altogether cost less than 12 rupees! Isn’t it wonderful what one can do here ? Margot

And now we see a very different and yet very significant picture in a letter to Miss J.MacLeod :

16 Bosepara Lane

Bagh Bazar, Calcutta.

Maundy Thursday 1899

[30.3.99]

My darling Yum

On Tuesday afternoon, Joginanda7 died. They were most of them with him, and asked him – “Brother how do you feel now? Any pain?” And he answered – “I am trying all the time for Brahma-Gnan, but my mind will cling to the personal. Read me the verses from the Gita.” They read them and he said “There is no pain now. Everything is melting. Brahma Gnan is coming.” And then saying “Om Ramakrishna!” in a sudden accession of voice and strength, he died.

Wasn’t it wonderful ?

Swami came over and dear old Mr. [Girish Ch.] Ghosh was afraid he was going to have an attack, and persuaded him to go back to the Math, for which I was most thankful. I went to the Mother, who was in tears. Jogin Ma who has nursed continually for months lay on the floor without a word or a tear. I was there a long time when we heard “Hari Om!” from 50 or 60 voices downstairs, and the Mother told me hurriedly to go and see. It was very very awful. The dead man wearing a great turban of yellow silk and covered with flowers Swami had thrown on him, was help up in the arms of Sadananda and another while burning camphor was waved before him, and the crowd within and without chanted the Sacred Name.

I wish you had seen the face of Sadananda. At such moments he is a saint. But a long wail broke out upstairs – and went forth with the sound of the worship from below – for the women knew that it meant that he who had so long been master of the house was about to leave it for ever. Jogin Ma’s icy calm was broken now – and I thought she and the Mother would break their hearts. And then he went. The bed was made so soft to receive him and he was covered with flowers – he with white, the bed with yellow. Down at the burning ghat, they built the pyre – and talked to him all the time, and then before the lighted straw was put beneath it by Brahmananda they all asked his pardon for anything they might have done.

Actual name Swami Yogananda; a direct disciple of Sri Ramakrishna and trusted attendant of the Holy Mother. She called him ‘Yogin’, a shortened form of his premonastic name ‘Yogindranath’; perhaps that is why Nivedita refers to him as ‘Yoginanda’.

“And his face was just as Shiva – in the fire” – says Sadananda.

Yesterday was all reaction of course. The men had suppressed their sorrow to a great extent and merged it in religious exaltation on Tuesday. Yesterday was a day of real mourning. Sadananda could talk of nothing else.

This worship of the Dead is very very impressive.

S. tells me of a boy who was dying, and the Mother ordered them to take him to the Ganges-side.

“What, am I going to die then?” he said, when they told him.

“The Mother orders it, they answered evasively. “Of course,” he said at once. “My, namaskara to Mother. I must obey. Let us go.” They then carried the bed out, and the Mother stood on her balcony and looked down on him and all over his body Trigunatita was writing in Ganges-mud the name of Sri R.K. [ Ramakrishna] and then of Krishna and other gods –but he watched the finger moving and saw the words. “No” he said, “rub them all off but the One

– I have lived in that Name, and it is enough to die in.” And when they had done this, he looked farewell to the Mother and they bore him away. And all the way, going, he chatted pleasantly but when they reached the river side, he died. It seemed so natural to me that all the time they were at the Ganges ghat on Tuesday a great storm raged and howled. Swami was safe by that time in the Math, and it seemed fitting that the wind should offer its great chariots of music to carry the departing soul. ...

Margot

... This death probably means that the Mother will be going back to her village shortly, for 6 months or a year.

M

And now in the next few letters we read an unchanging message.

Wednesday [10.4.1899]

My Sweet Yum [Miss J. MacLeod ],

... The Mother sends her love, her blessings and her wishes for good health to ‘Sara and Joy.’

April 19th 1899

My Sweet Grannie [Mrs. Ole Bull ],

... The Mother’s love and blessings.

16 Bosepara Lane,

Bagh Bazar, Calcutta

April 26th [1899]

My Sweet Grannie [Mrs. Ole Bull ],

... The Mother sends her love and birthday blessings. The death of Joginanda has seen a terrible blow to her and to Jogin Ma. She cannot now bear the sound of the word die. It has been such human grief. “Yes, he has gone to my Lord,” she said, “I know that. But it was my Joginanda, and he was taken away from me!”

Thursday [27.4.1899]

My Sweet Yum [Miss J. MacLeod]

... The Mother sends love and blessings. ...

And now we have a beautiful picture to meditate upon :

May 2nd [1899]

My Sweet Nell [Mrs. Eric Hammond],

... All round gongs are beating and bells are ringing, for it is the time of evening worship – I go up to my roof and lie there quietly to watch the stars come out and when I come down I shall talk to you again. ...

I call it the Hour of Peace – One seems to settle all one’s difficulties there – but tonight I have been called down – So I shall wait till bed time now. The idea of this worship is that ‘Candle-light’ has just begun, and when the servants bring up the lights the ladies in the zenana prostrate before a sacred picture or an image, and then it is the use of Sarada Devi’s household, which is really a convent, to go to meditation. For an hour or two before, you will see some of the ladies counting their rosaries quietly, while the Mother sits chatting with anyone who is there. ...

Yours lovingly

Margaret E.N.

And gradually Nivedita seems to grow a little in her understanding of what the Holy Mother really was :

C/o Srimati Sarada Devi

8, Bosepara Lane, Calcutta

June 18th [1899]

Sunday early

My sweet Yum [Miss J. MacLeod],

... How Sweet of Sri R.K. [ Ramakrishna] to let the mails come this morning. I am keeping Ekadasi – just for fun. Clothed in a white sari and spending the whole day with mother. And in these hours I sat down to write letters. ...

... which reminds me – what the Mother is – is only drawing on me now. You should have heard her defend Sadananda against horrid aspersion the other day! And when my zenana article comes out you will realize what it meant when she said quietly that in giving us the poses Santoshini’s mother had helped her.

Margot

Then Nivedita had to leave for England and America to get funds for work. From there she wrote frequently to the Mother; the Mother sometimes told Swami Saradananda to convey her blessings and sometimes even dictated a letter to be sent to her ‘Baby’. Here is a letter from Swami Saradananda to Miss J. MacLeod :

27th July 1899

Belur Math, Howrah, India

... I went with Margot’s letter to act as an interpreter to Sarada Devi, the other day. ...

Saradananda

And another from him to Nivedita :

Math, Belur, Howrah, India

16 November 1899

... The Holy Mother always sends for love and blessings to you and all those. ... Saradananda

A letter from Nivedita to Miss Mary Hale :

112 Lincoln Park, Boulevard, Chicago

Sunday afternoon [28.12.1899 ?]

... I wanted to give you a photograph of Sarada Devi – but will have to get new ones as I have none left. ...

Your loving niece

Margot

Letter from Swami Saradananda to Sister Nivedita :

Math, Belur, Howrah, India

April 11th, 1990

The Holy Mother is well and has written a beautiful letter to you. I send you the original as well as the translation for I know it will gladden your heart.

[Letter from Holy Mother to Sister Nivedita]

Jairambati 21st Chaitra

[probably 13.5.1900]

Sri Sri Gurupada bharasa –

May this letter carry all blessings! My dear love to you, Baby daughter Nivedita! I am so glad to learn that you have prayed to the Lord for my eternal place. You are a manifestation of the ever blissful Mother. I look to your photograph which is with me every now and then. And it seems as if you are present with me. I long for the day and the year when you shall return. May the prayers you have uttered for me from the heart of your pure virgin soul be answered! I am well and happy. I always pray the Lord to help you in your efforts and keep you strong and happy. I pray too for your quick return. May He fulfill your desire about the women’s home in India, and may the would be home fulfill its mission in teaching true dharma to all.

He, the Breath of the Universe, is singing His own praise, and you are hearing that eternal song through things that will come to an end. The trees, the birds, the hills and all are singing praise to the Lord. The Banyan of Dukineswar [Dakshineswar] sings of Kali to be sure, and blessed is he who has ears to hear it.

I was so glad to hear of the faith of Mrs. Waterman. She who thinks she has not lost her beloved, even after the fall of the body, has really attained to light; for the soul can never die, even when the body falls. I am glad to hear that it has strengthened her to hear of me. May she be a help to your work. My love and blessings to Mrs. May Wright Sewall. My dear love to you and blessings and prayers for your spiritual growth. You are indeed doing good work – but do not forget your Bengali! Or I shall not be able to understand you when you come back. It gave me such delight to know that you are speaking of Dhruba, Savitri, Sita-Ram and so on there!

The accounts of these holy lives are better than all the vain talk of the world! I am sure. Oh how beautiful are the Name and the doings of the Lord!

[Sister Nivedita’s comment ]

‘Oh what a sweet soul !’ – said Mr. Waterman, when I finished reading this last night, and I thought his words the finest expression of the quality.

My Sweet Granny,

I am sure you will be pleased with this letter, from the Holy Mother. ... Margot

## SWAMI PITAMBARANANDA

With the help of (i) mainly – the two volumes of letters of Sister Nivedita, edited by Prof. Sankari Prasad Basu, (ii) important extracts from the unpublished third volume and other material used by him in his article ‘Niveditar Dhruvamandire’ included in the Bengali book Shatarupe Sarada, (iii) some other articles from the same book, and (iv) the complete works of Sister Nivedita, published by the Advaita Ashrama, Calcutta, we have seen in the first part of this study that Nivedita’s first meeting with Sri Sarada Devi took place on March 17, 1898. In a letter written on May 22, 1898, i.e. two months after this first visit, Nivedita assessed the Holy Mother as one of the strongest and greatest of women and after five-and-a-half years she declared her to be ‘the greatest woman in the world today’. And in the letter of June 18, 1899, she has herself acknowledged – ‘what the mother is – is only dawning on me now.’ We concluded the previous part with the observation that the evolution of Nivedita’s understanding regarding Sri Sarada Devi from one of the greatest of women, to the greatest woman in the world today, was only the first step. Now let us see how far and further it went and what more facets of the divinely human personality of the mother were revealed to Nivedita. If we study Nivedita’s letters of the two years 1904 and 1905, we find that an unparallelled facet of the personality of the Holy Mother is continually impressing itself on Nivedita’s mind. There is nothing unchanging in this evanescent world. On the other hand, God, the infinite, the partless, the one-without-a-second, Existence-Consciousness-Bliss Absolute, though ever new, is eternal and unchanging. And the personality of Sri Sarada Devi, identified with the Absolute in her Consciousness, is similarly unchangingly same and ever sweet.

Let us have a look at the letters of this period :

Two or three things strike us most while going through these letters. First and foremost, there is this most covetable unchanging ‘state of Brahman’. Second is the evolution of Nivedita’s understanding of the Holy Mother whether it is ‘one of the greatest of women’ or ‘the greatest woman in the world today’ – these are assessments drawn from comparison with women in this world. But that the personality of the mother is incomparable, that is the ‘ideal’ to be followed by all – this is what we see coming home to Nivedita in these letters. The ‘ideal’ is not of this world but above it and we have to evolve by keeping our sight fixed on it. And what sort of an ideal is presented by Mother? Ideal Hindu, ‘ideal disciple’ – no, no

- ‘the ideal woman of all place and time’ – Nivedita seems to realize now that ‘SHE’ is the ideal woman. And the third thing which is obviously happening is Nivedita’s soul as expressed in her words, ‘She grows dearer and dearer’.

Brahman, which is Existence-Knowledge-Bliss to the philosophers, is Existing- Shining-Dear to the people of realization. Which means that they experience it to be existing unchangingly; to them It shines as It is ‘made of knowledge’; and it grows dearest to them due to Its Bliss-nature. Isn’t something like this emerging from Nivedita’s experience of the Mother’s unchanging-ness, the idealness in her personality shining on account of perfection of knowledge, and her growing dearer and dearer?

Sister Nivedita has very ably presented to the world a picture of the Holy Mother pertaining to the period 1898 to 1906, through her almost fully developed insight as described above, in the tenth chapter of her book The Master as I Saw Him, written during 1906-1907. Let us now see this masterly description and analysis of the various facets of the great

personality of the Holy Mother.2 This chapter has been named by Nivedita as ‘Calcutta and the Holy Women’. The paragraphs relevant to our study are given below :

## A GUEST SELF- INVITED

I arrived in Calcutta, alone, in the beginning of November [1898]. I was able to find my way at once, from the station to the north end of the town. But once there, with insular rigidity, I insisted on being made the guest of women. The Swami was himself staying, as it happened, at a sort of parish room of the order, in Calcutta. Through him, therefore, the negotiations were carried on. The widow of Sri Ramakrishna – Sarada Devi, or the ‘Holy Mother,’ as she is called amongst us – was living close by, with her community of ladies and in the course of the day, I was accorded possession of an empty room in her house. This is one of the occasions on which people look back, feeling that their courage was providentially determined by their ignorance. It is difficult to see how else a necessary solution could have been found. Yet, had I deeply understood at that time the degree of social embarrassment which my rashness might have brought, not only upon my innocent hostess but also on her kindred in their distant village, I could not have acted as I did. At any cost, I must in that case have withdrawn. As it was, however I imagined caste to be only a foolish personal prejudice – which must yield to knowledge – against some supposed uncleanliness of foreign habits, and thus cheerfully assuming all the ignorance to be on her side, confidently forced myself upon this Indian lady’s hospitality.

In the event, fortunately, the Swami’s influence proved all powerful, and I was accepted by society. Within a week or ten days, a house in the close neighborhood was found for me. But even then, I spent all my afternoons in the Mother’s room and when the hot weather came, it was by her express command that I returned to her better arranged house, for sleeping quarters. And then I occupied no room apart, but shared the cool and simple dormitory of the others with its row of mats, pillows and nets, against the polished red earthenware of the floor.

## THE MOTHER’S HOME

It was a strange household, of which I now found myself a part. Downstairs, in one of the guard-rooms beside the front door, lived a monk, whose severe austerities, from his youth up, had brought him to the threshold of death, from consumption, in the prime of manhood. To his room I used to go, for Bengali lessons. In the kitchen behind, worked a disciple of his, and a Brahmin cook; while to us women-folk belonged all above stairs, with roofs, terraces, and the sight of Ganges hard by.

Of the head of our little community, it seems almost presumptuous to speak. Her history is well-known. How she was wedded at five, and forgotten by her husband till she was eighteen; how she then, with her mother’s permission, made her way on foot from her village home to the temple of Dakshineswar on the Ganges-side, and appeared before him; how he remembered the bond, but spoke of the ideals of the life he had adopted; and how she responded by bidding him Godspeed in that life, and asking only to be taught by him as the Guru – all these things have been told of her many times over. From that time she lived faithfully by his side for many years, in a building in the same garden, at once nun and wife, and always chief of his disciples. She was young when her tutelage began and in hours of quiet talk, she will tell sometimes in how many directions his training extended. He was a great lover of order, and taught her even such trifles as where to keep her lamp and its appurtenances, during the day. He could not endure squalor, and notwithstanding severe This is probably the first pen-picture of the Mother to appear in print.

asceticism, he loved grace and beauty and gentle dignity of bearing. One story that is told of this period of her life, is of her bringing to him a basket of fruit and vegetables one day, with all the eagerness and pride of a happy child. He looked at it gravely, and said, ‘But why so extravagant?’

## SRI RAMAKRISHNA’S LOVE

“At least it was not for myself” said the young wife, all her sunshine gone, in sudden disappointment, and she turned and went away, crying quietly. But this Sri Ramakrishna could not bear to see. “Go, one of you,” he said, turning to the boys beside him, “and bring her back. My very devotion to God will take wings if I see her weep!” So dear she was to him. Yet one of her most striking traits is the absolute detachment with which she speaks of the husband she worships. She stands like a rock, through cloud and shine, as those about her tell, for the fulfilment of every word of his. But ‘Guru Deb!’ ‘Divine Master,’ is the name she calls him by, and not one word of her uttering ever conveys the slightest trace of self-assertion with regard to him. One who did not know who she was would never suspect, from speech of hers, that her right was stronger, or her place closer, than that of any other of those about her, it would seem as if the wife had been long ago forgotten, save for her faithfulness, in the disciple. Yet so deeply is she reverenced by all about her, that there is not one of them who would, for instance, occupy a railway berth above her, when traveling with her. Her very presence is to them a consecration.

## THE IDEAL WOMAN

To me it has always appeared that she is Sri Ramakrishna’s final word as to the ideal of Indian womanhood. But is she the last of an old order, or the beginning of a new? In her, one sees realized that wisdom and sweetness to which the simplest of woman may attain. And yet, to myself the stateliness of her courtesy and her great open mind are almost as wonderful as her sainthood. I have never known her hesitate, in giving utterance to large and generous judgment, however new or complex might be the question put before her. Her life is one long stillness of prayer. Her whole experience is of theocratic civilization. Yet she rises to the height of every situation. Is she tortured by perversity of any about her? The only sign is a strange quiet and intensity that comes upon her. Does one carry to her some perplexity or mortification born of social developments beyond her ken? With unerring intuition, she goes straight to the heart of the matter, and sets the questioner in the true attitude to the difficulty. Or is there need for severity? No foolish sentimentality causes her to waver. The novice whom she may condemn, for so many years to beg his bread, will leave the place within the hour. He who has transgressed her code of delicacy and honour will never enter her presence again. “Can’t you see, said Sri Ramakrishna, to one who had erred in some such way, can’t you see that the woman in her is wounded? And that is dangerous!”

And yet she is, as one of her spiritual chidren said of her, speaking literally of her gift of song, ‘full of music’, all gentleness, all playfulness. And the room wherein she worships, withal is filled with sweetness.

## SARADA DEVI’S CULTURE

The Mother can read and much of her time is passed with her Ramayana. But she does not write. Yet it is not to be supposed that she is an uneducated woman. Not only has she had long and arduous experience in administration, secular and religious; but she has also traveled over a great part of India visiting most of the chief places of pilgrimage. And it must be remembered that as the wife of Sri Ramakrishna, she has had the highest opportunity of

personal development that it is possible to enjoy. At every moment, she bears unconscious witness to this association with the great. But in nothing perhaps does it speak mare loudly than in her instant power to penetrate any religious feeling or idea. I first realized this gift in Holy Mother on the occasion of a visit that she paid us in recent years, on the afternoon of a certain Easter Day. Before that, probably, I had always been too much absorbed, when with her, in striving to learn what she represented, to think of observing her in the contrary position. On this particular occasion, however, after going over our whole house, the Mother and her party expressed a desire to rest in the chapel, and hear something of the meaning of the Christian festival. This was followed by Easter music, and singing, with our small French organ. And in the swiftness of her comprehension, and the depth of her sympathy with these resurrection hymns, unimpeded by any foreignness or unfamiliarity in them, we saw revealed for the first time, one of the most impressive aspects of the great religious culture of Sarada Devi. The same power is seen to a certain extent, in all the women about her, who were touched by the hand of Sri Ramakrishna. But in her, it has all the strength and certainly of some high and arduous form of scholarship. The same trait came out again one evening when, in the midst of her little circle, the Holy Mother asked my Guru-bhagini and myself, to describe to her a European wedding. With much fun and laughter personating now the ‘Christian Brahmin’, and again the bride and bridegroom, we complied. But we were neither of us prepared for the effect of the marriage vow.

## THE MARRIAGE VOW

‘For better for worse, for richer for poorer, in sickness and in health – till death us do part,’ wire words that drew exclamations of delight from all about us. But none appreciated them as did the Mother. Again and again she had them repeated to her. “Oh the Dharmik words! the righteous words!!”

We see three important points in this unique delineation which is the result of Nivedita’s highly developed perceptions. First is the statement ‘To me it has always appeared that she is Sri Ramakrishna’s final word as to the ideal of Indian womanhood’. This should not be taken to mean that Nivedita is circumscribing Mother’s personality by calling her the ideal for ‘Indian’ womanhood only because, before she made this statement in her writings of 1906-1907, i.e. in her letters of 1904 itself, she has unequivocally called her the ‘ideal woman of all place and time’ – rather ‘the ideal woman’. Hence when we try to reconcile these two types of statements we are led to the conclusion that being the disciple of the great Swami Vivekananda, Nivedita had heard from him and was naturally convinced that it was India’s providential role to set up spiritual ideals before the world and hence ‘the ideal of Indian womanhood’ meant the ‘spiritual ideal for world’s womanhood’. And this was the Holy Mother.

Along with this, we see what seems to be Nivedita’s question : ‘But is she the last of an old order, or the beginning of a new?’ Of course, any discerning reader knows that it is not really a question or an expression of doubt, but rather a meaningful proclamation put in a question form, for has Nivedita not already said that the Mother is the ideal woman of all place and time? Thus it is clear that Sister Nivedita is enchanted by the ideal in Holy Mother’s personality which is not confined within the limits of any time or country and which is complete in all respects.

And yet some idealistic sons of the Holy Mother feel that Nivedita is limiting the ideals manifested in the Mother by calling her the ideal of ‘womanhood’. They ask, “why can’t we, the ‘men’ – ‘sons of the Mother’ – emulate her?’ The answer is that the Sister is

not putting any restrictions on us but, being herself a ‘woman,’ is simply confining herself to speaking of her own kind.

The second important point emerging from the revealing per-picture so ably drawn by Nivedita is the Holy Mother’s unobstructed range of comprehension in spiritual field – in the field of true religious ideas and ideals – that there is nothing alien or unfamiliar to her in this field.

This is a very natural facet of the actual mission of Sri Ramakrishna and Sri Sarada Devi. It is this which would establish the harmony of religions. The Holy Mother, with her insight going to the very root, herself says while talking about Sri Ramakrishna, that the harmony of religions is not established by any ‘planning,’ but it is supreme renunciation which enables a person to live with God always and in all conceivable ways, which in its turn naturally brings about the harmony of all religions.3 It is this universality which has incarnated itself in the twin forms of Sri Ramakrishna and Sri Sarada Devi. The third point, the wonderfully significant aspect of the Holy Mother’s personality which stunned and enchanted the Sister, is also an offshoot of this universality or limitlessness. It is the unhindered vision or clear transparent insight of the Motor not only in the spiritual domain but even in social and all other dimensions of human problems related to the understanding of the functions of human mind. The Holy Mother’s expansive under-standing or ‘unerring intuition’, unobstructed by any walls, goes straight to the heart of the matter. This modest woman, who always kept her own face covered with a veil, this self-veiled Divinity in the form of Mother, had a crystal pure faculty of understanding, a transparent insight, which was never blocked or covered by any veil which separates persons by place or time or the feelings of own-alien, native-foreigner, etc. Remarkable indeed! And if we wish to understand this phenomenon, we can draw light from a section on Infinitude in the Chhandogya Upanishad, where Sanatkumara tells Narada : “That alone is Infinite where there is no otherness – what is below, that is above, and ... that is everything.”4 Such was the infinitude of the Holy Mother and her unobstructed insight. Thus we have seen the evolution of Nivedita’s understanding of the Holy Mother from a worldly, comparative level to the level of the transcendental ideal to be universally followed. We have also seen the enchanting pen-picture of the Mother so ably drawn by the highly developed insight of Sister Nivedita. Does anything more remain to be said ? That we shall see in the last part of this article.

See the Gospel of the Holy Mother, (Madras : Sri Ramakrishna Math, 1986), 395-96. Chandogya Upanisad, 7.24.1 and 7.25.1.
glory-of-sarada-devi-3:
The Glory of Sri Sarada Devi

As Seen by Sister Nivedita

A Chronological Study – (3)

## SWAMI PITAMBARANANDA

We have seen how Nivedita, in a letter written in April 1904, calls Sri Sarada Devi ‘an ideal woman of all place and time’, and also in another dated October 6th 1904, ‘the ideal woman’. We have also seen the complete pen-picture of the Mother drawn by Nivedita with keenly developed insight in a chapter of her book ‘Master as I saw him’ written during 1906- 1907. What remain are Nivedita’s letters of 1909-1911 and some material of which we have not been able to ascertain the dates. What shall we get from these? First, many endearing and touching scenes. Secondly, we shall see the Mother standing, as it were, beyond the ken of Nivedita’s understanding even after it has been stretched to its farthest limit! Of course, we shall also see to what great heights Nivedita’s own life had been lifted by the power that was Mother. So let us first see those letters of Nivedita.

My dear S.Sara [Mrs. Ole Bull],

I have been seeing a good deal of Saradananda lately, over publication – and also because I am beginning to gather facts for the authoritative life of Swamiji. So one seems to be much back in the early days when they used to go to Sri RK at Dukhineswar. And the dear Holy Mother remains as proof and witness of that time. Sept. 22, 1910

Dears [Mr. & Mrs. S.K.Ratcliffe],

... If I ever go to prison for a prolonged period, none of my friends need grieve about it – for I shall immediately take to meditation and try to climb those wonderful heights on which the Holy Mother [Sarada Devi ] lives. Such sweetness and serenity as hers, with such depth of experience and affection, are past all imagining. And how wonderful her life is – she lives in the midst of an elaborate system of worship spontaneously organized and maintained by others, for the adoration of her own Husband, whom she worships as GOD, but cherishes a deep human tenderness for nevertheless. “I loved simply to look at him!” I heard her say the other night! She simply doesn’t seem to regard that branch of criticism as her province.

In all these letters we have seen, apart from beautiful touching scenes, that the Holy Mother and the ideals manifested in her, appear to Nivedita, in a chronologically ascending sequence, as ‘extraordinary’, ‘perfect’, ‘beyond description’ and eventually ‘past all imagining’.

It is what the Taittiriya Upanishad describes as “who realizes the Bliss of Brahman, failing to reach which, words along with the mind turn back!”5

*

The culmination of all this is the inimitable letter written by Nivedita to Holy Mother herself on December 11th, 1910. We had quoted a few sentences from this at the very outset

Taittiriya Upanisad 2.4.1 and 2.9.1

in the first part of this article, and yet let us read the full letter here. Cambridge, Mass

11th Dec. 1910

Beloved Mother [Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi],

This morning, early, I went to church – to pray for Sara. All the people there were thinking of Mary, the Mother of Jesus, and suddenly I thought of you. Your dear face, and your loving look, and your white sari and your bracelets. It was all there. And it seemed to me that yours was the Presence that was to soothe and bless poor S. Sara’s sick room. And do you know? – I thought I had been very foolish to sit in your room, at the evening service to Sri Ramakrishna, trying to meditate – why did I not understand that it was quite enough to be a little child at your dear feet? Dear Mother! you are full of love! And it is not a flushed and violent love, like ours, and like the world’s, but a gentle peace that brings good to everyone and wishes ill to none. It is a golden radiance, full of play. What a blessed Sunday that was, a few months ago, when I ran in to you, the last thing before I went on the Ganges, and ran back to you for a moment, as soon as I came back! I felt such a wonderful freedom in the blessing you gave me, and in your welcome home! Dearest Mother – I wish we could send you a wonderful hymn, or a prayer. But somehow even that would seem too loud, too full of noise! Surely you are the most wonderful thing of God – Sri Ramakrishna’s own chalice of His love for the world – a token left with his children, in these lonely days, and we should be very still and quiet before you – except indeed for a little fun! Surely the ‘wonderful things of God’ are all quiet – stealing unnoticed into our lives – the air and sunlight and the sweetness of gardens and of the Ganges, these are the silent things that are like you! Do send to poor S. Sara the mantle of your peace. Isn’t your thought, now and then, of the high calm that neither loves nor hates? Isn’t that the sweet benediction that trembles in God, like the dew-drop on the lotus-leaf, and touches not the world? Ever, my darling mother, your foolish Khooki,6

Nivedita

Nivedita continued to be in this world for 10 months only after this letter. Two more letters refer to the mother after Nivedita’s return to India.

The Sister departed from this world on 13th of October 1991 at Darjeeling. Our objective of seeing things in a chronological order has been achieved. But why should we not taste the nectar a little more? Let us be blessed by sipping a few more drops gathered from here and there.

First let us see the picture of Nivedita’s service to the Mother.

‘Almost everyday Sister Nivedita used to visit the Holy Mother and take the dust of her feet. On Sundays she would unfailingly come to clean the Mother’s room. Dusting the bed, sweeping the floor, wiping the glass panes of doors and windows with soap and water –

Bengali equivalent of ‘Baby [girl]’

with all these she would make everything clean and shining. Nivedita had taken up this work as her paramount duty. ... She was so very alert for providing even the smallest convenience or comfort to the Mother.’

And how was this service accepted by the Mother? –

‘One day Nivedita herself cooked food, offered it to Sri Ramakrishna in the temple, and gave a portion of it to the mother who accepted it with great delight and partook of it. This created a furor in the circle of tradition-bound women and they even criticized the Mother harshly for it. Disgusted with that attitude, the Mother remarked, "Nivedita is my daughter. She has the right to offer food to our dear Lord; the food thus sanctified shall be accepted by me most gladly and without any hitch; if anyone finds anything improper in it, let them keep their own counsel.”8

‘The Mother treasured whatever she received from Nivedita. Once she had given her a small German-silver box in which the Mother kept Sri Ramakrishna’s hair and said, “When I worship it, I will remember Nivedita.” A scarf presented by Nivedita was carefully preserved by her in a trunk even after it was in rags and if someone suggested that it might be thrown away she said, “Don’t throw it away. Let it be. Nivedita lovingly gave it to me. I am reminded of her whenever I see it. What a wonderful person she was! ...”9 And what happened if the Mother herself gave her something as a token of affection? –

‘Sister Nivedita now came in, bowed to the Holy Mother and took her seat. The Holy Mother enquired after her welfare, and gave her a woolen fan made by herself saying, “I kept this for you.” The sister was very happy to receive it. She put it on her head, touched it to her heart and said, “How beautiful, how wonderful.” She showed it to us and said, “Just see how beautifully it is made!” The Holy Mother said appreciatively, “Do you notice her happiness upon receiving some small present!”10

Not only did Nivedita feel extremely happy in Holy Mother’s company but she used to become like a small baby and completely lose herself in love and bliss in her presence. Let us see two or three pictures of this ecstatic joy :

‘The Holy Mother used to stay now and then in the Udbodhan building in Bagh Bazar. Sister Nivedita and Sister Christine used to spend some time at least once every day with her there. Nivedita used to constantly look at Holy Mother’s face as a young baby would look at her mother’s. Sister Nivedita, a woman as brilliant as whom is rarely found in this world, by looking at the penetrative vision of whose eyes shining with light of intelligence one felt that it can solve any mystery in this universe, the same Nivedita when seen sitting near Sri Sarada Devi would appear to be a small girl of five, innocent, depending wholly on the Mother. When the Mother looked at her with an affectionate smile, she would totally melt like a baby being caressed by her mother. The day when she would get the privilege of spreading the seat for the Holy Mother, her joy would be indescribable – one could only realize it if one looked at her. She would kiss the seat several times and dust it very solicitously before spreading it; her expressions would reveal that she was finding the very fulfillment of life in being allowed to do that service for the mother.’11 Once Lakshmi Devi, the niece of Sri Ramakrishna, gladdened every one’s heart for some days consecutively. … Nivedita one day took on the role of a four legged lion and seating Lakshmi Devi on her back like the Goddess Jagaddhatri, began to roar like a lion. The Holy Mother and other ladies were beside themselves with laughter.’12 ‘Once it was decided that the Holy Mother would visit the school. On getting that
