forms-of-god:
Shri Ramakrishna, Shri Sarada Devi & Swami Vivekananda

On

Forms of GOD, Idol-Worship etc. etc.

-- Sw. Pitambarananda, Ramakrishna Kutir, Rishikesh

Q.1 Has anyone seen God in the form of Krishna, Rama, Shiva or is it just the image formed in the mind of people and they are following it blindly?

Answer : (a) Even today there are many people, I know, who see God in the form of Krishna or Rama or Shiva or ... Ramakrishna , some times even without their seeking to see God in that form. Let us first see some pages of recent history --

"Some time passed that way. Ramawat ‘fathers’ (Babajis) -- men of fervent renunciation, devout and dispassionate ... -- began to pour in. ... It was from one of them that ‘Ramlala’[A metal image depicting child Rama] came to me. ... That ‘father’ served the image for a long time. He took it with him wherever he went. He cooked whatever he got by Bhiksha and offered the cooked food to it. That was not all; he actually saw that Ramlala ate or wished to eat something or wanted to go for a walk or insisted on the satisfaction of a fancy, and so on. ... I also saw Ramlala doing all that. ... As days passed on, Ramlala’s love for me went on increasing. ... I actually saw -- just as I see you before me -- that Ramlala accompanied me. ... On some days the holy ‘father’ would cook food and offer it to Ramlala but could not find him. ... He would then run up here (to Sri Ramakrishna’s room) and find him playing in the room. ... he used to drag Ramlala to his place and feed him. ... The ‘father’ then came one day and said, ‘Ramlala ... has quenched the thirst of my life. My mind is now free from sorrow and pain. ... He lives happily with you and plays and sports; I am now in such a state that I feel happy at his happiness. Therefore, I can now leave him with you and go elsewhere. ...’ saying so and giving Ramlala to me he bade goodbye. Ramlala has been here since then." (Sri Ramakrishna The Great Master, P 526-531) Here everything is objectively real and much more real than the things of the world!

(ii) "The garden-house of Yadunath Mallick is situated to the south of the Kali temple at Dakshineshwar; the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) used to go there now and then for a walk. ... The officers would open the door of the parlour and ask him to sit and rest there for sometime. There were some good pictures hanging on the walls of that room. One of those pictures was that of the child Jesus in his mother’s lap. The Master used to say that he sat one day in that parlour and was looking at the picture ... when he felt that the picture came to life. ... The Master came back to Dakshineshwar temple. ... At last, when the third day was about to close, The Master saw, while walking under the Panchvati, that a marvellous god-man of very fair complexion was coming towards him, looking steadfastly at him. As soon as the Master saw that person, he knew that he was a foreigner. He saw that his long eyes had produced a wonderful beauty in his face, and the tip of his nose, though a little flat, did not at all impair that beauty ... and from the bottom of the Master’s pure heart came out with a ringing sound, the words, ‘Jesus!’ ... When we were visiting the Master long after this event, one day he raised the topic of Jesus and said, ‘Well, boys, you have read the Bible; can you tell me what is written in it about the physical features of Jesus? How did he look? We said, ‘Sir, We have not seen this mentioned anywhere in the Bible; but as he was born a jew, he must have been very fair in complexion, with long eyes and an aquiline nose to be sure.’... The Master said,’But I saw that the tip of his nose was a little flat; I don’t know why I saw him like that.’ (Because that is not what we see in the available paintings.) ... We thought, ‘How could be the form seen by him in ecstasy tally with the actual form of Jesus?’. But we came to know, shortly after the Master passed away, that there were ... descriptions of Jesus’s

physical features; according to one of them the tip of his nose was a little flat.’ (G.M. P.295- 296). (So when the actual person is seen, the photos etc. are left behind.)

(iii) Sri Ramakrishna told Narendranath "... over and over again, ‘God always hears the plaintive prayer of man and he can be seen, heard and touched palpably, being more real than the fact of this conversation of ours. I stake my credit on this.’ On another occasion he said to him, ‘If you cannot accept the form of God or the common well known ideas about Him because they are the products of human thought, but at the same time have faith in the existence of a God, the controller of the universe, He will certainly bestow His grace on you if you offer such a plaintive prayer as this, "O God, I don’t know Thy nature; please manifest Thyself to me as Thou really art".’ ... (Basing upon these instructions) Narendra adopted a new method of practising meditation from that time on. We have already said that in our meditation on the Lord, with or without forms, we can but think of Him anthropomorphically (i.e. through modes of the human mind). ... Coming to this conclusion ... he prayed to the effect; ‘O God, make me fit to see your real nature.’ He then removed all kinds of thought from his mind and keeping it still and motionless like the flame of a lamp in a windless place, tried to remain in that state. ... Narendra described -- ‘There flowed in my mind a current of serene bliss when I kept it still, devoid of all objects. I felt for a long time even after the end of the meditation, a sort of intoxication under its impulse. ... One day, when I was sitting in that condition at the end of the meditation, I saw the extraordinary figure of a monk appear suddenly, from where I did not know, and stand before me at a little distance filling the room with a divine effulgence ... as if he wanted to say something. ... That face has been indelibly imprinted in my heart. ... Very often it comes to mind that I had the good fortune of seeing Lord Buddha that day’." (Great Master P.797-798) [When God incarnated himself as the Buddha, he had practised same type of meditation, and that is why, perhaps, he wanted to share some of his experience with Swami Vivekananda!]

(iv) "... Oblivious of surroundings, the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) one day was pacing up and down the verandah extending east to west, to the north-east of his room in the complex of the temple where he was serving as a Pujari, Mathur (who was almost the proprietor of that temple -- a worldly man, sceptical and yet a devotee) was then sitting by himself in one of the rooms of the separate house. ... The place where the Master was pacing was within an easy range of vision from where Mathur was sitting. ... But the event turned out to be something unthinkable and incomprehensible, for Mathur himself ran up in a great flurry to the Master and started weeping. ... Afterwards ... he said, ‘Father, you were walking, and I saw distinctly that it was not you but my Mother in the temple (the Goddess Kali) over there as you were coming forward in this direction and that it was Mahadeva (God Shiva) Himself immediately when you turned about. I thought at first that it was an optical illusion; I rubbed my eyes well and looked, but saw the same thing. This happened as often as I looked.’"(Great Master P. 433)

(ii) "On 24 September 1926 Swami Shivananda (A disciple of Sri Ramakrishna) inaugurated the building of the new ashrama in Ootacamund. Later he recited this incident: ‘One year I visited the Nilgiri Hills. Learning that I was there, a Muslim doctor and his family came all the way from Bombay to see me. ... He had been educated in England and had a very good practice. He was accompanied by his wife. ... The doctor said to me, "... my wife is particularly eager to speak to you." ... His wife saluted me with great devotion, and disclosed many intimate things relating to her spiritual life. ... She worships the child Krishna and occasionally has visions of him. ... It is her conviction that her chosen deity, Krishna, has been born as Ramakrishna.’(God Lived with them, P.165)

Q.2 How did people get the idea of praying to Idols? Is it correct to worship idols? Should we believe in idol-worship?

Answer : Some funny confusion seems to have engulfed the Indians due to modern education, grossness of the mind, and ignorance of the ways of mind.

(a) Let us see what Swami Vivekananda has to say.

(i) It was in Rajasthan that Thakur Mangal Singhji, the Maharaja of Alwar, who had become much anglicised, asked, "Well, Swamiji Maharaj, I have no faith in idol worship. What is going to be my fate?" He smiled as he spoke ..."You see, I really cannot worship wood, earth, stone or metal like other people. Does this mean that I shall fare worse in the life hereafter?" The Swami answered, "Well, I suppose every man should follow the religious ideal according to his own faith."... his eyes lighted on a picture of the Maharaja which was hanging on the wall. The Swami commanded the Dewan: "spit on it" ... The Dewan cried out, "What, Swamiji! What are you asking me to do? This is the likeness of our Maharaja! How can I do such a thing?" ... Turning to the Maharaja the Swami continued, "See, your Highness; though this is not you in one sense, in another sense it is you. That was why your devoted servants were so perplexed when I asked them to spit on it. It is a shadow of you; it brings you into their minds. One glance at it makes them see you in it; therefore they look at it with as much respect as they would have in looking at your own person. Thus it is also with the devotees who worship stone and metal images of gods and goddesses. It is because an image brings to their minds their Ishta (that particular aspect of God which is most suitable for that individual), or some special forms and attributes of the Divinity, and helps them to concentrate, that the devotees worship God in an image. They do not worship the stone or the metal as such.

"I have travelled in many places, but nowhere have I found a single Hindu worshipping an image, saying, ‘O Stone, I worship Thee. O Metal, be merciful to me.’ Everyone, Maharaja, is worshipping the same one God who is the Supreme Spirit, the Soul of Pure Knowledge. And God appears to all according to their understanding and their representation of Him. Prince, I speak for myself. Of course, I cannot speak for you." Mangal Singhji, who had been listening attentively all this time, said, with folded hands, "Swamiji, I must admit that, looking at image worship in the light you have thrown on it, I have never met anyone who worshipped stone, or wood, or metal. Before this I did not understand its meaning. You have opened my eyes. ..." (Life of SW.V. Vol.I P.268-270)

(ii) And see what happened in Jaipur. Sardar Hari Singh, the Commander-In-Chief of the state ... did not believe in the value of images, and even after hours of discussion with the Swami remained unconvinced. In the evening they went out for a walk. As they were going along the footpath they came upon some devotees carrying the image of Sri Krishna and singing devotional songs as they went. The Swami and the Sardar watched the procession for a while. Suddenly the Swami touched Hari Singh and said, "Look there, see the living God!" The eyes of the sardar fell on the image of Lord Krishna, and he stood there transfixed, with tears of ecstasy trickling down his cheeks. When he returned to ordinary consciousness, he exclaimed, "Well, Swamiji, that was a revelation to me. What I could not understand after hours of discussion, was easily comprehended through your touch. Truly, I saw the Lord in the image of Krishna!" (ibid P. 278)

(b) And hence says Swami Vivekananda -- (i) All men are born idolaters. The lowest man is an animal. The highest man is perfect. And between these two, all have to think in sound and colour, in doctrine and ritual. The test of having ceased to be an idolater is : when you say ‘I’, does the body come into your thought or not? If it does, then you are still a worshipper of idols. (C.W.of Sw.V.,Vol.8, P.229-230)

(ii) The man who is bowing down before the idol; ... It is peculiar to the Hindus. The man is before the idol, and he shuts his eyes and tries to think, "I am He; I have neither life nor death; I have neither father nor mother; I am not bound by time or space; I am Existence

infinite, Bliss infinite and Knowledge infinite; I am He, I am He." ... this he repeats and then says, "O Lord, I cannot conceive Thee in myself; I am a poor man." ... You may take the most learned man you have and ask him to think of spirit as spirit; he cannot ... It is impossible to think of spirit without training. (Vol.8,P 210-211)

(iii) Among the Jews, idol worship is condemned, but they had a temple in which was kept a chest which they called an ark, in which the Tables of the Law were preserved, and above the chest were two figures of angels with wings outstretched, between which the Divine Presence was supposed to manifest itself as a cloud. That temple has long since been destroyed, but the new temples are made exactly after the old fashion, and in the chest religious books are kept. The Roman Catholics and the Greek Christians have idol-worship in certain forms. The image of Jesus and that of his mother are worshipped. Among Protestants there is no idol-worship, yet they worship God in a personal form, which may be called idol-worship in another form. Among Parsees and Iranians fire-worship is carried on to a great extent. Among Mohammedans the prophets and great and noble persons are worshipped, and they turn their faces towards the Caaba when they pray. These things show that men at the first stage of religious development have to make use of something external, and when the inner self becomes purified they turn to more abstract conceptions. "When the Jiva is sought to be united with Brahman it is best, when meditation is practised it is mediocre, repetition of names is the lowest form, and external worship is the lowest of the low." But it should be distinctly understood that even in practising the last there is no sin. Everybody ought to do what he is able to do; and if he be dissuaded from that, he will do it in some other way in order to attain his end. So we should not speak ill of a man who worships idols. He is in that stage of growth, and, therefore, must have them; wise men should try to help forward such men and get them to do better. But there is no use in quarrelling about these various sorts of worship. (Vol.3, P.362-363)

(iv) It has become a trite saying that idolatry is wrong, and every man swallows it at the present time without questioning. I once thought so, and to pay the penalty of that I had to learn my lesson sitting at the feet of a man who realised everything through idols; I allude to Ramakrishna Paramahansa. If such Ramakrishna Paramahansas are produced by idol worship, what will you have -- the reformer’s creed or any number of idols? I want an answer. Take a thousand idols more if you can produce Ramakrishna Paramahansas through idol-worship, and may God speed you! Produce such noble natures by any means you can. Yet idolatry is condemned! Why? Nobody knows. Because some hundreds of years ago some man of Jewish blood happened to condemn it? That is, he happened to condemn everybody else’s idols except his own. If God is represented in any beautiful form or any symbolic form, said the Jew, it is awfully bad; it is sin. But if He is represented in the form of a chest, with two angels sitting on each side, and a cloud hanging over it, it is the holiest of the holy. If God comes in the form of a dove, it is holy. But if He comes in the form of a cow, it is heathen superstition; condemn it! That is how the world goes. That is why the poet says, "what fools we mortals be!" (Vol.3,P.218)

(c) And what then is Sri Ramakrishna’s final advice? --

1. While raising a building, the scaffolding is indispensable; but when the work is completed, no one feels the necessity of it. So also image-worship is necessary in the beginning but not afterwards.

2. A marksman learns to shoot by first having big objects to shoot at; and as he acquires more and more facility in shooting, he aims more and more easily at the smaller marks on the target. So when the mind has been trained to focus on images having forms, it is easy for it do so on things having no form.

3. As a toy fruit or a toy elephant reminds one of the real fruit and the living animal, so do the images that are worshipped remind one of God who is formless and eternal.

4. You were talking of images made of clay. There arises a necessity for them too. These various forms used for worship have been provided to suit the needs of different men at different stages of spiritual evolution.

5. Why call it an earthen image? The Divine image is made of spirit (consciousness) .

6. Why do these images rouse the idea of mud and clay, stone and straw, in your mind? Why can you not realise the presence of the eternal, blissful, all-conscious Mother (The Supreme Reality) even in these forms.?

7. If a worshipper is convinced that the images of the Deity in the shape of various gods and goddesses are verily divine, he reaches God through their worship. But if he holds them to be nothing better than mud and straw and clay, to him the worship of such images does no good.

8. If there is anything wrong in image-worship, does He not know that all worship is meant for Him? He will surely be pleased to accept that worship, knowing that it is meant for Him alone. Love God; that is the duty nearest to you.

9. When one sees God, one realises that everything, images and all, is a manifestation of the Spirit. To him the image is not made of clay but of spirit (consciousness). (Sayings of Sri Ramakrishna,P.100-101)

Now we are in a position to find answers to all questions on idol worship by ourselves.

Q.3 Is it necessary to offer Prasad to God? How does He accept it?

Answer : Let us correct our language a little. When we ‘offer’ anything to God, it should be called Naivedya. (Naivedya = offering); it becomes prasad (sanctified food) only after God has accepted it.

(a) God has created the world; God has created everything in the world; God has created us; God has created our capacity to do anything; God has created food; God has created the capacity in us to eat food. Everything is God’s. Everything belongs to God. If we understand this thoroughly, should we not think and feel every time that we owe to God our eating food or enjoying the world or doing things? If we do not, we will be thieves, and our eating etc. will be sinful and we shall be sinful -- says the Bhagavad Gita.(3, 12-13)

(b) If we love anyone really -- do we not feel much more happy by feeding him/her first and then eating the residual? If we do not feel that way, aren’t we too selfish and love our enjoyments more than anything else? Those who ‘love’ God feel that way. And hence they offer everything to God or rather they try to make God eat first before they do so.

(c) Similarly, if you have high regard for some one do you not feel like serving him/her? Those who have highest regard for God feel like this. Offering food etc. becomes a part of those acts of service. All these actions help us to feel the living presence of God.

(d) How does God accept the food offered? Let us read some narration from ‘Sri Ramakrishna The Great Master’ (P.146-147)

" Formerly when he(Sri Ramakrishna) offered cooked food etc, to the Mother (Goddess Kali) he used to see an extraordinary ray of light coming out beaming from Her eyes, touching all the offered articles, taking their essential parts and withdrawing itself again into Her eyes. Now he saw that even before the offering was made, the same Mother sat down to take the offerings in Her very Person, illumining the temple with the effulgence of Her holy person. One day Hriday(Sri Ramakrishna’s nephew) came suddenly at the time of the worship and saw that the Master (Sri Ramakrishna) had taken in his hands an Arghya

consisting of Chinaroses and Bilva Leaves, which he was going to offer to the lotus feet of the divine Mother. He was absorbed thinking of Her, when he cried out suddenly, saying, "Wait, wait. Let me utter the Mantra first, and then Thou mayest take it." He then offered the food ritually before finishing the worship.

(e) There is an independent corroboration with some more explanation in a passage from the "The Gospel of the Holy Mother"(P.101-102) --

Disciple : Does the Master really partake of the food that you offer him? Mother (Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi) : Yes, He does.

Disciple : But we do not see any sign of it.

Mother : A light comes out of his eyes and licks all the articles of food. His ambrosial touch replenishes them again. So there is no decrease. ... Why? Does the Master require any food? He doesn’t. He eats the food offering only for the gratification of the devotees. The sacred prasad purifies the heart. The mind becomes impure, if one eats food without first offering to God.

Disciple : Does the Master really partake of the food offering?

Mother : Yes, do I not notice whether he partakes of the food or not? The Master takes his seat before the plate and then partakes of the food.

Disciple : Do you then actually see it?

Mother : Yes, In the case of some offerings, he actually eats and in other cases he merely looks at them. Take your own case. You don’t like to eat all things at all times. Nor do you relish the food offered by anyone and everyone. It is like that.
scriptures-and-sri-ramakrishna:
Scriptures and Sri Ramakrishna

--Swami Pitambarananda, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh

[Edited version of a lecture delivered at Tunuku (Andhra Pradesh) on 19.1.1997 on “Shastree-kurvanti Shastrani – Sri Ramakrishna ”]

Let me start with an incident which you perhaps might not have read in the books. Sri Ramakrishna’s disciple Swami Shivanandaji or Mahapurush Maharaj was in the Belur Math. If you have seen his photo, you will observe that he is sitting with his hands folded, head slightly bent. Also along with that, which has not come in the photo is that, he would be utter-ing, as if to himself, “Ramakrishna, Ramakrishna, Ramakrishna”. That was almost the regular posture and habit of his. One of his dear disciples from whom I had the privilege to hear this incident, approached him and deliberately poking him he asked, “What is this Maharaj, that you are sitting like this and saying Ramakrishna, Ramakrishna, Ramakrishna. What does it mean, Maharaj?” He became little grave and said, “Why my boy, why are you asking like this? Don’t you know who was Sri Ramakrishna?.” The disciple replied, “Yes, I know that he was a man like us.” “Why do you say so?” “Why, when we read his life we find that he per-formed rigorous austerities, rigorous sadhanas, wonderful sadhanas. So he was a human be-ing like us; because it is only a man who does sadhana and attains perfection. That’s why …” Mahapurushji became spiritually charged up and stood up from the chair on which he was sitting. He said, “My dear boy, tell me which sadhana reveals him as a human being. Pick up any sadhana. Take up Vedanta sadhana –Tota Puri only instructed him about Vedan-ta sadhana and he almost immediately entered into Nirvikalpa Samadhi. Can a man do like this? Can a saint do like this? Can a superman do like this? Take up his Tantra Sadhana – Bhairavi Brahmani brought a naked woman, asked him to sit on her lap and do japa. The moment he sat there, he entered into Samadhi. Can a man do like this? Can a saint do like this? Can a superman do like this? Take up any sadhana. Take up his Vatsalya Bhava Sadha-na. The Ramayat Panthi Babaji was worshipping that Ramlala for his whole life and he was having wonderful experiences. And Sri Ramakrishna, just at a look, not only knew his expe-riences but himself started getting much more intimate experiences, and finally Ramlala stayed with him. Can a man do like this? Can a saint do like this? Can a superman do like this? Tell me which sadhana reveals that he was a human being? You are only looking at the fact that he did sadhanas; but see through and analyze. It was more through his sadhanas that it was clearly revealed that he was God, Parabrahman Himself. If by anything his absolute divine nature is revealed it is through his sadhanas. Take up any sadhana and see that every sadhana of his has revealed supremely that God incarnated on earth to show man what is sadhana, what could be ideal sadhana!”.

I referred to this incident in the beginning as the subject given to me today is ‘Shas-tree-kurvanti Shastrani – Sri Ramakrishna.’ In English translation it may read – “Sri Rama-krishna is a person who made the scriptures really worth the name of ‘scriptures’.” It reminds one of a line in the Narada-bhakti-sutras, though it is slightly different from this. It says ‘Sat- Shastree-kurvanti Shastrani’ – ‘(they) validate the scriptures’. The reference in Narada- Bhakti-sutras is to devotees who are called Mukhya Bhaktas –‘the principal devotees’. While instructing the Gaun bhaktas or secondary devotees, Narada says, “Remember that those are really the devotees, who are fully devoted to God” – “Bhaktah ekantino mukhyah”. And while describing these ‘fully devoted to God’ he says, “Teertheekurvanti Tirthani; Sat- Shastree-kurvanti Shastrani; Sukarmeekurvanti Karmani” – “They impart holyness to holy places; they validate the scriptures, they change certain works into spiritually elevating activi-ty”. But Sri Ramakrishna does not belong to that category. And that is why perhaps that line has been changed a little.

Now let us first understand this idea of Narada-Sutras. What are shastras (scrip-

tures)? We will have to start from that point – what are shastras? Shastras mean that which can authoritatively guide us for reaching the ultimate spiritual goal. They have the authority to guide us. Of course, there are other functions – they inspire us, they impress the spiritual truths on our minds, they give us spiritual strength etc.. But the main purpose is to authorita-tively guide us on our path to the ultimate spiritual goal. Thus Vedas, specially the ‘knowledge portion of the Vedas, otherwise known as the Vedanta Upanishads are the prima-ry shastras and then we have the Smritis and the Puranas. And when we extend this defini-tion we can include the religious scriptures of all the religions of this world. Talking of shastras in this sense, we should know one more thing. Millions do now accept ‘The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna’ as the most authoritative Shastra. And I earnestly request this gathering not to forget ‘Sri Sri Ramakrishna Lila Prasanga’ (‘Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master’) also. Such a scripture the world has not yet seen. My teacher once wrote to a disciple, “These days we are studying ‘Sri Ramakrishna Lila Prasanga’, the scripture of scriptures, the greatest scripture”. That disciple of his was himself a great devotee of ‘Lila Prasanga’. But due to his keen analytical mind, he asked him a question in his letter, “To me Lila Prasanga is greater than many of the Upanishads, but are you placing it on the top of all Upanishads including the Mandukya Upanishad which speaks of the Brahman in the most wonderful way?” To that this great teacher replied, “I am not comparing it with any particular Upanishad. Take all the Upanishads and in them you find Brahman revealed through the words and ideas of the Rishis. The realizations of the Rishis have come to us in words. But herein we find Brahman revealed in flesh and blood. That is why I am talking of it as the scripture of scriptures and the greatest scripture”.

Let us go back to that line of the Narada-Sutras – “They validate the scriptures”. This is something which we have to understand. There is a scripture, it tells us out of the Rishis experience that if you follow these steps you will surely reach the goal”. I used the word ‘au-thoritatively’; another word should be added to that – ‘unfailingly’. The Sanskrit word is ‘Amogha’. Narada says – “Bhavatu Nischayadardhyadoordhwam Shastra-rakshanam” – “When your conviction has become very firm but you have not yet realized God, you should take recourse to the shastras and then only you will reach the goal”. So these Mukhya Bhak-tas take recourse to the shastras and reach the goal. Now as soon as they reach the goal and tell us that they have reached the goal, what they have done is -- ‘Sat-Shastree-kurvanti Shas-trani’ -- validated the scriptures. Shastras have been proved to be real spiritual guides. They have been verified, because many have taken the guidance and reached the goal. This is the function of the Mukhya Bhaktas. And for us it is surely wise to follow the scriptures. But we are living in these modern times and modern psychology tells us that by this method we are conditioning our minds. They say – “People have told you that Rama was like this, you are thinking that Rama is like this, so you are seeing Rama like that”. This is ‘condi-tioning of the mind’. So the very fact of validating the shastras is totally rejected by modern psychology. Modern psychology itself may not be very valid, but that is a thought current which we have to take into cognizance. What the Mukhya Bhaktas do is very valid; they vali-date the shastras by following those steps. But the modern trend of thought tells us that we have conditioned our minds. They say that the Rama which you saw does not relate to the nature of truth, rather it relates to the conditioning of your mind. So the very shastrahood of Shastras is imperiled, whether they are sat-shastras or not is a distant thing. Now there are two ways left open to us – One is like Buddha’s way, because during ancient times also such a doubt was there. So what did Buddha do? He threw away all the Shastras and rediscovered the truth all by himself. But there is a danger in this method that we come to a negative thought process called heterodoxy. If we understand through Sri Ra-makrishna, we can understand that the result of Buddha’s sadhana itself validated the Vedas, though Buddha’s followers may not say so. Because Sri Ramakrishna himself had all the re-alizations of Buddha. Some people ask that while Sri Ramakrishna performed sadhanas of every known religion, why did he not do sadhana according to Buddha’s teachings? Swami Saradananda has raised this question in ‘Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master’ and quoted Sri

Ramakrishna himself in reply – “There is no difference between the faith founded by him and the Vedic path of knowledge”. So we can understand through Sri Ramakrishna that Buddha validated the Vedas by apparently rejecting them, doing sadhana independently and reaching the same goal, exactly as declared in Vedanta.

But Sri Ramakrishna has done much more, much more. He is called the prophet of harmony. What did he do? He did not reject the shastras, but, at first, did not go to the shas-tras and so performed sadhana without refering to the shastras; got all the desired results and then subsequently took recourse to different methodologies prescribed in all the known Shastras!. Something unique and unthought of before! In an essay titled ‘Hinduism and Sri Ramakrishna’, Swami Vivekananda says – “The Divine, whose embodiment is the Vedas, almost wholly neglected literary education in this incarnation, in order to show how the eter-nally existing shastra reveals itself in the heart of a Rishi wherefrom all Sanskaras have been erased; so that when the Truth of the shastras is thus proved, religion would be rediscovered and re-promulgated.”1 So there was no chance of his mind being conditioned. Sometimes ‘rejecting’ can itself become a condition, a negative condition. But Sri Ramakrishna was practically an unlettered man -- not in literal sense, but in this sense that – there was no con-ditioning of his mind. In that same paragraph Swami Vivekananda has explained how the Vedas have come. Generally we hear the world samskara. ‘We must develop spiritual sam-skaras, we must develop the right samskaras and then we will reach the goal’ -- that is what we have been taught throughout, and it is not wrong. But here again the modern psycholo-gists will object. Hence Swami Vivekananda has said, “…in the heart of a Rishi wherefrom all Sanskaras have been erased” – i.e., there are no ‘impressions’. The ‘impressions’ start from individuality – ‘I am a Jiva’. This ‘I am a Jiva(an individual being)’ accumulates all the samskaras. If there is no ‘I’ there is no accumulations of samskaras. The Rishis travel by the reverse path. As the Shruti (Kathopanishad 2.1) puts it: "Kaschid dhirah pratyagatmanam aikshat avrittachakshuh amritattwam ichchan" ….desiring immortality, a rare discriminating man, turns his eyes away and the sees the indwelling self…. They remove this ‘I’ totally. ‘I’ is the peg on which all the samskaras gather. When ‘I’ is totally removed there are no sam-skaras left and then what happens? Truth in its original form shines in the hearts of the Rishis and that is why the Vedas have been called ‘apourusheya’ (not made by man). When an indi-vidual loses his individuality what he remains is Brahman only “brahmavit brahmaiva bha-vati” – “The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman”. Then he is no more an individual, this limitation of ‘I’ is totally eradicated and Brahman shines in its own nature. The ultimate Truth, by whatever name you call it God or Brahman or Atman manifests itself in the con-sciousness of that rishi. And that is why they say, “tasya nihshwasitam veda” – “it is from God himself, like his natural breathing, that the Vedas have come out”. God resides inside the pure heart of the Rishi; from there these have come out.

So Swamiji explains in that paragraph why ‘Vedamurti Sri Ramakrishna’ did not take recourse to external education. By dint of one single asset, vyakulata (intense yearning) he realised the ultimate Truth. Now that is exactly according to the Upanishad, though he was not aware of what the Upanishads say! He has spontaneously followed everything. Kathopan-ishad tells us that no sadhana leads to God except Vyakulata -- ‘Yam eva eshah vrinute tena labhyah; tasya esha Atma vivrinute tanum swam’—i.e. ‘That very Atman which is most yearningly sought for by this aspirant is realised by him; This Atman reveals its true nature in his consciousness’. And it is for increasing this yearning that we do all the sadhanas. Every sadhana is valid because ultimately it makes this yearning for God cent percent complete. Sri Ramakrishna himself tells us that when this mumuksha or vyakulata (intense yearning) be-comes cent percent, it is like the dawn, and the sunrise of full realisation must follow. It is a matter of only a little time then. And this is what the Kathopnishad tells us. So this is how the Vedas came in the beginning. Of course, we have alresdy seen that he was God incarnate, God in the role of sadhaka. So by his very constitution, his vyakulata was unique, unparal-

(‘Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master’ , fourth edition 1970 P.325)

leled. That is why in every respect he has said, “if I have done sixteen annas, it is enough for you if you do one anna”. But the model is there. The absolute ideal model is there. Those who have read the 5th Volume of ‘Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master’, called ‘Divya Bhava and Narendranath’ will find Narendranath representing the ideal modern man who stumbles at every point and gets corrected when Sri Ramakrishna tells him what to do next. So we need two types of examples. What mistakes we can posibly make and how to come out of those mistakes is one model. And what is sadhana without a mistake should be another model. And that can be done only by God incarnate. That is why Mahapurushji said – His greatest glory as incarnation, as God Himself is his sadhanas. In the very beginning of the ‘Sadhaka bhava’ of the ‘The Great Master’ (vol.ii) Swami Saradanandaji has explained this fact. When we read of his panting and yearning, we may think that he was yearning for the vision of Mother Kali in a personal sense. But that was not true. To understand Sri Rama-krishna it is better to go through Swami Vivekananda. In his lecture on ‘My Master’ he says that the query in his mind was whether this image in the temple was a stone or there was a reality behind. And also when we read the description of his experience, -- waves in the ocean of consciousness engulfed and drowned his separate ‘I’ -- we understand that it was the Nirvikalpa Samadhi, absolute I-less consciousness. Thus this sadhana of his validated the Vedanta. Now he was not Buddha who rejected the Vedas, he is born in this modern age, as the prophet of harmony. So though he began his sadhanas without reference to scriptures and achieved the goal, yet afterwards he took recourse to all the known shastras and all the known methodologies.

Some people wonder, why was it necessary for Sri Ramakrishna to practice Islam etc when he had done all the Sadhanas according to Hindu religion, The answer is – was it nec-essary for him to practice any sadhana at all. What was necessary for him? To fulfil the cosmic need of this age. Our need, my need, your need, the need of this world -- that need when felt by God results into incarnation. So it was for the sake of establishing harmony of religions in this modern age that he took recourse to all the known methodologies. This is something wonderful, unique, because many people tell us that sadhana of bhakti does not lead to the Absolute. Sri Ramakrishna proved it is not so.He said, `Pure Bhakti and Pure Jnana are one and the same. Through every sadhana he reached the same Absolute non-dual Truth! What was the formula? What was the basis? He himself has said, “Advaita Jnan Anchale Bendhe Ja Ichha tai karo” – “Tying advaita knowledge in a knot of your cloth, do what you like”. ‘Do what you like’ means perform any sadhana you like. So the fundamental truth manifests itself when the ego drops. That is the purpose of every sad-hana. There are stages, there are degrees, there are varieties of human nature and so there are varieties of paths.

And it was because of his unique nature that he undertook sadhana of all the scrip-tures, all the methodologies separately. That is why when he talked of the Truth and of the methodologies he talked in such a harmonious manner, all in the same breath. He would say that at such and such a stage the experience is like this, the yogis describe like this, the bhaktas call it like this. The same experience, that same level of experience – the Jnanis de-scribe in a particular way, the Yogis in a different way, the bhaktas in still another way -- of the same level. This he could do because he had performed the sadhanas according to all known scriptures.

Now it is again a rare, unique thing. We find incarnations of the past laying stress on different particular aspects of the Supreme Truth. The Rigveda tells us – “Ekam Sat Viprah Bahudha Vadanti” – “Truth is One, the Sages call It variously”. There is no confusion in the minds of the sages; but sometimes it leads to confusion in the followers. We are not belittling any incarnation or any prophet. It is God Himself who incarnates every time. But according to the need of the age, a particular facet has to be emphasized. So the prophet emphasises a particular facet, and later on, due to our narrowness, due to limitedness of our mind that em-phasis leads to one-sidedness. Then will it not happen in the case of Sri Ramakrishna too? What has he emphasised? He has emphasised the harmony. That is the need of the present

age. Because the world has come so close together physically, and yet is mentally drifting further away. So nobody can be an island now. I cannot sit in a corner and say that only my sadhana is alright, I do not care for others. Either I have to love or I have to quarrel, because we have come so close to each other. And that is why the need of the age is harmony. And the need of the age is to bear the onslaught of modern science and also to harmo-nise the findings of modern science with the truths of religion. Modern science wants proof for everything. He has given all the proofs. Then again, science asks us how do the different scriptures speak differently – one contradicting the other? How can they be true? But we have already seen that Sri Ramakrishna took recourse to all scriptures and each time got the same ultimate result and removed this confusion once for all that if God can be seen this way how can he be seen that way also. He showed that in reality no sripture conflicts with any other scripture, they are different approaches to the same goal!

We have seen that he started with an unconditioned mind. But then for practical need of the sadhakas they have to follow the shastras. And to generate that faith, that supreme faith in the scriptures, Sri Ramakrishna undertook sadhanas meticulously according to scrip-tures under qualified teachers. Not of one particular kind, because he had to validate all the scriptures of the world. Swami Vivekananda calls him Avatara-varishtha, sar-vadharamsvarupee (embodiment of all religions) and dharamasya sthapkah – ‘he has put Re-ligion itself on a firm foundation’. To explain that ‘Religion in itself’ Swami Saradananda calls him ‘saravadharama-sthapkah’ – ‘he has put all religions on firm foundation’. So he had not only to validate each scripture separately but also to reconcile and harmonise them. That is why he went to different scriptures, different methodologies and then told us that ac-cording to the different minds, the paths appear different, but the levels or the steps or the stages will be the same looked at in different ways. So we find him describing the evolution of sadhak’s consciousness according to saptabhumikas ( 7 levels) of Vedanta. And then he said that in Yoga it is described thus, in Bhakti it is described like this and so forth. So he val-idated the scriptures by going independently of them and reaching the same truth, and he re-validated all the scriptures by following them. He also reconciled or harmonized all the scrip-tures by telling us how at different levels the experiences appear differently. And one more thing has to be understood. Sri Ramakrishna could not use the word ‘I’ with reference to himself, and yet so much uniqueness was in that frail appearing personality of his, that he himself said, “Know that the many Hari-sabhas and the other religious institu-tions that you see are due to this (referring to his own person). Did they formerly exist? Eve-rything had been lifeless, but since this (referring to his person again) came, all this have come to life again and a current of religion is now flowing just a little below the surface”.2 So about Sri Ramakrishna’s 12 years of sadhana, one has to understand this very important point. Through his superhuman efforts and sadhana he roused the tremendous cosmic spiritu-al power for the upliftment of whole humanity. Thus if you and I and generations to come feel the need of God, feel the zest for sadhana, we must understand and remember it is Sri Ramakrishna who is inspiring us to do this sadhana. His was the cosmic mind. God incarnate as man has the cosmic mind. When the vibration of sadhana is raised in that cosmic mind all our minds for generations together become filled up with such thoughts – ‘I want to see God, I want to do sadhana, I want to take recourse to scriptures, etc’.

Let us summarize –

Sri Ramakrishna did not pay heed to external education in the beginning. Hence he did not know what the Vedas or other scriptures told of sadhana. Hence there was no chance of his mind being conditioned by them. Nor was there any chance of his rejecting the Vedas or scriptures and entering a sort of negative conditioning. He practiced sadhanas prompted by his asset of intense yearning for realising the Ultimate Truth and when he succeeded, his real-isation tallied with the scriptures and thereby they were re-established as scriptures. Then he took recourse to the method given in all the known scriptures, under competent guides and

(‘Great Master’, P.619)

reached the same truth through all of them thereby not only validating all of them but estab-lishing a harmony of scriptures based upon direct experiences. Thus he fulfilled the following needs of the age.

(a) There should not be any conditioning of the mind—positive or negative.

(b) Truths should be proved by demonstration.

(c) Apparent antagonism between different scriptures should be removed and harmo-ny established.

(d) Men and women should be inspired to try to realise the Ultimate Reality.

(e) So many validated paths should be available to them so that they can proceed by that which suits them most individually without mental conflicts.

How could Sri Ramakrishna achieve all this, even accepting that he was God incar-nated as man, can be better understood through another supremely wise personality —Holy Mother Sri Sarada Devi. A sannyasi disciple once asked her, “Mother, is it for the establish-ment of the harmony of all religions that the Master came this time?” The Holy Mother re-plied, “Look here. I never felt that he practised all the religions with the intention of teaching the harmony of all religions. He was always immersed in God-conciousness. He followed all the disciplines—those of Christians, Muslims, Vaishnavas, etc.—for the sake of God-realisation, and he enjoyed the Divine lila (play) in different ways, entirely unconscious of how time passed. But still, do you know, my dear, in this age renunciation has been his speci-ality. Has anyone ever seen at any time that kind of spontaneous renunciation? What you have said of the harmony of religions is also true. In other Incarnations one Ideal or another was emphasised over others.”3 What did she mean? ‘I want to see God in a such and such particular form’ is also clinging to one's own ‘I’. The ultimate renunciation makes one trans-cend even this specification! Sri Ramakrishna has described it through a beautiful analogy. He says, “A man kept a solution of dye in a tub. Many people came to him to have their clothes dyed. He would ask a customer, “What colour should you like to have your cloth dyed?” If the customer wanted red, then the man would dip the cloth in the tub and say, “Here is your cloth dyed red.” If another customer wanted his cloth dyed yellow, the man would dip his cloth in the same tub and say, “Here is your cloth dyed yellow.” If a customer wanted his cloth dyed blue, the man would dip it in the same tub and say, “Here is your cloth dyed blue.” Thus he would dye the clothes of his customers different colours, dipping them all in the same solution. One of the customers watched all this with amazement. The man asked him, “Well! What colour do you want for your cloth?” The customer said, “Brother, dye my cloth the colour of the dye in your tub.”4 Now this is what Sri Ramakrishna has de-scribed about God; and to our minds that dyer is Sri Ramakrishna himself, that special cus-tomer is Swami Vivekananda who wants God as He is. But the fun with Sri Ramakrishna is that people want God in different ways. So he says, “Here you are”. That is why the Holy Mother said that his renunciation was supreme. And then she said, “What you say of harmo-ny also is true”. In the previous incarnations emphasis was given on some aspect of God, be-cause of which the other aspects had got suppressed. But this time emphasis has been been given on all the aspects. Thus she has explained the uniqueness of Sri Ramakrishna. In conclusion, let me again refer to the person who had questioned Mahapurush Ma-haraj about his attitude towards Sri Ramakrishna. It so happened that the same person went to Swami Saradananda and asked him, “Why are you writing this ‘Lila Prasanga’?” He replied

– “In order that all the sadhakas belonging to all the denominations in the world could see light in their spiritual struggle”. So this unique ‘Shastree-kurvanti Shastrani’ was possible only for Parabrahma-swarupa (The Supreme Reality embodied as--) Sri Ramakrishna. So we understand that He is the goal and He is the way, and He has validated all the ways, and also it is He who is inspiring us to follow the way most suitable to us. That will lead us ultimately to sure success in our own spiritual endeavors.

-------x-------

(‘The Gospel of the Holy Mother’, P.395-96)

(‘Tales and Parables of Sri Ramakrishna’, P.171-72)

## Observations: (Swami Pitambarananda)

1. Both the translations are wrong; “Sadhanakaler samaya hoite” can neither be “from the time he completed his Sadhanas” nor “from the period after his sadhana”. It rather means from the period of his Sadhanas.

2. The translations do not correspond with the contents wherein “mainly” the events of the time of his Sadhanas are recorded and not of the time “after” its completion.

3. A great point indicated by the Seer Saradanandaji has been missed in both these translations, viz., he is not writing about a human being who becomes perfect by Sadhanas and then per chance becomes a teacher, but he is writing about God who incarnated himself in the form of a man and so is a born teacher.
swami-gahananandaji:
What I remember of Revered Swami Gahananandaji Maharaj

By Sw. Pitambarananda

It was between A.D. 1970 and 1972 that I remember to have seen Rev. Gahananandaji for the first time. I was a Brahmachari then at the Ramakrishna Ashrama, Nagpur. One day, all of a sudden, Rev. Gahananandaji who was the Secretary of Ramakrishna Mission Seva Pratisthan at Calcutta (now Kolkata) arrived at Nagpur Ashrama accompanied by Sw. Akunthanandaji, the Secretary of Ramakrishna Mission Institute of Culture, also at Calcutta. When asked about the purpose of their visit, Rev. Gahananandaji replied, “As the old man (referring to Most Revered Swami Bhaskareswaranandaji, the then President of that Ashrama) is getting older, there is no knowing when he would drop his mortal coil so we wanted to pay our respects to him before that.”

One day, during that very short visit of theirs, I saw Rev. Gahananandaji coming out of the bathroom. He had finished his bath and had washed his clothes himself and was carrying the wet clothes in his hand. I went forward, took the clothes from his hand, and spread them on the drying rope, but alas, not as properly as they should have been put. He quickly came there and showed me how to do it properly and then narrated his own similar story.. He was a young monastic at the Belur Math and Most Revered Swami Sankaranandaji Maharaj was the President of the order. When once he entered President Maharaj’s room he found that his blanket was yet to be folded after his getting up from the bed. So he folded it as he thought best. At which Revered Maharaj exclaimed in his natural grave tone, “kaaj baadhiye laabh nei”, in Bengali, meaning “there is no use in increasing the work”. An unknown loving respect in my heart and a loving kindness in his heart had sprung up at Nagpur.

My second meeting with Revered Maharaj came about in 1978 at Belur Math. I was transferred from Nagpur and was awaiting my next posting. Maharaj, along with some more sadhus, was going to Kamarpukur from Belur Math. I asked them whether I could also join them. They told me to get necessary permission from Rev. Gambhiranandaji Maharj who was the General Secretary of the Ramakrishna Math. But when I went to ask him, he sternly said, “No”, and I communicated the same to them. So they left without me. A few days after this, Revered Kishori Maharaj, a disciple and sevak of the Holy Mother, left his body at the Seva Pratisthan at Calcutta whose chief was Rev, Gahananandaji. It was Kishori Maharj’s wish that his body should be cremated at Jayarambati. So it was loaded in a jeep and with some sadhus from there could have gone straight to Jayarambati. But Rev. Gahananandaji phoned Rev. Gambhiranandaji that the jeep would go to Belur Math first and pick me up as a necessary additional escort and then proceed to Jayarambati via Kamarpukur. So I was asked to go with the jeep. While halting at Kamarpukur on the way, the Head of that Ashrama told us that after completing the rites of cremation ceremony, we must return to Kamarpukur for night food and sleep and return to Calcutta next day. When I returned next day Rev. Gahananandaji lovingly asked me, “So your desire to go to Kamarpukur has been fulfilled, isn’t it?” And then only I understood that it was Maharaj’s grace which had made it possible!

The third meeting was also at Belur Math in 1978. Rev. Maharaj had come to attend the Trustee Meeting after which I went and paid my respects to him. He then told me, “You are getting infamous here for not accepting any proposal for your posting. You should better accept their next proposal." Within a couple of days the call came and I was asked to go to Deoghar. Keeping Maharaj’s advice in mind, I accepted it.

Some time after 1982, when I was at the Mission’s Students’ Home at Madras (now Chennai), Swami Veetabhayananda and myself had gone to the Airport to see off Rev.Maharaj after one of his visits. Somebody mentioned some wrong criticism about me, to which I reacted quite angrily. Revered Maharaj then said, “Pitambar, you should always keep an ice-bag on your head.”

The next time I met him was in AD 1995 at Chandigarh when I was the Head of Chandigarh Ashrama and Rev. Maharaj was the Vice-President of the Ramakrishna Math. He had come there on our request to initiate the aspirant devotees with 'mantra diksha'. In the the necessary forms to be filled-up by the candidates, there was a column “If you are a girl, have taken the permission from your parents?” One girl had left the column blank and I showed it to him. He asked me “What do you say?" I replied, “She would never get permission.” To which he again asked me, “What do you say?" I replied, 'It would be better if you are kind enough to bless her.” He immediately agreed.

One day during that visit, a question-answer session was arranged for revered Maharaj with the newly initiated devotees and he made me sit near him and answer the questions on his behalf. One of the questions was “Why are we asked to repeat our mantra at least 108 times. He suggested the following answer : “In Indian calculation one day was divided into 60 ghatikas, each ghatika into 60 palas and each pala into 60 vipalas which gives a total of 60x60x60 = 21600 moments of time. The Rishis want us that at least once for 1000 moments we should remember the Lord once. Now 108 times in the morning and another 108 in the evening makes a total of 216 which is once for each 1000 moments during the day."

Rev. Maharaj's second visit to Chandigarh Ashrama was in 1999 for a similar purpose. In Ambala which is 50 kms. away from Chandigarh, there lived a great philanthropic devotee named Shri Pannalalji and he was well known to all our senior Monks. The husband of one of his married daughters Smt. Sudesh Garg, was so much against sadhus that she could not freely meet them except in her father’s house. For this reason she could not receive ‘initiation’ though she was fully devoted to Shri Ramakrishna. But she desired very much to have it this time. As soon as I told this to Revered Maharaj, he said, “Doesn’t matter. On the spare day we shall go to Sri Pannalalji’s house at Ambala and she can come there and I can easily initiate her in Pannalalji’s shrine room.” When I phoned Pannalalji, he said, ”This will not be necessary. I shall bring her with me to Chandigarh after her husband leaves for his factory and she should be allowed to join the initiation programme a little late. Only thing is that she should not have to wait for Annaprasad there, so that I shall bring her back to Ambala before her husband comes back home for his lunch." Rev. Maharaj graciously agreed for this. Simplicity and grace personified!

These are the 2 pictures taken of his Chandigarh visits. The first one is his visit to the famous Rose garden and second seems to be in the train while seeing him off and there is some time for the train to start.

Revered Gahananandaji Maharaj left his mortal coil on 4th November 2007. I was at Rishikesh spending time in solitude. But I was invited by our Kankhal (Haridwar) Ashrama for a special feast preceeded by a memorial meeting on the 16th day as per the tradition in the Sadhu Samaj. Many outside Sannyasis were, of course, invited. Now one of them was speaking about his experiences of Revered Maharaj and his topic was Maharaj’s undisturbed mind. He was talking about the days when Rev. Maharaj was the Head of Ramakrishna Mission Seva Pratisthan and he had gone to meet him for some purpose of his own. At that time one Communist leader entered Maharaj’s office and started abusing Maharaj vehemently. The visiting Sadhu felt that he shoud slap that intruder. And yet Maharaj himself was calmly listening till the person cooled down!”

May he continue to shower his unbounded grace on all of us!

*****

palace-for-the-poor:
(Ramakrishna Mission Students' Home, Madras)

Shri Ramakrishna Mission Students' Home at Madras, an affiliated branch of the Ramakrishna Mission, is the direct outcome of the message of service to the poor and destitutes, in the field of education, with a view to helping the manifestation of the Divine in man. It was started under the guidance and inspiration of Srimat Swami Ramakrishnanandaji Maharaj, one of the direct disciples of the Master, who was sent as the apostle to South India by the great leader Swami Vivekananda.

After starting the Ramakrishna Math in Madras in 1899, Swami Ramakrishnanandaji Maharaj surveyed the needs of the people and thought of an orphanage where orphan and destitute boys could be educated under the Gurukula system and put on their legs as properly oriented and useful members of society. At his behest, the cousins, Shri C. Ramaswami Iyenger and Shri C. Ramanujachariar started the "Home", nurtured it, and built it up. The "Home" was inaugurated on the 17th February, 1905, in a small house in the Kesava Perumal, South Mada Street, Mylapore, given free of rent by Dr. M. C. Nanjunda Rao. It had then 5 orphans to take care of. It was afterwards shifted from one rented house to another to accommodate more and more boys. When Swami Ramakrishnananda died in 1911, Swami Brahmananda, the spiritual son of Shri Ramakrishna took over the mantle of guiding and inspiring the activities of the Home. In 1916 some land was obtained in Mylapore itself and he laid the foundation stone of the new buildings on the Akshaya Tritiya in May 1918. Again he himself inaugurated the new building when the Home was brought to its own permanent site, on Akshaya Tritiya, the 10th May, 1921, of which the present postal address is 101 Sir P.S. Sivaswami Salai, Mylapore, Madras 600 004.

In the beginning the object was to provide a home for destitutes and orphans giving them free board and lodging and at the same time to secure for them general supervision in their education, conduct and regulation of life. But for a fuller realisation of the Gurukula ideal, a Residential High School was started in 1922. Vocational training was also started immediately which now has taken the form of a fully developed residential Technical Institute. An Elementary School for the children of the locality was also opened in 1936. Some land was received as gift at Malliankaranai Village in Chingleput District and the educational activities were extended to the village level with a Higher Elementary School started there in 1945 and an attached hostel started in 1947.

Today the Students' Home has under its management six sections: The Collegiate, the Technical, the Secondary and the Elementary education at Mylapore, Madras, and the Higher Elementary education at Malliankaranai Village (Uttiramerur Taluk, 603 406, Chingleput District), as well as the Agricultural Estate in Malliankaranai.

(1) THE COLLEGIATE SECTION: The "Home" provides only free lodging and boarding and the boys study in different colleges or (2) courses in the city. Present strength: 30.

(2) THE TECHNICAL SECTION: The "Home" runs the Ramakrishna Mission Technical Institute which is fully residential for 3 years' Diploma course. Present strength 126. The Technical Institute also conducts a part-time P.D. Course and A.M.I.E. classes having a combined strength of 46.

(3) THE SECONDARY SECTION: The "Home" runs the Ramakrishna Mission Residential High School for boys from standards VI to X. Present strength: 175.

(4) THE ELEMENTARY SECTION: The "Home" runs the Ramakrishna Centenary Primary School for day scholars only. Present strength: 359.

(5) THE HIGHER ELEMENTARY SECTION: The "Home" runs the Ramakrishna Mission Middle School at Malliankaranai. Present strength: 424. Number of boys in the attached Hostel: 44.

Thus the total number of free boarders is 375 and the combined strength of the Students in various educational Institutions, is 1130.

(6) AGRICULTURAL ESTATE AT MALLIANKARANAI: The Students' Home owns some agricultural land and cattle heads in this village.

The Home, besides giving an up-to-date education, bestows special attention upon character-building, emphasis being on a harmonious development of body, mind, intellect and heart.

PUJA, PRAYERS AND RELIGIOUS CLASSES: The Home has separate Shrine Halls for the juniors and seniors where Puja is done by the students themselves both morning and evening. In the morning boys are taught the Bhagavadgita and Vedic chanting with explanations; devotional songs are sung and a silent meditation ends the programme. In the evening there is Arati with songs and meditation. Religious classes are conducted for the boys both morning and evening. In the month of Margazhi (December-January) Bhajans are conducted every morning with singing of Tiruppavai and Tiruvembavai.

Birth Anniversary of Bhagavan Shri Ramakrishna, Shri Sarada Devi, Swami Ramakrishnananda and other festivals are celebrated with processions, cultural programmes, and meetings, etc.

All the inmates of the Home are under the care of monastic warden and lay ward-masters. Three staff members of the High School and eight of the Technical Institute are provided with residential accommodation in the Staff Quarters opposite to the Home.

Classwise and overall competitions are held for both Junior and Senior wings in Oratory, Recitation, Extempore Speech, General Essay writing, Religious Essays on the Gita, Tirukkural etc. and general knowledge in English and Tamil, as also in pencil-drawing and colour-drawing. Competitions are also held in chanting the Vedas, the Gita, the Vishnusahasranamam, the Kambaramayana, etc.

Almost all the domestic activities of the Home are carried out by the boys themselves under their respective captains allotted by the wardens. Special duties e.g. maintenance of electrical installations and water pumps, carpentry, vegetable gardening and flower gardening, etc., give ample scope for training of boys with special aptitudes. Serving in the dining hall is another very useful training activity. Stationery Stores for all inmates are also being managed by the boys.

Physical exercises are taught and conducted daily for all inmates of the Home in the early morning between 5 and 5.30 a.m. Gymnastics and outdoor sports are also provided for. A qualified doctor and a compounder visit the Home every day between 5 and 6 p.m. and boys requiring observation and rest are kept in the Medical Ward.

The Home organises Film Shows for the boys for inculcating spiritual and moral values.

Excursions are arranged classwise to places of religious interest, natural beauty, and industrial development.

In 1932 a gift of about 200 acres of land in this Malliankaranai Village (about 85 Kms. away from Madras) was received by the Students' Home with the idea that the income derived from paddy grown here could be used for supporting the students in Mylapore, Madras.

However when the Mission workers took over this place, the first thing noticed by them was the backwardness of this remote place with no educational or any other facilities whatsoever and hence as per the ideals of the Students' Home educational activities were started here though there was considerable expenditure involved in the process. It was also noticed that the land was highly alkaline and hence unfit for good agriculture. However, the Students' Home workers over a number of years have tried to improve the agricultural produce, the educational facilities, and the overall condition of the villagers. Thus today one can see here:

(1) A School with more than 400 Children housed in a pucca stone building with shrine and prayer hall of its own.

(2) Extension of the Home in the form of free board and lodging to 45 students.

(3) Agricultural pattern changed to long term investments like: 1200 coconut trees, Mango, Tamarind and Guava trees, Casurina groves; along with Paddy cultivation and Vegetable garden.

(4) Mechanisation by digging several wells and installation of pumpsets, wind-mills, bio-gas plants, etc.

(5) Dairy products for consumption and marketing in future.

Almost all the students who are admitted to the Students' Home are from the lowest rung of society, either due to their orphanhood or due to extreme poverty, and also, in most cases, due to the backwardness of their family background. And yet they are made to forget all these and encouraged to strive to gain the highest in life, in various fields for which they possess the required potential.

Swami Brahmananda declared the Students' Home to be the "Palace for the poor" and "a temple of learning" on the day of inauguration of the new buildings in 1921. True to that spirit, the heights reached by the old boys of this Home in various fields in the last 83 years since its inception in 1905, are too numerous to mention. A few of these students turned into outstanding monks of the Ramakrishna Order, and other Maths.

Anna N. Subramanian who came to the Home as a college student, and now the President of the Home, has authored the Tamil translations of almost all scriptural books published by the Ramakrishna Math, Madras.

One student of this Home who earned Padmabhushan is Dr. T. R. Seshadri (1917-24). Two others were awarded Padmashri, Dr. T.M.P. Mahadevan, and Shri O.S. Murthy. Besides this, the Home students have turned out to be distinguished scientists and scholars like Dr. V.S. Swaminathan (1919-23), Dr. A. Appadurai (1921-23) and others.

The Home has contributed high ranking officers of the Indian Army, Navy and Air Force, the highest rank being that of Major General S.P. Mahadevan (1939-40) who retired as G.O.C. in C., Southern Command and then was made the Chairman of Tamil Nadu Public Service Commission.

Many distinguished I.C.S., I.A.S. and other officers have come out of this Home. In the field of politics Shri N.M. Lingam, a student of this Home from 1929 to 1934 was elected to the Indian Parliament in 1952. Very prominent in the field of Law was Shri V. Rajaram Iyer (1912-1913) who retired as Advocate General, Hyderabad State.

These are only a few names out of hundreds of successful lawyers, administrators, engineers, and other distinguished citizens of India who were blessed with the grace of Shri Ramakrishna and His holy followers in this 'Palace of the poor', which is also a 'temple of learning.'

## EDUCATION ACCORDING TO VEDANTA

(Revised form of a paper presented at the Panjab University Department of Education on December 9th 1996)

--Swami Pitambarananda, Secretary, Ramakrishna Mission Ashrama, Chandigarh

## PREAMBLE

The need

Academicians believe that Education in any society is designed to preserve, modify and transfer its culture to the coming generation. So far as India is concerned, most unfortunately, however, our education was designed by the British Rulers"1 to make us forget our culture, to make us think of ourselves as inferior to our rulers and to make us ape our rulers as best or as much as we could. And, still more unfortunately, even after gaining political freedom, no worthwhile attempt has so far been made to overhaul this educational policy !. There have been commissions and their reports,2 but except for some cosmetic changes and changes of 'patterns', no 'Indian' thoughts regarding 'policy' have ever been implemented. More recently,3 a name 'New Education Policy' was circulated, publicised and made current without ever concretely defining what it meant ! The result of this 'drift' is that the thought of Inferiority of Indian ideas, designated as primitive etc. and the superiority of Western ideas has permeated and eaten up the entire nation; the only difference, perhaps, is the substitution of 'American' for 'British' as the role model. It was on this background that the Education Department of the Panjab University invited me to talk on 'Education according to Vedanta'. They wanted to find out if India really had any worthwhile thoughts on Education which could really meet the needs of our society at the present time to preserve, improve upon and transfer its culture to the coming generation.

Various organisations like the Ramakrishna Mission have their ideas on Education, but they are not known in the 'Official Academic Circles' -- the schools, colleges and universities funded by the Government which still think in terms of purely American idiom.

Now in India itself human society has always been thought of as a graded organisation consisting of varieties of types of individuals, social groups and cultures and hence innumerable educational ideas and ideals were always available. Hence it is impossible to discuss the gamut of Indian ideas on education in a single paper.

But then why should we single out the 'Vedantic' ideas for discussion ?

Because all Indian thoughts have been influenced by Vedanta to lesser or more degree and also all Indian thoughts tend towards it. Hence an attempt is being made here to bring out from the Vedantic literature the ideas on education under (A) The Goal, (B) The process, (C) Testing and evaluation as also the allied topics e.g. (i) Preparatory education (ii) Continued education and the most important topic – (iii) Teachers' education. And while doing so once again we wish to inform the readers that we are not dealing with Indian educational thought in its entirety for which we would have to pay attention to the entire Vedic literature and not merely its Vedantic part.

Now, the original source books for this Vedantic system of thought and culture are (i) The Upanishads, (ii) The Bhagavad-Gita and (iii) The Aphorisms of Vyasa. We shall try to stick mostly to these sources and avoid taking recourse to the vast philosophic literature growing in the name of Vedanta.

If we think of broadening its scope and applying it to the modern day needs we may have to take recourse to what Sri Ramakrishna and Swami Vivekananda demonstrated in their own lives and preached to the world at large. But that will take us beyond the scope of the present article though we may make some references to these thoughts here and there. Similarly what the present writer thinks or feels can only be mentioned as reflections here and there as the main theme proposed for this paper is "Education according to ‘Vedanta’.”

We wish to clarify one more issue before we make the actual start.

Any theme such as ‘Vedantic ideas of education’ can justifiably be presented in its own idiom and hence it may not always be possible to use totally the American idiom current in the present day academic circle, though we may attempt to take note of it whenever possible.

## INTRODUCTION

What is Education

Let us then start on neutral grounds.

When we say, "Education in any society is designed to preserve, modify and transfer its culture to the coming generation", we are not really defining education but are merely indicating as to how it should be ‘designed’, utilised or used or handled or planned, and, we are also limiting it by a kind of social selfishness. This social selfishness, again, is itself based on the shallow western idea of continuity of life through society, and, thrives only in the absence of the real concept of continuity based on the Immortality of the Soul or Atman. Vedanta tells us that every human being educates himself or herself in this life in continuity of what was already learnt in past lives, and that he or she would, in the next life, start from where they would end in this life. Thus they would go on evolving till they reach infinitude or absolute perfection. Swami Vivekananda says, "Education is the manifestation of perfection already in man."4 If man is thus helped or guided towards his natural goal of absolute perfection, the well being of society is automatically taken care of. On the other hand 'social selfishness' may curb the human growth and in its turn defeat even the purpose of social well-being! Hence, though the one definition appears 'social' and hence 'broader' and the other 'individual' and hence ‘narrow’ to the superficial view, the deeper view reveals the second to be based on the 'ultimate nature of things' and hence really universal and everlasting while the first one is narrow, divisive, chauvinistic, giving rise to Macaulayism and would serve only to achieve temporary objectives. However, to strike a neutral path, let us turn to the dictionary of the English language to 'define' the word education itself. We find -

The new Webster Dictionary defines `education' as "instruction or training by which people learn to develop and use their mental, moral and physical powers". Paying particular attention to `mental powers' in the definition of education we find the same dictionary stating that `mental' means "of or pertaining to the mind", and `mind' means "the seat of consciousness, thought, feeling and will". If we combine all these definitions we find that education is that instruction or training by which people learn to develop their powers of thought, feeling and will as well as moral or physical powers (thereby making their life more and more valuable and worthwhile to themselves and to society at large).

The present scenario

On this background, if we look at the present scenario in the field of Education, neither we see attention being given to moral training, nor to training of feeling and will. It is only concerned with intellectual gathering of information and development of certain skills. It appears that education has become totally divorced from its own meaning.

Swami Vivekananda says, " Education is not the amount of information that is put into your brain and runs riot there, undigested all your life. We must have life-building, man-making, character-making, assimilation of ideas."5 And again, "The training by which the current and expression of will are brought under control and become fruitful, is called education."6 " The education that does not help the common mass of people to equip themselves for the struggle for life, which does not bring out strength of character, a spirit of philanthropy and the courage of a lion -- is it worth the name?"7 The human society is what education makes it and hence we are passing through the darkest period where we are facing steep decline of moral values, rise and dominance of anti-values like corruption, apathy towards neighbors and nation, etc. etc. and drifting towards chaos where nobody seems to know what human life is meant for. Does it not imply that the present education system has failed and has lost its meaning? Where is the solution?

It is an evident fact that, today, every field of human endeavor is primarily being influenced by what could be called `the western mode of thinking'. In this context, Arnold Toynbee, perhaps the greatest historian of the present age, says -- "Today we are still living in this transitional chapter of the world's history, but it is already becoming clear that a chapter which had a western beginning will have to have an Indian ending if it is not to end in the self-destruction of the human race. In the present age, the world has been united on the material plane by Western technology. But this Western skill has not only `annihilated distance'; it has armed the peoples of the world with weapons of devastating powers at a time when they have been brought to point-blank range of each other without yet having learnt to know and love each other. At this supremely dangerous moment in human history, the only way of salvation for mankind is an Indian way. ... The primary reason is that this teaching is right -- and is right because it flows from a true vision of spiritual reality." 8

What is this `Indian' `teaching' which `flows from a true vision of spiritual reality'? This is what is called `Vedanta'.

What is Vedanta

`Vid' is `to know'. Hence `Vedas' means knowledge; and when this knowledge reaches its culmination, it is called `Vedanta', the end of knowledge. We have already seen (in the preamble) that three primary sources are universally accepted as authoritatively dealing with this ultimate knowledge known as Vedanta. In Swami Vivekananda's words: " First of all there are the Revelations, the Srutis, by which I mean the Upanisads (which form part of the most ancient Vedic literature). Secondly, among our philosophies, the Sutras(aphorisms) of Vyasa (known as `Sariraka-Mimansa' or `Vyasa-sutras', `Vedanta-sutras', or `Brahma-sutras') have the greatest prominence on account of their being the consummation of all the preceding systems of philosophy. ... Then between the Upanisads and the Sutras, which are the systematising of the marvelous truths of the Vedanta, comes in the Gita, the divine commentary of the Vedanta (which itself is called an Upanisad though it does not form part of the ancient Vedic literature)".9

Education according to Vedanta

What system of education does this Vedanta enunciate and how it fully meets the requirements implied in the very meaning of the term `education' is to be discussed in this paper devoted to ‘Education according to Vedanta'. This we shall try to do under three heads: (i) The Aims; (ii) The Process; and (iii) Evaluation, and further under (iv) Preparatory education, (v) Continued education and (vi) Teachers' education

## THE AIMS OF EDUCATION ACCORDING TO VEDANTA

The ultimate aim of all education ought to be to make the human individual perfect in all respects – physically perfectly healthy, perfect in thinking, feeling and will, perfectly moral, and with fully evolved consciousness.

In the words of Swami Vivekananda, " the end of all education, all training, should be man-making. The end and aim of all training is to make the man grow."10 " We want that education by which character is formed, strength of mind is increased, the intellect is expanded and by which one can stand on one's own feet."11

The Goal of Education is to achieve omniscience and personal perfection

In the Mundaka Upanisad [1.1.3] we find --

" O adorable sir, (which is that thing) which having been known, all this becomes known?" Thus Vedanta or ultimate knowledge is what makes a person all-knower or omniscient through the knowledge and realisation of the Universal Absolute which is denoted by the word Brahman. Why ? What is its value in life ?

Because:
