The answer given here is very significant, for it elaborates upon all the objectives: " Since He is the Ear of the ear, the Mind of the mind, the Speech of speech, the Life of life, and the Eye of the eye, therefore the intelligent (wise) men, after giving up (self-identification with the senses) (i.e., being freed from all imperfections resulting from such an imperfect view of oneself) and transcending this world of limitations, become immortal (i.e., attain infinitude of Existence- Consciousness-Bliss)." 16

Bhagavadgita on the Aims

Let us now turn our attention to the Gita.

In the seventh chapter Bhagavan Sri Krsna tells Arjuna:

In the thirteenth chapter `knowledge' is equated with perfection of character and Sri Krsna tells Arjuna -- " Humility, unpretentiousness, non-injury, forbearance, uprightness, service to the teacher, purity, steadiness, self-control, renunciation of sense-objects, absence of egoism, reflection on the evils of birth-death-old age-sickness and pain, non-attachment and non-identification of self with wife, home etc., constant even-mindedness in desirable and undesirable occurrences, unswerving devotion to God by the yoga in which one does not feel himself to have any existence separate from God, resort to sequestered places, distaste for the gatherings which serve no purpose, constant application of one's mind to spiritual knowledge, and understanding of the purpose of true knowledge -- this is called knowledge, and whatever is different from this is ignorance."19

## THE PROCESS OF EDUCATION

Absolute correspondence between the Goal and the Means

Before we discuss the details of the process, the method and the means, we should understand that in Vedanta every thing is derived from the very nature of the Ultimate Truth and thus the means is nothing but the reflection of the Goal itself. For example, the Universal Absolute is found to be of the nature of Homogeneous Existence-Knowledge-Bliss and this itself is the real nature of the individual. Hence it follows that:

All knowledge is inside

"Knowledge is inherent in man, no knowledge comes from outside; it is all inside. What we say a man `knows', should, in strict psychological language, be what he `discovers' or `unveils'. What a man `learns' is really what he `discovers' by taking the cover off his own soul, which is a mine of infinite knowledge. We say Newton discovered gravitation. Was it sitting anywhere in a corner waiting for him? It was in his own mind; the time came and he found it out. All knowledge that the world has ever received comes from the mind; the infinite library of the universe is in your own mind. The external world is only the suggestion, the occasion, which sets you to study your own mind. The falling of an apple gave the suggestion to Newton, and he studied his own mind. He rearranged all the previous links of thought in his mind and discovered a new link among them, which we call the law of gravitation." 21

Like fire in a piece of flint, knowledge exists in the mind; suggestion is the friction which brings it out." 22

Need of the Teacher

" But this ... does not preclude our receiving help from outside; nay in the vast majority of cases such help is absolutely necessary. This quickening impulse cannot be derived from books. The soul can only receive impulses from another soul, and from nothing else. ... The person from whose soul such impulse comes is called the Guru -- the teacher; and the person to whose soul the impulse is conveyed is called the Sisya -- the student." 23

That is why the Mundaka Upanisad says:

" For knowing that Reality he should go, with sacrificial faggots in hand, to a teacher alone, versed in the Vedas and absorbed in Brahman." 24

This raises the most important question – who can be the teacher ? But we shall take it up later when we discuss teachers’ education.

The Ideal Method

The first point to be carefully noted here is that the teacher and the student are praying together. Let us understand what it means. The teacher has discovered the Universal Absolute to be his own Self and as the Self of all including, of course, the student. It is this knowledge which he wishes to impart or transmit to the student or rather awaken it in him by removing the coverings. The channel of communication also has to be Love which again is the expression of the Reality common to them. Hence this prayer `together'. Commenting on the last clause of the prayer -- "May we not cavil at each other", Sri Sankaracarya says -- "There is occasion for ill-feeling on the part of the student in the matter of learning, as also on the part of the teacher, consequent on unwitting lapses; hence the prayer, `May we not cavil' etc., is made in order to forestall this." 26

For, unhindered love and mutual respect are the key-factors in the process called education according to Vedanta.

And then we see how the ideal process of education is revealed here : (i) firstly, Varuna placed some data before Bhrgu, gave a definition to guide him to think and hinted at concentration as the means to get at the knowledge; (ii) Bhrgu caught the hint, got an answer but was not satisfied with it and hence referred back to the teacher; (iii) who in turn confirmed Concentration as the means, saw that the direction of his search was right and encouraged him to proceed further and further till the definition could be pushed no further; and lastly (iv) that the Upanisad chooses to call this process by the name of the taught-and-the-teacher and also declares it to be available for all. Sankaracharya, while commenting on the above passage, says, “Thus becoming pure in mind through concentration … Bhrigu penetrated inside by degrees and … realised the innermost Bliss as Brahman.”

Let us concentrate a little more on `concentration' as the means to get at knowledge. Swami Vivekananda says:

So it is in every case; with the professor in his chair, the student with his book, with every man who is working to know. ... The more the power of concentration, the greater the knowledge that is acquired. ... this is the one call, the one knock, which opens the gates of Nature, and lets out floods of light. ... the power of concentration is the only key to the treasure-house of knowledge." 29

How do the organs come into play? The student is bent upon not only analytically thinking of the Reality and feeling it but also is keen to see it, sense it in every way. And this effort of discovering the Universal Absolute hidden as it were under all the coverings of the ever-changing phenomenal world of `I' and `you' and names and forms may be called `concentrated meditation'. It involves (i) analytical thinking and (ii) devotional feeling or loving absorption which takes a student deeper and deeper with (iii) a will or determination to know, together with (iv) the application of the power of restraint not allowing the mind or the senses to pull him outside in different directions. Ordinarily, the ever-changeful multiform world of appearances pulls our mind and organs outside and makes the mind scattered, while the search for the Reality which is Unchanging and Universally One requires exactly the opposite -- to collect the mind and the senses to one focus, to concentrate and to make them penetrate the appearance to look for the Reality. This is meditation. And through this meditation Bhrgu reached the Goal of education under the infallible guidance of his teacher. To feel the imperative need of meditation, we go over to Svetasvatara Upanisad which we have already seen for the details of the Goal and objectives -- how the exact nature of the cause of whatever happens in our life in this world is asked for. In the next verse we find that those students discussed all possible theories of the origin -- " Time, inherent nature, fate, chance, the elements, the (so called) individual soul, as the source, were considered and found insufficient. But their combination is not the source because they exist for the soul. The soul too is not independent on account of joy and sorrow."

During this process they clearly found the deficiency of logical intelligence itself in finding the answer conclusively.

Sankaracarya says -- "After having thus demolished the different views, and not finding another means of determining the Entity that defies all other means of realisation, they themselves realised the supreme primary Source by practising the yoga of meditation. The Upanisad declares this in:

" By practising the yoga of meditation they realised..." 31

Variation in methodology to suit the needs of students with differing aptitudes or psychoses.

The question naturally arises that though the method of concentrated meditation may be available for all, can all really benefit from it or rather are all ready or fit for it? If the student does not have the capacity for such concentrated meditation, what does he do? Obviously, the teacher has to devise methods and means of bringing the ever-active mind of the student to the serene state to enable him to achieve this capacity. The Vedanta tells us that on one side the Universal Absolute is the One Self of all and on the other side each individual is differently or uniquely constituted and hence though the Goal is same for all, viz., the realisation of the Universal Absolute Reality as their own Real Self, yet the starting points and hence the methods of approach necessarily vary. This we clearly see demonstrated in the Chandogya Upanisad where several methods have been mentioned in connection with the acquisition of the same true knowledge by different students. Let us have one such example to convince ourselves of this variety.

The following narrative is taken from the fourth chapter of Chandogya Upanisad. " Once upon a time, Satyakama Jabala accosted his mother Jabala with, `Honorable mother, I wish to live (in a teacher's house) as a celibate. Of what lineage am I?'

" She said to this one: `O my son, I do not know this, the lineage to which you belong. I got you in my youth when I was busy performing many duties, and remained engaged in serving. Being as I was, I do not know this as to which lineage you belong. But my name is Jabala and your name is Satyakama. So you speak of yourself as Satyakama Jabala.

" He having approached Haridrumata Gautama, said, `I shall live as celibate with you, the worshipful one. Therefore, I have come to you, the venerable one.

" To him, he said, `To what lineage do you, O good looking one, belong?' He ... (repeated his conversation with the mother and) said, `Sir, such as I am, I am Satyakama Jabala.' " To him he said, `... Fetch faggots for sacrifice, O good looking one. I shall initiate you since you did not depart from truth.' After initiating him (in the process of meditation etc.), he , having separated four hundred heads of cattle from among the thin and weak ones, said, `O good looking one, you follow them.' While driving them on he said, `I shall not return without a thousand.' He lived in exile for years. When they became a thousand --

To him he said: `The eastern side is one part, the western side is one part, the southern side is one part, the northern side is one part. Sri Sankaracarya in his commentary points out -- (i) "The story is meant for showing that faith and austerity are accessories of meditation on Brahman;" and (ii) "A knower of Brahman is possessed of tranquil organs and a smiling face; he is without care, and contented. Therefore the teacher said `You shine verily like a knower of Brahman'."

Let us also remark on two things. The family or social backgrounds of Bhrgu and the students referred in the Svetasvatara Upanisad on one hand and Satyakama on the other are very much different and so is their receptivity or capacity or faculties available to them. Bhrgu takes the hints from the teacher, directly goes inside himself, crosses layer after layer through powerful penetrative concentrated meditation and reaches the truth as guided by his teacher who is his own father. So do the other students after they have used up their analytical reasoning. Satyakama may not be having that purity and transparency of mind, but has perfect faith, purity of purpose, loving devotion and the capacity to translate it in terms of service. This helps in his meditation and finally he also reaches the goal by a different method. However we also see that in spite of these differences, meditation seems to have been the prescription in all the methodologies.

The Bhagavadgita on different methodologies

Sri Krsna tells us -- "Through meditation, some realise the Self in their being with the help of the internal organ, others through the yoga of analytical knowledge and others through the yoga of action. Others, again, who do not know thus, take to their heart what they hear from others(i.e.

Chhandogya 4.4.1 to 4.9.3

teachers); they too who are devoted to hearing, certainly overcome death (by realising their real Self)."

Sankaracarya explains: " Meditation means contemplation on the Self after withdrawing the organs of hearing etc. from the objects like sound etc. into the mind, and then withdrawing the mind into the indwelling conscious Self. Thus ... meditation is a constant and uninterrupted current of thought (and feeling) like a line of pouring oil. Through that meditation some yogis realize the indwelling consciousness i.e. the Self with the help of the internal organ that has been purified by meditation."

As for the others, we easily understand by the context that those who do not possess the capacity to be totally devoted to meditation take the help of analytical thinking along with meditation, and those whose mind is too restless use their activity itself to make it one-pointed etc. by dedicating their actions to God. Others may lack understanding but use their faith to finally achieve the same concentration and meditation.

Examples of various methods to suit different students

Let us now see a few more methods, suitable for different individuals, used by teachers in imparting knowledge.

We continue our study of the Chandogya Upanisad in this light and go to the sixth chapter. We have already seen Svetaketu's father showing him the inadequacy of the education received by him up to that point, because he had not realised that by knowing which what is unknown becomes known! Now we continue with the narrative to see the method of instruction employed by his father. " Svetaketu said, `May yourself, venerable sir, tell me that., `O good looking one, so be it', said he. "

" `O good looking one, in the beginning this was Existence alone, One only, without a second. With regard to that some say, "In the beginning this was non-existence alone, one only, without a second. From that non-existence issued existence." '

" `O good looking one, by what logic can existence verily come out of non-existence? Surely, in the beginning all this was Existence, One only, without a second.

" `That (Existence) saw(visualised), "I shall become many. I shall be born." That created fire. ... water. ... food. ...

" `That Deity which is such saw: "Let it be that now, by entering into these three cosmic elements Fire, Water and Food, in the form of the soul of each individual being, I shall clearly manifest name and form." ...

" `Food when eaten becomes divided in three ways. Of it, that which is the grossest ingredient, that turns into faeces. That which is the medium constituent becomes flesh. That which is the subtlest becomes mind.

" `Water(fluids) when drunk becomes divided in three ways. Of it, that which is the grossest ingredient, that turns into urine. That which is the medium constituent, that becomes blood. That which is the subtlest, that becomes the vital force.

" `Fire (in the form of fats etc.) when eaten becomes divided in three ways. Of it, that which is the grossest ingredient, that becomes bone. That which is the medium constituent, that becomes marrow. That which is the subtlest, that becomes (the organ of) speech.

" ...' `May the venerable sir explain to me over again (with examples ... firm conviction has not risen in me).' So be it, O good looking one', he said.

" `O good-looking one, in this very way, of food when it is eaten, that which is the subtle part, that rises upward, and that becomes mind.' ...

" `O good looking one, mind is surely made of food, vital force is made of water, and speech is made of fire.' (The idea is, `What I have said is logical.') (Svetaketu said: `But I do not get an absolutely firm conviction that the mind is made of food alone. Therefore) `May the venerable sir explain to me over again.' `Let it be so, O good looking one', he said.

" `O good looking one, a person has sixteen parts. Do not eat for fifteen days. Drink water as much as you like. The vital force is made up of water. It will depart if you do not drink.' " He did not eat for fifteen days. Then he approached him (saying), `Sir what shall I speak of?' He said, ` O good looking one, (recite) the Rik-mantras, the Yajur-mantras.' `Sir, they indeed do not flash in my mind.'

" To him he said, `O good looking one, as a single ember of the size of a fire-fly remains as a residue of a big fire, and by that nothing bigger than that is burnt -- in this way, O good looking one, one of your sixteen parts remains as a residue. With that you do not remember the Vedas at this time.' " He took food. Then he approached him. Whatever he asked him, he understood all of it. " To him he said, `O good looking one, as a single ember of the size of a fire-fly remaining as a residue of a big fire, should it be made to blaze up by adding to it a heap of grass, then, by that is burnt much more than itself. O good looking one, surely mind is made of food, vital force is made of water, speech is made of fire.' That (statement) of his he learnt, he learnt."34

Shall we call it `the example and experiment method'?

Several examples and experiments continue throughout this chapter and finally the father leads the son to the realisation of the Supreme Truth -- "Thou art That" -- the Reality of the individual is the same Universal Absolute..

And let us mention that in the next chapter, we find Sanatkumara using a completely different procedure to help his student Narada, who is already a venerable sage, to realise that his true nature was Infinite -- One without a second.

`Life with the teacher' as an important aspect of the `process'

One salient feature to be noted in all these narratives is the student's life with the teacher. Swami Vivekananda, the modern representative of Vedanta, has this to say -- "My idea of education is Gurugriha-vasa (living in the abode of the teacher). Without the personal life of the teacher, there would be no education." 35

And again, " One should live from his very boyhood with one whose character is a blazing fire and should have before him a living example of the highest teaching. In our country the imparting of knowledge has always been through men of renunciation." 36

## EVALUATION

Evaluation: its purpose and levels

Let us now consider Vedantic ideas of `evaluation' in education. Usually evaluation has to be thought of on three levels: (i) before admission to a particular course; (ii) during the process; and (iii) at the end of the course. Evaluation `during the process', again, is (a) regarding the progress made by the individual students, and (b) regarding the ability of the teacher, and (c) the efficacy of the method itself.

The most important feature of Vedantic evaluation at any stage is that its purpose is never to reject a student etc. But rather to find out ways and means of applying changes in the `methods' by which the student will ultimately pass.

Evaluation at the `end'

Applying this principle `at the end', Sri Krsna asks Arjuna:

" O Partha(Arjuna), has this been listened to by you with a one-pointed mind? O Dhananjaya (Arjuna), has your delusion caused by ignorance been destroyed (For which purpose has there been this effort on your part for hearing the scripture, and on My part, the effort of being a teacher)?" 39 Sankaracarya comments: " In order to ascertain whether or not the disciple has comprehended the meaning of the Scripture, the Lord asks (this question), the intention of the questioner being, `If it is known that it has not been comprehended, I shall again make him grasp it through other means.' Hereby is shown the duty of the teacher that a student should be made to achieve his goal by taking the help of a different method."

In this connection, let us again remember the incident in the Chandogya Upanisad (discussed at the beginning of this article). When Svetaketu returned home thinking that he had completed his education, his father said to him, `O Svetaketu, O good looking one, now that you are conceited, proud of being a learned man, and immodest like this, did you ask about that instruction --(about the Supreme Brahman) through which the unheard of becomes heard, the unthought of becomes thought of, the unknown becomes known?' `O venerable sir, in what way is that instruction imparted?' " `O good looking one, as by knowing a lump of earth, all things made of earth become known. All transformation has speech as its basis, and it is name only. Earth as such is the reality.'" and then " Svetaketu said, `Those venerable teachers did not certainly know this. For if they had known this,

why should they not have told me? May yourself, venerable sir, tell me that., `O good looking one, so be it', said he. " 40

Testing the competence

Here, again, the purpose is not to reject but (i) to show him the way to become competent, and also (ii) to find methods of education suiting the available talents of the individual; and (iii) still more important is to make the student conscious of his ability, so that he feels confident and encouraged to undergo the process set up before him.

We move on to Kathopanisad, where Nachiketa has gone to a great teacher Yama and is asking him -- " This doubt that arises, consequent on the death of a man -- some saying, `It exists', and others saying, `It does not exist' -- I would know this, under your instruction."

The teacher, while testing him, apparently tries to put him off by saying: "With regard to this, even the gods entertained doubts in days of yore: for being subtle, this substance (the Self) is not easily comprehended. O Nachiketa, ask for some other boon; do not press me; give up this that is demanded of me."

Nachiketa replies: "Even the gods entertained doubt with regard to this thing; and O Death (Yama), since you too say that It is not well comprehended and since any other instructor like you, of this thing, is not to be had, therefore there is no other boon comparable to this one." Although told this, still Yama says by way of testing: "Ask for sons and grandsons that will be centenarians. Ask for many animals, elephants and gold, and horses, and a vast expanse of the earth. And you yourself live for as many years as you like. If you think any other boon to be equal to this, ask for that. ... I make you fit for the enjoyment of all delectable things. Whatever things there be that are desirable but difficult to get -- pray for all those cherished things according to your choice. Here are these women with chariots and musical instruments -- such are not surely to be had by mortals. With these, who are offered by me, you get yourself served. o Nachiketa, do not enquire about death." Although tempted thus, Nachiketa, not to be perturbed like a vast lake, said: "O Death, ephemeral are these, and they waste away the vigour of all the senses that a man has. All life without exception, is short indeed. Let the vehicles be yours alone; let the dances and songs be yours. Man is not to be satisfied with wealth. ... What decaying mortal who ... knows of higher goals, will take delight in a long life while conscious of the worthlessness of music, disport, and the joy thereof? O Death, tell us of that thing ... whose knowledge leads to a great result. Apart from this boon, which relates to the inscrutable thing, Nachiketa does not pray for any other."

Having tested the disciple and found his fitness for knowledge, he said : "The preferable is different indeed; and so, indeed, is the pleasurable different. These two, serving divergent purposes, bind men (to their respective courses). Good befalls him who accepts the preferable among these two. He who selects the pleasurable falls from the true end. The preferable and the pleasurable approach mankind. The man of intelligence, having considered them, separates the two. the intelligent one selects the electable in preference to the delectable; ... O Nachiketa! you, such as you are, have discarded, after consideration, all the desirable things that are themselves delightful ... . You have not accepted the path of wealth in which many a man comes to grief. That which is known as knowledge (which has for its object the preferable) and that which is known as ignorance (which has for its object the pleasurable) are widely contradictory, and they follow divergent courses. I consider Nachiketa(`you') to be an aspirant for knowledge, because the enjoyable things, multifarious though they be, did not tempt you. (This he said by way of making him conscious of (i) the mental tendencies underlying this fitness and (ii) the great asset which he (the student) possessed.) And then the praise: "The wisdom that you have, O dearest one, which leads to sound knowledge ... is not to be attained through argumentation. You are, O compassionable one, endowed with true resolution. May our questioner be like you, O Nachiketa."

And the full encouragement: "I consider that the mansion (of Brahman) is wide open to Nachiketa."41

Sankaracarya says that as the effect of such declarations Nachiketa felt: `I am fit and you, too, sir, are pleased with me' and proceeded (enthusiastically) with his query.

The Mundaka Upanisad says: " To him who approaches duly, whose heart is calm and whose outer organs are under control, that man of enlightenment should adequately impart that knowledge of Brahman by which one realises the true and immutable Purusa." 42

Sri Krsna tells Arjuna: " This, that I have taught you, should not ever be taught to one who is devoid of Tapas and to one who is not a devotee; also, neither to one who does not render service, nor as well to one who cavils at Me."

And again, " He who, entertaining supreme devotion to Me, will speak of this highest secret to My devotees, will without doubt reach me alone." 43

If the reference to `Me' in these verses raises doubt as to whether the intended meaning is `The Teacher' or `The Supreme God', we get the answer in Svetasvatara Upanisad, which tells: " He who has supreme devotion to God (The Effulgent One), and as much of it to the teacher as to God, to him, indeed, to the great-souled one, these subject-matters that have been spoken become revealed." 44

## THREE MORE ASPECTS OF EDUCATION

It is not possible to do full justice to these topics in this paper devoted to the study of higher or real education according to Vedanta. However a few ideas are being noted.

Preparation for Education according to Vedanta

It must have been noticed that Education according Vedanta chiefly is what could be termed as `Higher Education'. And this is clearly stated in the Mundaka Upanisad -- " There are two kinds of knowledge to be acquired -- the higher and the lower. ... Of these the lower comprises the Rgveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvaveda, the science of pronunciation etc., the code of rituals, grammar, etymology, metre, and astrology. Then there is the higher knowledge by which is realised that Immutable ... that which cannot be perceived and grasped; which is without source, features, eyes, and ears; which has neither hands nor feet; which is eternal, multiformed, all-pervasive, extremely subtle, and undiminshing; and which is the source of all." 45

What is described as lower knowledge here can easily be taken to mean the `preparatory education.' But if we apply the principle of absolute correspondence between the goals and the means here, we understand that such training of Intellect, heart, will and limbs, and self-control should make up the Preparatory education which will make the student possess the required aptitude for the higher or the real education.

We find this beautifully depicted in the prayer in the beginning of Kenopanisad. " Aum ! May my limbs, speech, vital force, eyes, ears, as also strength and all the organs, become well developed. Everything is the Brahman revealed in the Upanisads. May I not deny Brahman; May not Brahman deny me. ... May all the virtues that are spoken of in the Upanisads repose in me who am engaged in the pursuit of the Self; may they repose in me. Om peace! Peace! Peace!" 46

The obvious implication is that the proper development of the personality results in the conviction that `all is Brahman which has been revealed in the Upanisads (has been realised by the sages) and it is very natural that I can and should also realise the same. For that I need those traits of personality which have been spoken of in the Upanisads. (Which we have discussed at great length in various contexts.)' This dynamic conviction is tantamount to aptitude for real knowledge. In Swami Vivekananda's words: " We want that education by which character is formed, strength of mind is increased, the intellect is expanded and by which one can stand on one's own feet."47

And again: " the training by which the current and expression of will are brought under control and become fruitful, is called education." 48

In the Taittiriya Upanisad we find some brilliant ideas of the preparatory education should be so designed so as to make the individual evolve to receive the real, higher education Mundaka. 1.2.13

Gita 18.67-68

Svetasvatara 6.23

Mundaka 1.1.4-6

Kena: Prayer

CW Vol.5 p.257

CW Vol.4 p.423

“We shall speak of the science of pronunciation. The things to be learnt are the alphabet, accent, measure, emphasis, uniformity, juxtaposition. " 49

We see later on that while teaching juxtapositions, counting numbers etc., the Upanisad is always trying to present cosmic, noble and widening ideas to the student. For example “The earth is the first letter. Heaven is the last letter. The sky is the meeting-place. … The teacher is the first letter. The student is the last letter. Knowledge is the meeting-place. …” 50

Education Continued Or the Cycle of Education

If "Education is the means to preserve, modify and transfer its culture to the coming generation", when does such education start ? It should certainly start with the would be parents themselves being educated to be ready to impart education to the forthcoming child. Because the process of education starts from the pre-natal influences on the child and continues till the end of life. Let us read two passages from the Taittiriya Upanisad instructing the would be parents. " Righteousness and learning and teaching or self-recital of Vedas (are to be practised). Truth and learning and teaching or self-recital. Austerity etc. and learning and teaching or self-recital. Control of the outer senses and learning and teaching or self-recital. Control of the inner organs and learning and teaching or self-recital. The fires (for daily worship) and learning and teaching or self-recital. The daily worship and learning and teaching or self-recital. Guests (are to be looked after) and learning and teaching or self-recital. Social good conduct and learning and teaching or self-recital. Children and learning and teaching or self-recital. Procreation and learning and teaching or self-recital (are to be practised). A grandson and learning and teaching or self-recital. Truth is the thing -- this is what Satyavacha Rathitara thinks. Austerity is the thing -- this is what Taponitya Paurushisti thinks. Learning and teaching or self-recital alone (are the things) -- this is what Naka Moudgalya thinks. For this indeed is the austerity; that indeed is struggle of life."

Having completed the task of education, the preceptor imparts this post-instruction to the students :

"Speak the truth. Practise righteousness. Make no mistake about study. Having offered the desirable wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the line of progeny. There should be no inadvertence about truth. There should be no deviation from righteous activity. There should be no error about self-protection. Do not neglect activities leading to prosperity. Do not be careless about learning and teaching.

“There should be no error in the duties towards the gods and forefathers. Let your mother be a goddess unto you. Let your father be a god unto you. Let your teacher be a god unto you. Let your guest be a god unto you. The works that are not blameworthy are to be resorted to, but not the others. Those actions of ours that are commendable are to be followed by you, but not the others. “You should, by offering seats, remove the fatigue of those learned virtuous people who are more praiseworthy among us. The offering of gifts or money should be with honor; the offering should not be with dishonor. The offering should be in plenty. The offering should be with modesty. The offering should be with awe. The offering should be with sympathy.

“Then, should you have any doubt with regard to duties or customs, you should behave in those matters just as the learned virtuous people do, who may happen to be there and who are able deliberators, who are adepts in those duties and customs, who are not directed by others, who are not cruel, and who are desirous of merit. Then as for the accused people, you should behave with regard to them just as the learned virtuous people do, who may happen to be there and who are able deliberators, who are adepts in those duties and customs, who are not directed by others, who are not cruel, and who are desirous of merit.

“This is the injunction. This is the instruction. This is the secret of education. This is the Divine Command. This is how the character is to be cultivated. This is how the character must be cultivated. 51

How would these parents teach the children ?

By their own actions and attitudes and by their way of dealing with the children. The Vedanta tells us, “" Each soul is potentially divine; and the Goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal.”52 This has clearly two dimensions or aspects. One Taittiriya 1.2.1

Taittiriya 1.3.1-3

Taittiriya 1.8.1; 1.11.1-4

CW Vol.1 Page

is to be followed in one’s own life and the other is to mould our attitude towards everyone including our children. This should be understood along with the other most important truth that each individual is unique in his/her manifestation of the same inherent divinity.

So the parents look upon their own lives as a relentless struggle to manifest the inherent divinity and hence do not give up the cultivation of knowledge till death, and they look upon their children as embodiments of the same divinity with their own individual unique features in manifestation and try their utmost to help the children evolve towards this manifestation of divinity in their individual unique manner.

The child grows till he becomes qualified to approach a suitable teacher for his higher education.

Teachers’ Education according to Vedanta

This brings us to most vital part of the education system – dealing with the education of the teacher.

Swami Vivekananda says, “He who is learned in the scriptures, sinless, unpolluted by lust, and is the greatest knower of the Brahman is the real teacher.” 53

He elaborates, “In regard to the teacher, we must see that he knows the spirit of the scriptures. The whole world reads Bibles, Vedas, and Korans; but they are all only words, syntax, etymology, philology, the dry bones … . The teacher who deals too much in words and allows the mind to be carried away by the force of words loses the spirit. It is the knowledge of the spirit of the scriptures alone that constitutes the true … teacher. … The second condition necessarry in the teacher is – sinlessness. … The third condition is in regard to the motive. The teacher must not teach with any ulterior selfish motive – for money, name, or fame; his work must be simply out of love, out of pure love for mankind at large.” 54

What if one has not realised this state of perfection ? Should he aspire to be a teacher or not ? He can – provided he knows that he is not perfect, that life is a struggle for perfection, that when he helps the student to manifest his perfection, it helps him (the teacher) also and so looks upon his student with love and respect and above all is utmost sincere in his own struggle for perfection. This is the spirit which should guide all concerned when they think of educating the teachers.

Implementation of Swami Vivekananda's Ideas on Education

-- Swami Pitambarananda, Chandigarh

A letter written by Swami Vivekananda on March 3, 1894 from Chicago to Shri Singaravelu Mudaliar in Madras, is so vital in understanding the basic tenets of his `creed' that it has been published in the `Complete Works' (Vol.IV, Page 358) under the significant title "What we believe in - ". In this letter Swamiji says --

" Education is the manifestation of perfection already in man.

" Religion is the manifestation of divinity already in man. "

These two sentences written together and in this order in this letter of vital importance provide the key to Swami Vivekananda's ideas on Education as well as on its relation with religion, which again is the main theme of his thoughts on the development of man.

Swami Vivekananda's ideas about the very goal of human life and the means of its achievement are only the elaboration of the above quoted thought on religion. In what could be called his 4 aphorisms on religion, he says --

" Each soul is potentially divine.

" The goal is to manifest this Divinity within, by controlling nature, external and internal. " Do this either by work, or worship, or psychic control, or philosophy -- by one, or more, or all of these, and be free.

" This is the whole of religion. " (C.W.,I,124)

Now, if the very goal of life is achieved by religion, what is the place of `education' in his scheme? In this context we mark that his ideas on Education and Religion are expressed in very much similar terms and that also together in a sequence.

On this background, let us study their correlation. Both are processes of manifestation; one manifests `perfection' and the other `divinity'. The use of two different words in successive sentences in different definitions implies that he does not use them as synonyms, otherwise education will be same as religion and vice versa and there would be no need of two separate definitions at all. And yet the similarity of expression and the very fact of their togetherness strongly suggest a deep and direct inner relation between the two. And it seems that in Swami Vivekananda's vision, education is the first step or base on which religion comes as completion of the process or fulfilment.

This is exactly the place of education in the Taittiriya Upanishad where the Shikshavalli (Chapter on education) is followed by Brahmanandavalli (Or the chapter on fulfilment through religion) and, next, their inner connection through the common methodology is revealed in Bhriguvalli (i.e., chapter on methodology).

More clearly, in the Bhagwadgita (Chapter XVIII Stanza 50), we find --

" Siddhim prapto yatha brahma tathapnoti nibodha me

Samasenaiva kaunteya nistha jnanasya ya para "

--" Know from me, O son of Kunti, how a human being, who has already attained `perfection' attains `divinity' (the all-pervading God) through the culmination of steadfastness in the pursuit of `knowledge'. "

[ In Indian history we find Shri Shankaracharya (8th century A.D.) and Shri Vishwambhar, the elder brother of Shri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (15th century) and innumerable others, devoting themselves fully to the pursuit of religion immediately after completing education.]

It is now absolutely clear what Swami Vivekananda has in his mind as to the relation between perfection and divinity and thus between education and religion.

More specifically, he says, about education --

1. " Perfecting the instrument and getting complete mastery of my own mind [is the ideal of education]." (C.W.,I,510)

2. " We want that education by which character is formed, strength of mind is increased, the intellect is expanded, and by which one can stand on one's own feet. " (C.W.,V,342)

3. " The training by which the current and expression of will are brought under control and become fruitful is called education. " (C.W.,IV,490)

4. " The education that does not help the common mass of people to equip themselves for the struggle for life, which does not bring out strength of character, a spirit of philanthropy and the courage of a lion -- is it worth the name ?" (C.W.,VII,147)

5. " It is one of the evils of your Western civilisation, that you are after intellectual education alone and take no care of the heart.It only makes men ten times more selfish." (C.W.,I,412)

6. " Intellect has been cultured with the result that hundreds of sciences have been discovered, and their effect has been that the few have made slaves of the many -- that is all the good that has been done. Artificial wants have been created; and every poor man, whether he has the money or not, desires to have those wants satisfied, and when he cannot, he struggles, and dies in the struggle. This is the result. Through the intellect is not the way to solve the problem of misery, but through the heart. If all this vast amount of effort had been spent in making men purer, gentler, more forbearing, this world would have a thousandfold more happiness than it has today. Always cultivate the heart; through the heart the Lord speaks, and through the intellect you yourself speak. (C.W.,I,414-415)

7. " ... the laws which develop this personality, and by proper attention to those laws and methods, each one can grow and strengthen his personality. This is one of the great practical things, and this is the secret of all education. " (C.W.,II,16)

8. " The goal of mankind is knowledge. ... Now this knowledge, again, is inherent in man. No knowledge comes from outside; it is all inside. What we say a man `knows', should, in strict psychological language, be what he `discovers' or `unveils', what a man `learns' is what he `discovers', by taking the cover off his own soul, which is a mine of infinite knowledge." (C.W,I,27-28)

9. " The teacher spoils everything by thinking that he is teaching. Within man is all knowledge, and it requires only an awakening, and that much is the work of the teacher." (C.W.,V,366)

Thus education evolves `man' from the mere `biped', and religion evolves `God' from that `man'.

This also gives us a clue to the methods to be used in education which is the stepping stone to religion. Training of will, culture of heart, strength of mind and power of concentration, and broad philosophical outlook and wisdom are the essentials of education.

It is on this background that we can understand all his ideas on education and think out the ways of implementing them.

1. Role of Educators :-

All the people involved in the process of education have to understand and assimilate first of all the first two aphorisms mentioned above, viz., each soul is potentially divine and the goal of life is to manifest this inherent Divinity.

(a) In the first place it should give them a vision about the purpose & plan of their own lives -- " man is man so long as he is struggling to rise above nature, and this nature is both internal and external " (C.W. II, 64-65). It is then and then only that an educator can really contribute anything in the process of education.

(b) Next, he has to see the part his activities in the field of education are going to play in his own life -- His educatorship is the means by which he is going to struggle to manifest his divinity. The students, the school, the lessons are the means, just as for a worshipper the images, the paraphernalia of worship and the worship itself are the instruments, for his struggle towards perfection.

(c) Then, he has to look upon the students as potentially divine and potentially perfect and his work for them helps in his own evolution and so he is obliged to them and not they to him.

(d) The process of education should not be that of spoon-feeding but that of encouraging to think, feel and act freely and correctly.

2. Aptitude tests and vocational guidance

The idea of `Manifestation' of `potential' perfection and divinity when understood in the context of ShriRamakrishna-Vivekananda's emphasis on the acceptance of `variety of human nature' implies that development of an individual should take place along lines more natural to each individual. Hence, an elaborate method of finding out the special aptitudes of the students has to be worked out. This will help the students (i) to know which special line they should pursue while going in for higher education, and/or

(ii) which talent should be cultivated as special hobby in life. There has to be an interaction with the parents also in order to educate them on this key to real success in life. This will put an end to the rat-race in different fields of human endeavour.

3. What values are universally accepted and really conducive to man-making?

Answer: The Supreme values are :-- i) Awareness of potential divinity in oneself resulting in real stable Self-Confidence and healthy positive attitude.

ii) Awareness of potential divinity in others resulting in love and respect for all others irrespective of their caste, creed or nationality.

We can also add :

a. Fearlessness / Boldness b. Purity of Heart c. Constant Pursuit of Higher Values d. Austerity and Struggle for Perfection e. Steadfastness in the pursuit of knowledge.

f. Self-control g. Truthfulness / Uprightness h. Tranquillity / Steadiness / Even-mindedness i. Charity / Nobility / Spirit of sacrifice j. Kindness to Beings k. Humility / Gentleness / Modesty l. Forgiveness / Forbearence / Fortitude m. Cleanliness n. Dignity of manual labour o. Reverence to the teacher p. Introspection q. Non-attachment r. Faith and love for the Almighty God s. Absence of Jealousy, ill-feeling and hatred t. Freedom from Slander u. Absence/Control over Anger v. Non-craving for Enjoyments or Absence of Self-Indulgence w. Absence of Greed x. Absence of Conceit y. Absence of Arrogance and Rudeness.

z. Absence of Ostentation

4. What methods of implementation do you suggest at school, college and University levels?

Answer: We should orient the entire education system towards it so that education becomes true education.

a) For example, the very appearence and upkeep of the educational institutions and their Surroundings must be thought of as integral parts of `education'.

(i) The campus and buildings in every educational institution have to be kept spotlessly clean and most of the cleaning should be done by the staff and the students supervised by the Principal to inculcate

(a) dignity of manual labour, (b) love and regards for that section of the society who keep our city etc. clean, ( c) Cleanliness as a value, and (d) mental and moral benefits derived from cleanliness.

(ii) Great and noble thoughts should be prominently displayed in all possible places.

b) Similarly, we should use all direct and indirect methods of inculcating and strengthening values.

c) At least at school level there should be teacher-parent association -- a forum where values should be discussed and encouraged.

d) At college level groups should be formed under a tutor or counseller to discuss ways and means of imbibing values.

The approach must necessarily be multi-dimensional e) Some of the means suggested are i) compulsory class on moral education at every level ii) the course content, especially of language and literature topics must contain inspiring passages from the lives and teachings of great men of all countries whose lives have been shining examples of values leading to real success and glory of life.

iii) Teachers should be trained for counselling and this must be introduced in all educational institutions for guiding individuals.

iv) Activities like Boy-scouts, N.S.S., etc. should be made a part of education.
teacher-taught:
## T E A C H E R - T A U G H T R E L A T I O N S H I P

## I N I N D I A N C U L T U R E

Its Deterioration; and how to revive and promote it.

[Paper for the seminar on September 14 and 15, 1996

organised by the Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan, Chandigarh]

-- Sw. Pitambarananda, RAMAKRISHNA MISSION ASHRAMA

Epitomised Statement

What Indian Culture has to say about the teacher has been epitomised in the most popular Guru-stotra in the Visvasaratantra. The first three verses of this hymn run as follows :

"The teacher is the creator of this universe, its preserver and destroyer; he himself is the Reality beyond this universe; salutation to that teacher.

"the Reality which is partless, all-encompassing and which pervades the universe of sentient and non-sentient beings, was shown to the disciple by the teacher; salutations to that teacher.

"The eyes of the disciple were blinded by the disease of ignorance. the teacher gave him eyesight by curing his decease by the collirium of knowledge; salutation to that teacher." 1

This is not a mere sentiment. There are important factors ingrained in the Indian Culture which make up this unique relationship.

Firstly, it is held that the process of learning does not depend upon the mass of `information' made available to the student, but it consists of the `formation' of his mind and personality -- or rather the `transformation' of man, the biped mammal to man, who knows how to think, feel and act, and from such a man to the perfect individual who is a fit channel or vehicle for manifestation of the Divine on this earth.

Secondly, Indian Culture has discovered the fundamental truth that the human soul is the repository of infinite knowledge, purity and power which are lying dormant, covered by his ignorance and its reactions in the form of animal instincts etc.

Hence the teacher has to go within his student as it were, and help, guide and inspire him to manifest his divine potential by ably tackling the covering dross. And thus the process of learning becomes a process of discovery and unfoldment.

Examples from the most ancient literature

1. The best example of this teacher-taught relationship may perhaps be shown from the Taittiriya Upanishad.

The most ancient record of the Indian Culture is contained in the Vedas. All the Vedas have two distinct portions -- the ritual portion and the knowledge portion. This knowledge portion is

[[ORIG]]

called the Upanishads. Almost invariably the Upanishads present to us knowledge of religion, philosophy, character-building, culture etc. through teacher-taught relationship and dialogues. The third chapter of the Taittiriya Upanishad runs thus :

"May He protect us (the teacher and the taught) together. May He nourish us both together. May we both acquire strength together. Let our study be brilliant. May we not cavil at each other. Aum Peace Peace Peace.

"Bhrgu, the well-known son of Varuna, approached his father Varuna with the request, `O revered sir, teach me Brahman (the all-pervading reality)'. To him he said this : `Food, vital force, eye, ear,mind,speech -- these(are the aids to the knowledge of Brahman).' To him he (further) said: `Crave to know well that from which all these beings take birth, that by which they live after being born, towards which they move and into which they merge. That is Brahman.' He practised concentration. He, having practised concentration --.

"(He) realised food (consciousness associated with matter) as Brahman. For it is verily from food that all these beings take birth, on food they subsist after being born, and they move towards and merge into food. Having realised that, he again approached his father Varuna with the request, `O revered sir, teach me Brahman.' To him he said: `Crave to know Brahman well through concentration; concentration is Brahman.' He practised concentration. He, having practised concentration --

"(He) knew the vital force (consciousness associated with energy) as Brahman; for from the vital force, indeed, spring all these beings; having come into being, they live through the vital force; they move towards and enter into the vital force. Having known thus, he again approached his father Varuna with the request, `O revered sir, teach me Brahman.' To him he said: `Crave to know Brahman well through concentration; concentration is Brahman.' He practised concentration. He, having practised concentration --

"(He) knew the mind (consciousness associated with mind) as Brahman; for from the mind, indeed, spring all these beings; having been born, they are sustained by the mind; and they move towards and merge into the mind. Having known that, he approached his father Varuna again and made the request, `O revered sir, teach me Brahman.' To him he said: `Crave to know Brahman well through concentration; concentration is Brahman.' He practised concentration. He, having practised concentration --

"(He) knew knowledge (awareness) as Brahman; for from knowledge, indeed, spring all these beings; having been born, they are sustained by knowledge; they move towards and merge in knowledge. Having known that, he approached his father Varuna again with the request, `O revered sir, teach me Brahman.' To him he said: `Crave to know Brahman well through concentration; concentration is Brahman.' He practised concentration. He, having practised concentration --

"(He) knew Bliss (undividedness) as Brahman; for from Bliss, indeed, all these beings originate; having been born, they are sustained by Bliss; they move towards and merge in Bliss. This knowledge realised by Bhrgu and imparted by Varuna terminates in the Supreme, established in the cavity of the heart. He who knows thus becomes firmly established ..."

The points to be carefully noted here are that (i) firstly, Varuna placed some data before Bhrgu, gave a definition to guide him to think and hinted at concentration as the means to get at the knowledge; (ii) Bhrgu caught the hint, got an answer but was not satisfied with it and hence referred back to the teacher; (iii) who in tern confirmed Concentration as the means, saw that the direction of his search was right and encouraged him to proceed further and further till the definition could be pushed no further; and lastly (iv) that the Upanishad chooses to call this process by the name of the taught-and-the-teacher and also declares it to be universally applicable.

2. While introducing the Kathopanishad, Sri Sankaracharya exclaims -- "Salutation to Most revered Yama, son of Sun and the imparter of the Supreme Knowledge, and salutation to Nachiketa

[the ideal disciple];" -- thereby showing how important and relevant are both for the process of learning.

3. The Mundakopanishad tells --

"For knowing that Reality he must go, with sacrificial faggots in hand, to a teacher, versed in the Vedas and absorbed in Brahman.

"To him who approaches duly, whose heart is calm and whose outer organs are under control, that man of enlightenment should adequately impart that knowledge of Brahman by which one realises the true and immutable Purusha." (1-2-12,13).

4. The Prasnopanishad tells us a beautiful story. There were six seekers who were stuck up at different points in the course of their search for higher and higher truths. They with common intent and mutual consent went to Pippalada, a sage known for his almost omniscience. "To them the seer said, `Live (here) again for a year in a fitting manner, with control over the senses and with brahmacharya and faith. Then put questions as you please. If we know, we shall explain all your questions." (1-2)

And when everything was most satisfactorily answered, "to them he said, `I know this supreme Brahman thus far only. Beyond this there is nothing'." (6-7)

And then "while worshipping him they said `You indeed are our father who have ferried us across nescience to the other shore. Salutation to the great seers'." (6-8)

The idea is that the `father' gives us this body with which we begin our instinctive life, but the `teacher' transforms our being in such a way that then we have a personality in which the light of knowledge is always functioning. This is our second birth -- the birth in knowledge.

5. The Svetasvataropanisad concludes its teaching by saying --

"He who has supreme devotion to God and the same to his teacher, for him the words spoken here will reveal their inner meanings."

Krishna and Arjuna

Coming down from the Upanishads with the course of history, we reach the age of Mahabharata which should be called the medieval age if we think of Indian history as a whole. Here we find a brilliant example of what really teacher-taught relationship could be. If anyone could be a `friend, philosopher and guide' as the modern expression goes, it could not have a better example than Bhagavan Sri Krishna in relation to Arjuna.

We turn to Gita to find some salient features of the teacher-taught relationship.

1. Due to the onrush of attachment to the kith and kin, Arjuna's thinking process gets completely vitiated and he talks of running away from his duty. At this point Sri Krishna says --

"From where has this dirt entered your thinking in this critical time, which is not befitting a noble person, not conducive to virtue nor to good name ? O Son of Kunti, do not yield to impotence, it does not befit you. Giving up this mean faintheartedness, get up O scorcher of foes !"

The two things to be noted here are (i) He uses no uncertain terms to condemn the mistaken thinking and yet (ii) He raises Arjuna's morale by saying `it does not befit you' and by the use of the significant adjective `scorcher of foes' thus bringing out the best potential in him. This results inevitably in Arjuna's acceptance not only of his mistakes in thinking but of his supreme faith in Krishna's capacity to guide him which he expresses by saying -

"My nature is lost due to lop-sided thinking" and "I surrender to you; please teach me."

2. We now turn to 6th chapter to find another salient feature.

Krishna has given a masterly discourse on `meditation'. Arjuna introspects in that context and finds his own weakness which would not allow him to follow those instructions successfully. He does not hypocritically nod his head or hide his own findings but lays his mind bare before his teacher. He says --

"The Yoga which you you have spoken of as consisting of evenness of mind, O Madhusudana, I find it difficult to adhere to on account of the restlessness of mind. It is really not only restless, but also turbulent, strong in erring and adamant. I find its control as difficult as the control of wind."

This is what a genuine learner should do.

And the teacher ? Does he condemn him for his shortcoming ? No. He readily accepts that the weakness mentioned is already known. And a solution for the same is already at hand.

Remarkable teacher and taught indeed !

And yet this is not all.

3. We now turn to the 18th chapter. The dialogue is practically over. Arjuna seems to have got answers to all his doubts and difficulties. But now it is the teacher who comes up with the `million dollar question' -

"Have you, O Partha, listened to all my words with due attention ? Has your delusion born of ignorance vanished ?"

The great commentator Sankaracharya explains this interrogation thus : "In order to ascertain whether or not the disciple has comprehended the meaning, the teacher has asked this question. The intention of the questioner is - `if it is known that it has not been comprehended, I shall again make him grasp it through other means.' Hereby is shown the duty of the teacher that a student should be made to achieve his goal by taking the help of a different method. ... `for which purpose has there been this effort on your part for hearing and on my part the effort of being a teacher'."

What more do we seek in a teacher-taught relationship ?

A Modern example

But now let us turn to our own times to see the relevance of all this.

We come across Sri Ramakrishna the great master and Swami Vivekenanda the ideal disciple.

Talking about this relationship, Swami Vivekananda says --

"It is difficult to explain to others how blissfully I spent my days with the Master. There is no limit to our astonishment when we think of how, through play, merriment and other ordinary daily activities, he gave us high exalted spiritual education and moulded our lives without our knowledge. Just as a powerful wrestler, at the time of teaching a boy, keeps his skill in reserve and displaying a part only of his power, as suits the purpose of teaching the boy, produces self-confidence in him by defeating him sometimes seemingly with great effort, and sometimes allowing himself to be defeated by him; so on many occasions the Master assumed that attitude in dealing with us at that time. He always saw `a whole sea in a drop of water', as they say."

And again --

"Ever since our first meeting, it was Master alone, and no one else, ... who always had uniform faith in me. That faith and that love of his have bound me for ever."

Causes of deterioration

Well, if this be the ideal and if it be intact in ideal examples even now, how and why is the relationship deteriorated in general?

There are two causes

1. Indians in general, whether they are teachers or students by occupation, have lost the moorings of our own culture. The basic theme of our culture is to "struggle to manifest Divine within by controlling nature external and internal". But we have fallen prey to the drag of enjoyment, external glamour and `drift' of character. As Swami Vivekananda has pointed out about the religious teacher in the west - (and I quote from P.52 of Complete Works of Swami Vivekananda)

"While in those countries which have neglected to keep up this kind of relation the religious teacher has become a mere lecturer, the teacher expecting his five dollars and the person taught expecting his brain to be filled with the teacher's words, and each going his own way after this much has been done.....They think they can obtain it with dollars......But unfortunately it can not be".

This has become true of almost all teachers and students in our own country today.

2. Of course there is another important factor. The present education system imposed by English people on India and unfortunately continued even now has some inherent defects. Out of the various faculties making up the human mind like thinking, feeling, will, self-control etc., this system recognises only the first to the total neglect of all the rest. And even in thinking the emphasis is on data collected by the five senses to the utter neglect of transcendental perceptions which alone take mankind towards higher and nobler life. This has affected all our lives and the institutions of education are becoming commercial markets and `drift' is becoming all-encompassing.

How to revive the Ideal ?

The situation is alarming. And a serious view has to be taken by all concerned and immediate and perhaps drastic remedial measures have to be taken and sacrifices made by the teaching community to enable the country to raise itself once again.

The first and foremost is to be keenly aware of both the causes mentioned above and side by side to build up determination to be positive about it and not to use these causes as( allies)? for our own drift.

Cause No. 2 mentioned above can be tackled by supplementing the present education by teachers giving more time to students even outside class hours and building up heart to heart relationship and present their own lives as models of continuous struggle for improvement more and more.

The teachers have to understand that life does not become meaningful by money and enjoyments, but by struggle for improvement. The students, the school and the educational activities are the means with the help of which our lives are enriched. Each soul is potentially divine. This divine potential in the students should always be kept in mind by the teachers to develop the healthy relationship.

The teachers should constantly read and think about and associate with ideal personalities and try to imbibe all the higher values of life till they become completely absorbed in our personality. Similarly we have to encourage students to do the same. Then a healthy teacher taught relationship will be built which is a key to all progress.
